author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their time and feedback. Here are our answers and clarifications for the reviewers; the final version will be modified accordingly. == Title of the paper == In order to avoid any confusion about the scope of our study, we decided to modify the title (“Are Foundational Models Less Biased Than Specialized Models?”) with the following addition “An Ultrasound Study”. == Implementation details and comparison of architectures== We will clarify in the manuscript that the foundation model (FM) was finetuned in all its parts: encoder, decoder, up to the final classification layer. Regarding the exact architecture of the specialized model, it is entirely available in the referenced work of Pegios et al [1]. We will further emphasize that we reimplement exactly their architecture (SA-Sononet). == Are foundation models only for few-shots scenarios? == Deep learning models have some prominent domain shift issues such as scanner bias, where foundation models can hopefully help. FM have already been shown to improve robustness and mitigate biases on larger finetuning datasets [2,3]. And our results confirmed that these models can improve performance over specialized models on two different tasks. Therefore, FM, beyond their special fitness for few-shots scenarios, can also be valuable in other scenarios. == Effect of intersectionality on the outcome == We believe the intersectionality between factors cannot be expected to fundamentally alter the outcome of this paper. This outcome was, given two models, to answer this question: is the first model considerably less biased than the other? Given enough factors, two very similar bias profiles already tell us that the two bias behaviors correspond in their major directions, which was what we wanted to know. But the intersectional analysis could indeed add to that in revealing some additional and more subtle differences. Hence, we did acknowledge the absence of intersectional analysis as a limitation in the discussion, but we will make this part even more clear in the final version. == Results without pretraining for ViT-B == We recognize this comparison of architecture can be of interest. However, as our purpose here was to compare foundation models to specialized models, we did not consider the ViT-B architecture without the pretraining as it would not be considered a foundation model anymore. == Bias similarity index == Our goal with this index to associate some familiar metric value of overlapping (Dice Similarity Index) next to the two visuals of the bias profiles. (We didn’t intend to introduce a new metric with specific properties.) We will clarify this in the methods sections. == Granular reporting of subgroup analysis == We agree with the reviewer that an exhaustive reporting of all subgroups and biases would be valuable in appendix. Unfortunately, supplementary figures are not allowed, and this reporting would have to replace another important part of the paper. Hence, we chose to select three important subgroups for granular reporting (Ethnicity, Device, Birth Year). [1] Pegios, P. et al. (2023). title: AS-TIME: Time-Conditioned Multimodal Modeling of Aortic Stenosis Progression
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically meaningful and challenging problem, and the overall approach is well motivated. The use of multimodal data (echo videos and reports) combined with explicit conditioning on elapsed time is intuitive and aligns with how clinicians think about disease progression. The architecture is clean and modular, and the results show consistent (if modest) improvements over reasonable baselines. I also appreciated the effort toward interpretability, with modality weighting and expert routing providing some insight into model behavior, which is important for clinical applications.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The primary weakness I see is the evaluation. The dataset is relatively small and limited to a single institution, with no external validation, making it difficult to assess generalization. The performance gains over baselines are also modest, and it is unclear whether they are statistically significant. While the paper emphasizes clinical relevance and robustness, these claims are not strongly supported by the experiments, which limits confidence in the practical impact of the method. In addition, despite the “longitudinal” language, the model only uses Delta t for its predictions. The model cannot actually condition on trajectories, just on the elapsed time. Finally, the paper does not sufficiently cite many of the methods that it integrates. For instance, using attention aggregation for frame embeddings should be cited (added references below).
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Strength 1: Novel and Well-Motivated Time-Conditioned Architecture Explicit Δt conditioning at multiple hierarchy levels (modality fusion and expert routing) is innovative and well-motivated for trajectory-aware prediction. The disagreement-aware gating mechanism is clever: using cosine similarity between modalities reveals complementarity (avg: -0.33, suggesting modalities capture different information), which informs adaptive weighting. MoE with time-dependent expert specialization is elegant and interpretable: different experts activate for different Δt intervals, reflecting heterogeneous AS progression patterns. The hierarchical design (token MIL → modality gating → MoE) is principled and mirrors clinical reasoning about disease progression. Strength 2: Strong Empirical Validation with Rigorous Ablation Studies Comprehensive baseline comparisons: temporal embeddings alone, unimodal (video/report), multimodal fusion strategies (TAMME, concatenation, cross-attention), and foundation models (EchoPrime, BERT, MedGemma). Strong results: 80.4% AUC, 73.8% BAcc, up to 15.29% AUC improvement over baselines. Systematic temporal ablation (Table 2) demonstrates clear value of Δt conditioning: no Δt (73.91% AUC) → gated fusion (79.42%) → full AS-TIME (80.40%), with reduced variance suggesting stabilization. Statistical rigor: results reported with standard deviations across 5 seeds, showing reproducibility. Reasonable dataset size: 4,124 patient pairs with 35,658 total echo videos across 3 views (A5C, PLAX, PSAXAo). Strength 3: Multi-Level Interpretability and Clinical Alignment Explainability at instance, modality, and expert levels provides transparency for clinical deployment. Observed modality weights (96% video, 4% report) align with clinical practice where reports are interpretations of videos. Expert routing patterns show meaningful temporal specialization (Expert 8 for early intervals, Expert 3 for longer follow-up), suggesting the model learns clinically relevant progression dynamics. Well-calibrated predictions (Figure 2) are essential for clinical trust and decision-making. Only requires single baseline echo without additional clinical variables, addressing practical deployment challenges. Strength 4: Strong Clinical Motivation and Impact Potential AS is a prevalent and growing problem (global aging population), and current surveillance is suboptimal. Heterogeneous progression patterns make individualized risk stratification critical for optimizing follow-up schedules. The framework supports adaptive, risk-guided surveillance, particularly valuable for resource-limited settings and rural/remote communities. Clear future directions outlined: subgroup analysis, multi-visit longitudinal modeling, time-to-progression estimation, external validation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Weakness 1: Missing Comparison to Time-Aware Baselines and Simple Ablations Issue: The reviewer specifically notes: “No comparison to simple time aware model that only use either report or images alone are done, in this past few years multiple methods were proposed across MICCAI and ISBI.” While the paper compares against TAMME [10] (which underperformed), there are no comparisons to other recent time-aware multimodal methods from MICCAI/ISBI 2024-2025.- Critically missing: simple baselines using EchoPrime+Δt or BERT+Δt with time-conditioned architectures similar to AS-TIME (e.g., MoE routing on unimodal features). This would isolate the value of multimodal fusion vs. sophisticated temporal modeling on single modality. The TAMME underperformance is attributed to “requiring multiple input data across multiple time points,” but this should be investigated more rigorously. Why not adapt TAMME to single timepoint? Specific references: Recent time-aware medical imaging methods should be compared: Liu et al. 2025 [3] (cited in paper but not compared), Susetzky et al. 2025 [10] (TAMME), and other temporal modeling approaches from recent MICCAI proceedings. Weakness 2: Insufficient Dataset and Experimental Details Issue: The reviewer requests: “Very detail on the split distribution and how was the ablation study perform and which set the results are reported.” The paper states “70% training, 15% validation, 15% test set, stratified by class distribution while ensuring patient exclusivity” but lacks critical details: Exact sample sizes for train/val/test splits not reported Event rate (significant AS %) in each split not provided (only overall: 63.4% early, 36.6% significant) How is patient exclusivity ensured when there are 4,124 pairs from 2,605 patients? Are pairs from the same patient split consistently? Temporal distribution of Δt in each split not reported - is there temporal bias? Random seed for split not mentioned Ablation study details: Are all experiments (baselines, ablations) evaluated on the same test set? Or is hyperparameter tuning on validation set followed by final evaluation on test set? No external validation cohort - all experiments are on single institution data, limiting generalizability claims. Weakness 3: Limited Analysis of MoE Expert Behavior and Architectural Justification Issue: While expert routing patterns are described (Expert 8, Expert 3, etc.), the analysis is superficial: Why 12 experts? Was this number ablated (e.g., 4, 8, 16 experts)? How diverse are the learned expert behaviors? Are some experts redundant? No visualization of what features each expert focuses on (e.g., saliency maps per expert) No analysis of failure cases: When does the MoE fail? Which experts misroute? The modality gating shows strong video preference (96%), raising the question: Why not just use video-only model with better architecture? The 4% report contribution seems marginal. Missing architectural ablations: What if we use attention pooling instead of MIL? What if we use different temporal encoding (learnable vs. sinusoidal)? Weakness 4: Limited Reproducibility Issue: No statement about code/model release is provided. Dataset is private (single tertiary medical center), limiting reproducibility. Some implementation details are provided (AdamW, lr=3.8e-6, batch=16, 50 epochs), but others are missing: MIL architecture details (attention mechanism, hidden dimensions) Gating network architecture (number of layers, activation functions) MoE routing mechanism specifics (top-k selection? soft vs. hard routing?) How are 32 frames sampled from videos (temporal distribution, selection criteria)? Foundation model versions (EchoPrime, BioClinical-ModernBERT specific checkpoints)

author_feedback: We extend our sincere gratitude to the Area Chair for the opportunity to clarify our work. We appreciate the reviewers’ thoughtful comments and are encouraged that they found AS-TIME clinically meaningful and well motivated. We address the key concerns below: 1.Model Framing/Clinical Relevance (R1,R3): AS-TIME is intended as a horizon-conditioned risk estimator: given a baseline echo study, clinicians can query personalized progression risk across plausible follow-up intervals (0-10 years) to support individualized surveillance planning. We will revise the “longitudinal” wording to clarify this framing and discuss future extensions for multi-timepoint trajectory modeling and direct time-to-progression prediction. 2.Novelty (R1): We agree that attention-based MIL and MoE build on established methods, and sincerely thank R1 for suggesting additional references. We will include them in our paper. We would like to respectfully emphasize that our contribution is not MIL or MoE in isolation, but their integration into a time-conditioned framework where ∆t dynamically modulates multimodal fusion and expert specialization. We will make our novelty clearer, in line with R2 and R3’s recognition of time-conditioned formulation as central to our work. 3.Dataset (R2): The data were split into train/val/test sets of 2,933/594/597 study pairs, stratified by class, with about 64% no progression and 36% progression in each split. Patient exclusivity was enforced by splitting on patient IDs, thus all pairs from the same patient remained in a single split. Mean ∆t was comparable across train/val/test: 2.35/2.46/2.46 years. All results in Tables 1 and 2 were evaluated on the same held-out test set and averaged over five seeds. Hyperparameters were tuned on the val set. We will revise the Experiments section of our paper for clarity. 4.Statistical Significance (R1,2): In comparison to Cross-Attention which achieved the highest baseline, AS-TIME consistently outperformed across all seeds. Paired t-tests confirmed statistically significant differences in both AUC and BAcc. We will make this clearer in our final manuscript. 5.External Validation/Baseline (R1-3): We agree that lack of external validation limits generalizability. This was challenging because AS-TIME requires longitudinal echo studies with reports and clearly defined AS severity labels. Despite our best efforts, we were unable to identify a publicly available or accessible external dataset containing this combination of data. We will include this limitation in the final paper and acknowledge that further validation is important for assessing generalization. Additionally, we appreciate R2 and R3’s suggested extra baselines and will incorporate them into our future work. 6.Modality Weighting/MoE/Performance Across ∆t (R1-3): We agree that the strong video weighting warrants further discussion. We do not view it as evidence that reports are uninformative, but rather, it likely reflects the clinical relationship between raw echo videos and report summaries. We will acknowledge that further analysis is required to better characterize the contribution of the report modality. AS-TIME uses a soft weighted expert combination, with the number of experts selected by validation. AUROC remained stable across ∆t bins, suggesting preserved discriminative performance across time horizons. BAcc showed slight decrease in longer horizons, likely reflecting increased prediction difficulty and significantly reduced sample sizes in these subgroups. 7.Reproducibility/Citations/Figure (R1-3): We will add the suggested citations, implementation details, and release code upon acceptance. We will also revise the method figure with a clearer color scheme. We will revise the final manuscript to address feedback outlined above. If these clarifications address your concerns, we kindly ask you to consider revising your score.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper addresses an important clinical problem and presents a well-motivated time-conditioned framework for aortic stenosis progression prediction. The paper is generally well executed, with supportive ablations and good overall clarity. The main concerns are around validation and clinical framing. The reported gains, while encouraging, should be better supported with statistical testing and more complete split details. | This paper addresses an important clinical problem and presents a well-motivated framework for modelling aortic stenosis progression using multimodal echocardiography data and explicit time conditioning. The proposed integration of elapsed time into multimodal fusion and prediction is intuitive, clinically relevant, and supported by consistent improvements over competitive baselines. The work is strengthened by comprehensive ablation studies, interpretability analyses, and a reasonably large longitudinal cohort. The rebuttal satisfactorily clarified several concerns regarding data splitting, statistical significance, model design, and clinical framing. While the lack of external validation remains an important limitation, and additional time-aware baselines would further strengthen the study, these issues do not outweigh the overall methodological contribution and clinical relevance of the work. Overall, the paper presents a well-executed and practically meaningful contribution that is likely to be of interest to the MICCAI community. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers recommend acceptance and judge the paper positively. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): One reviewers highlighted several key concerns including: 1.Missing Comparison to Time-Aware Baselines and Simple Ablations 2.Insufficient Dataset and Experimental Details 3.Limited Analysis of MoE Expert Behavior and Architectural Justification 4.Limited Reproducibility And also highlighted that this work needs a substantial work and new experiments, which cannot be done during rebuttal phase.

title: BDFR-Net: Boundary-Aware Dual-Domain Feature Reconstruction Network for Fetal Ultrasound Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper proposes Boundary-Aware Dual-Domain Feature Reconstruction Network for Fetal Ultrasound Image Segmentation, and Extensive experiments on the MICCAI IUGC 2024 benchmark and cross-dataset are conducted in the paper. 2.The low-frequency and high-frequency decompositions are separately designed for multi-scale feature enhancement on boundary segmentation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Paper mentioned speckled noise and low signal-to-noise ratio obscure anatomical boundaries. What’s the difference? 2.The proposed modules added in the UNET are more like a combination of different feature enhancement modules, although a performance improvement is observed. Because the spatial attention and different pooling operations are fundamental in unet-based segmentation. 3.The difference between BDFR-B1 and BDFR-B2

reviewer_2_strengths: The paper focuses on segmenting the fetal head and pubic symphysis in transperineal ultrasound, which matters for obstetric measurements used in delivery decisions. The main novelty is that the proposed BDFR-Net combines frequency-domain boundary cues with spatial-context modeling instead of relying on only one type of feature. The results show that BDFR-Net appears especially helpful on segmenting the pubic symphysis, which is anatomically challenging and clinically relevant.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The clinical task of this study is automated AoP measurement, but the results mainly focus on segmentation accuracy. The paper does not clearly demonstrate the impact on downstream AoP measurement or real clinical workflow. For instance, what is the accuracy of AoP estimation by BDFR-Net? 2.The architecture includes multiple specialized components. While this may improve accuracy, it also increases implementation and deployment complexity. Metrics such as the number of parameters and inference speed should be reported to assess efficiency. 3.The cross-dataset results show a clear performance drop compared to the FHPS-AoP results. This raises my concerns about the generalizability of the proposed BDFR-Net. 4.In addition, the results on the IUGC2024 dataset show performance drops across all evaluation metrics compared to FHPS-AoP. This further raises my concerns about the robustness of BDFR-Net. 5.The training epoch is set to 50 for the IUGC2024 dataset, but the reason for using a different setting is not explained. reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The main strength of this paper is to propose a DDBE module which synergistically models frequency-spatial complementarity to enhance boundary perception and structural fidelity. Specifically, DDBE addresses the issue of boundary blurring by decomposing features into frequency-decoupled edge responses and spatial contextual cues, and then integrating them through channel-attentive cross-domain fusion.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) Although the high-frequency branch is introduced to enhance boundaries, its robustness to ultrasound-specific noise and artifacts is not fully validated. Ultrasound images usually contain considerable noise and various artifacts. As a result, the extracted high-frequency components may include not only true anatomical boundaries, but also speckle noise and false edge responses. The current paper does not provide enough analysis to explain how the proposed design can effectively suppress these unwanted responses. The authors are encouraged to provide more visual evidence, especially on challenging cases with severe speckle noise, blurred boundaries, and obvious artifacts. For example, feature response maps or segmentation comparisons would help support the analysis. (2) Some parts of the method description are not sufficiently clear or rigorous. The definition of the Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) seems closer to a CBAM-style channel attention module than to a standard ECA module. In addition, several equations and notations should be presented in a clearer and more consistent way. (3) The computational cost of the proposed method is not discussed in enough detail. Since wavelet decomposition is integrated into the network pipeline, it seems to be performed in every forward pass during both training and inference. This raises concerns about the extra computational burden, as well as the training and inference time, compared with conventional convolution-based designs. The authors are encouraged to provide a clearer analysis of model complexity, including parameter count, FLOPs, and runtime overhead.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers (R) and the Meta-Reviewer (MetaR) for reviewing and recognizing our clinical motivation (R1,R2),SOTA performance (R1,R2,R3) and clear ablation (R1,R3).The code will be released upon acceptance. Q1.Speckle vs.low SNR(R1).Both are major ultrasound degradations noted in [21],but they affect boundaries differently.Speckle introduces granular false responses that obscure existing boundary cues,whereas low SNR,often caused by attenuation or shadowing,weakens echoes and reduces boundary visibility. Q2.Module-combination concern(MetaR-W1,R1).BDFR-Net is a boundary-driven decoder, not a generic block assembly. Prior decoders [Attention U-Net,SegNet] enhance spatial feature decoding, and frequency-based models [Wave-ViT] introduce spectral representation, but they are not tailored to the speckle-induced ambiguity between weak anatomical boundaries and texture-like responses in FH/PS ultrasound. DDBE addresses this ambiguity through frequency–spatial decoupling and cross-domain coordination. Prior skip refinements [UNet++,UCTransNet] improve feature reuse, whereas ACAM aligns encoder–decoder semantics before fusion. Q3.B1 vs.B2(R1).Only the encoder backbone differs (PVTv2-B1 vs.PVTv2-B2[27]); all other components are identical.This will be clarified in the camera-ready. Q4.AoP clinical relevance (R2). AoP is a key clinical indicator of labor progression [15] and, as reported in the PSFHS challenge report [MIA 99(2025), 103353], is derived from segmented FH and PS via deterministic geometric fitting. AoP is not learned as an independent target, where its accuracy depends directly on segmentation boundary fidelity. A standalone AoP-error table was omitted due to space limits, but the most pronounced PS gain (the AoP baseline structure) in Table 1 already supports clinical relevance. A quantitative AoP-error comparison will be presented in future work. Q5.Computational cost(MetaR-W2,R2,R3).Due to space limitations,parameter count,FLOPs and runtime analyses are not included; a systematic evaluation will be presented in future work. Q6.Cross-dataset drop,IUGC 2024 drop and 50-epoch setting(MetaR-W3,R2).The drops are mainly attributable to distributional differences across datasets rather than a failure specific to BDFR-Net.The cross-dataset protocol trains on JNU-IFM[17] and tests on PSFHS[5] with no overlap in centers,scanners or patients; IUGC 2024[1] tests on 300 standard-plane images from disjoint videos.Both introduce higher variability,so absolute scores decrease for all methods,yet BDFR-Net still achieves the best overall mean metrics (Table 1),evidencing stronger generalization.The 50-epoch setting on IUGC 2024 follows its smaller training scale and prior practice[1],and is applied uniformly to all compared methods for fairness. Q7.Dice+CE loss(R2).Inspired by [TransU-Net,6;I²U-Net,8],we adopt an equally weighted combination of Dice and cross-entropy losses,where Dice provides robustness to foreground-background imbalance and cross-entropy provides dense pixel-level supervision for boundary discrimination. Q8.HF robustness to speckle/artifacts(MetaR-W3,R3).We agree that speckle may enter the high-frequency response,but HF is not used in isolation: under segmentation supervision,DWT-decomposed subbands are projected and refined to bias toward anatomical edge responses,and then re-weighted with the LF and CTX branches via channel-spatial gating (Eq.6) to suppress branch-specific artifacts.Prior work has also established the robustness of wavelet-based high-frequency representations to speckle [Wavelet-CNN,CVPR’20;Wave-ViT,ECCV’22]; This will be clarified in the camera-ready.Due to space limitations,finer-grained feature response maps will be included in future work. Q9.”ECA” naming(R3).This module is a CBAM-style channel attention in which the shared MLP is replaced by two independent 1×1 convolutional branches.We will refine the description and unify the notation in the camera-ready version.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Please address the concerns about limited novelty, missing efficiency analysis, and insufficient validation under ultrasound-specific conditions. | two accept and one reject. i read through and would accept subject to minor Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper addresses a clinically relevant fetal ultrasound segmentation problem and reports competitive results on several benchmarks. However, after considering the reviews and rebuttal, I recommend rejection because the current submission remains below the acceptance threshold for a methodological contribution. 1) The methodological novelty is limited. Frequency-domain decomposition, high-/low-frequency feature modeling, boundary enhancement, and attention-based skip-feature refinement have already been widely explored in medical image segmentation, including ultrasound-related settings. The proposed DDBE and ACAM modules appear to be a task-oriented combination of these existing ideas rather than a clearly new technical formulation. The rebuttal mainly restates the intended roles of the modules, but does not sufficiently distinguish the concrete technical contribution from prior frequency-domain, boundary-aware, and attention-based decoder designs. 2) The baseline comparison is not sufficiently targeted. Since the paper’s central claim is boundary-aware dual-domain reconstruction, the comparison should include closely related frequency-domain segmentation methods, boundary-enhancement methods, and ultrasound-specific segmentation approaches. In addition, the baseline set does not adequately cover recent architecture families such as Mamba- or RWKV-style medical segmentation models. Without these stronger and more relevant comparisons, the claimed superiority over existing methods is not fully convincing. 3) The evidence for the claimed boundary and ultrasound robustness is incomplete. The method is motivated by speckle noise, low SNR, and ambiguous anatomical boundaries, but the paper does not provide sufficient boundary-specific evaluation, feature visualizations, or stress analysis under challenging ultrasound artifacts. The downstream clinical relevance to AoP measurement is also not quantitatively demonstrated, even though this is a key motivation for segmenting the fetal head and pubic symphysis. 4) The practical value of the added architectural complexity is not well established. The framework introduces multiple components, including wavelet-based frequency decomposition, frequency-spatial reconstruction, contextual aggregation, and adaptive feature alignment. However, the ablation study shows relatively limited gains from several individual components, and the paper does not provide complexity or runtime analysis to justify whether these added modules are worthwhile compared with simpler alternatives. Overall, although the paper is well organized and addresses an important application, its core technical contribution is not sufficiently novel or distinctive for a methodological paper at MICCAI. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The rebuttal clarified several presentation and implementation details and parts of the experimental setup. However, the main issue remains that the proposed method does not provide sufficient methodological novelty. In particular, the overall design still appears to rely on relatively standard frequency-feature fusion and attention-based refinement ideas, and the rebuttal does not sufficiently establish these components as a more distinct technical contribution. Considering the remaining post-rebuttal reviewer concerns, I do not support acceptance.

reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The ablation study is incomplete because it does not isolate the main claimed innovations: signed reflectivity, exact beam integration, and Harris initialization are not individually ablated. 2.The physics model is still approximate: interference is reduced to signed scalar reflectivities plus rectification, not a full RF/phase model. 3.Reproducibility details are incomplete, including limited experimental protocol detail.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive and insightful feedback. We address each concern below. Regarding the incomplete ablation study [Reviewer 3 W1; Reviewer 1 W3]: We agree with the reviewer on the importance of additional ablation studies. We have added new ablation experiments that individually isolate the effects of signed reflectivity, exact beam integration, and Harris initialization, and these results will be included in the camera-ready version. These experiments were conducted during the development of our method and demonstrated the importance and contribution of each component individually. Regarding our physics model is approximate [Reviewer 3 W2]: Our model is a deliberate approximation that balances physical accuracy with optimization tractability. A full RF/phase model, while theoretically richer, is extremely difficult to optimize end-to-end, as per our initial experiments, where we tried to develop full RF/phase model but it failed due to the following: Gauge symmetry in (a,φ) ≡ (a,φ+2πk), causing the optimizer to drift. A phase saddle at φ=0 where ∂C/∂φ vanishes leaves no escape signal. B-mode envelope detection discards phase, so an explicit φ has no supervisable target. We therefore opt for a simpler but more physics-aware approximation, which produces the higher-fidelity novel view synthesis evidenced by our state-of-the-art results. Regarding the reproducibility details [Reviewer 3 W3]: Complete implementation details, hyperparameters, and experimental protocols will be made fully available through the code repository linked in the camera-ready version, ensuring complete reproducibility. Regarding the vulnerability to inaccurate pose priors [Reviewer 1 W1]: Gaussian splatting is an explicit representation; therefore, the reconstruction quality is inherently dependent on the accuracy of the input poses. Consequently, errors in pose estimation propagate to the reconstructed volume and affect reconstruction fidelity. In our experiments, we evaluated the method on freehand ultrasound datasets that naturally contain pose noise arising from the acquisition process itself. Therefore, all reported results already reflect realistic pose inaccuracies present in practical settings. Furthermore, to explicitly study the sensitivity of the method to pose perturbations, we added additional synthetic pose errors and observed a degradation in reconstruction quality, confirming the strong dependency between pose accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Nevertheless, pose estimation is treated as an external input to our pipeline, and handling pose correction or refinement lies outside the scope of the current work. Regarding the clinical validation of BFS [Reviewer 1 W4]: Clinical validation is an unreliable process for measuring speckle-pattern fidelity. Speckle is noise-like by construction, and subjective judgments between two speckled reconstructions do not consistently discriminate well-preserved patterns from poorly-preserved ones. We therefore introduce BFS as a qualitative and standalone measure of speckle preservation. The signal-level preservation it promotes is not only aimed at clinical viewing, it is also aimed at downstream tasks that consume speckle as information, such as sensorless pose estimation via speckle decorrelation, tissue characterization, and speckle-based tracking and segmentation. Regarding method behavior in different and artifact-rich scenarios[Reviewer 2 W1,2]: Our method requires posed ultrasound datasets that are scarce. We evaluated the three publicly available datasets that we could find at the time of submission. These datasets cover low-, mid-, and high-speckle regimes as well as spanning over multiple anatomical regions from forearms to brain. Regarding moving organs such as the heart, this would require 4D (dynamic) Gaussian Splatting, which is orthogonal to our contribution and constitutes a compelling direction for future work.

title: Boosting Ultrasound Image Classification via Attribute-Guided Dual-Branch Framework
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses an important problem in ultrasound imaging, where interpretability and robustness are critical. 2.The framework is clearly described and easy to integrate into existing models. 3.The idea of incorporating attribute-based priors is well-motivated.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty is limited, as the approach largely builds upon existing ideas such as attribute-guided learning, concept bottleneck models, and feature fusion. 2.The performance improvements are relatively modest in some cases, particularly for certain backbones, which limits the overall impact. 3.The attribute design relies on manually defined expert knowledge, which may limit scalability and generalizability to other tasks or domains. 4.The evaluation is conducted on relatively limited datasets, with no strong validation under domain shifts or across diverse clinical settings. 5.While interpretability is claimed, the analysis remains somewhat limited, lacking deeper validation
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper attempts to incorporate attribute-level priors into ultrasound classification in order to improve both predictive performance and interpretability. This general direction is meaningful, and the idea of providing semantically meaningful cues for decision-making is potentially interesting.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Limited novelty and insufficient clarification of the role of the medical attribute semantic space. The overall novelty appears limited. The method mainly relies on CLIP to construct a medical semantic space and uses a dual-branch framework for prediction. However, the manuscript does not clearly explain what specific role this medical attribute semantic space plays in the proposed method. The authors use customized prompts to obtain language embeddings and compare them with image features, but CLIP is originally trained on natural image-text pairs. The paper does not sufficiently justify why such a semantic space can be expected to work effectively for a medical ultrasound task without further adaptation or evidence. 2.The notion of “domain-agnostic medical attribute priors” is not clearly defined. The manuscript repeatedly emphasizes domain-agnostic medical attribute priors, including in the abstract, but this concept itself is not clearly explained. If these attributes are truly domain-agnostic, it is unclear why they would be effective for a specific ultrasound classification task. On the other hand, if they are indeed informative for the task, then their relationship to the specific imaging modality, disease categories, or clinical context should be more clearly explained. At present, this key concept remains vague, and the methodological motivation is therefore not sufficiently convincing. 3.The description of the attribute branch and Figure 2 is unclear. The paper states that the attribute branch is derived from CLIP, but Figure 2 does not clearly show the corresponding modules, making the connection between the figure and the text difficult to follow. In addition, several important details are missing: What exactly are the ultrasound-specific prompts? How are these prompts designed? How is the patch-level attribute similarity map generated? How are the text attributes matched with image patch features? Since prompt design and attribute similarity computation are central to the proposed method, these components should be described more explicitly and concretely. 4.The category definition of the private dataset is incomplete. The manuscript mentions that the private dataset contains seven classes, but it does not specify what these seven classes are. For a classification task, the class definition is a basic and necessary part of the dataset description, and it should be clearly provided. 5.The experimental design is not sufficient to support the effectiveness of the attribute module. In Table 1, the authors seem to aim to demonstrate the benefit of the proposed attribute module. However, if the goal is to show that this module is effective, the more appropriate design would be to report results with and without the attribute module across all evaluated backbones, rather than only presenting the BU-Mamba results. The current experiments are not sufficient to show that the proposed module consistently improves performance across different backbone architectures. 6.The claimed interpretability is not yet convincing. Figure 3 attempts to demonstrate interpretability, but the current evidence is not sufficiently convincing. If the interpretability mainly comes from predicting attributes corresponding to manually designed prompts, then this seems closer to matching predefined semantic labels rather than genuinely explaining the model’s decision-making process. In other words, since the attributes themselves are predefined by the authors, it remains unclear whether predicting these attributes should be considered true interpretability. The authors need to better justify why these attribute predictions constitute meaningful explanatory evidence rather than merely reflecting the predefined prompt design.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1Practical plug-and-play design: Requires only minimal modifications to existing backbones (ResNet, ViT, Mamba) and delivers consistent gains without re-training the whole model. 2Clinical relevance: Explicitly uses domain-agnostic medical attributes derived from public guidelines, providing human-readable evidence (attribute prediction accuracy 83–87%) that clinicians can verify. 3Efficiency: Extremely low overhead (e.g., +0.16–1.93 min per fold, +0.5–1.3 M parameters) while improving strong baselines (e.g., BU-Mamba from 87.86% → 88.72% on BUSI; ViT-B +4.3% Acc on BUSI). 4Thorough validation: Extensive experiments across two datasets (public BUSI + private fetal 7-class), multiple backbones, multi-task settings, and detailed ablations showing the necessity of both branches and learnable fusion.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1The improvement on the strongest baseline (BU-Mamba) is relatively modest (+0.86% Acc). 2The fetal dataset is private, limiting direct reproducibility of that experiment. 3Novelty is incremental rather than groundbreaking: the approach combines ideas from Concept Bottleneck Models and CLIP-based attribute guidance, but does not introduce a fundamentally new paradigm compared to recent MICCAI works on prompt-based or attribute-guided medical VLMs (e.g., refs 7–9, 17–18, 20–24).
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the significance of our work. Q1: Generalizability and task coverage (R1,R2,R3) A1: (1) We validated our method on four mainstream backbones: CNN (ResNet), Transformer (ViT), Mamba (BUMamba), and Diffusion (DiffMIC-v2). It improved their performance by 1.8%, 4.3%, 0.86%, and 3.4%, respectively, showing backbone generalizability. (2) We added a thyroid ultrasound dataset with a 4.3% gain. Consistent improvements across fetal, breast, and thyroid ultrasound tasks validate task generalizability. Q2: Ablation studies (R1,R2) A2: (1) Attribute-table robustness: The attribute table is LLM-generated without manual expert annotation. It is robust: under the same prompt, three generated tables yielded stable accuracies (85.4%, 85.6%, 84.9%). Furthermore, a progressive analysis shows that manual expert selection further elevates performance to 86.4%, demonstrating the potential for even higher gains when manual expert knowledge is integrated. (2) Automatic attribute learning: Self-learned embeddings achieve 82.8%, showing utility without semantic vocabularies; however, our explicit attributes with offline encoding are stronger. (3) Medical CLIP: Replacing standard CLIP with MedCLIP improves accuracy (85.4% to 86.3%), showing medical text priors benefit the model. Q3: Attribute priors and method comparison (R1,R2,R3) A3: (1) Attribute priors: Attribute priors encode discrete attribute tables into semantic anchors via offline CLIP. Attributes such as shape and margin serve as domain-invariant priors; our fetal dataset was collected from three hospitals, reflecting cross-center differences. (2) Comparison and versatility: Existing methods like medical VLMs, alignment methods, and CBMs often need scenario-specific designs, limiting plug-and-play versatility. In contrast, our method uses LLMs to auto-generate task-specific discriminative attributes. Via a dual-branch structure, we introduce attribute priors in a plug-and-play manner while preserving the original backbone. This significantly enhances generalization and universality across clinical tasks with 5% overhead (see Q1). Q4: Interpretability, qualitative cases, clinical use, and reproducibility (R1,R2,R3) A4: (1) Interpretability: Attribute prediction accuracy (83.28%) provides reliable decision clues. CAM attribute-region maps will be released with the code. (2) Qualitative analysis: On the breast test set, we report three-branch predictions and top-5 attributes per sample. Cases show our attribute/fusion branches correctly predict malignancy when the visual branch misjudges it as benign, proving fusion corrects visual-head errors. (3) Clinical utility: We plan to invite senior physicians to evaluate diagnostic accuracy and clinical acceptance. (4) Reproducibility: We will release code and model weights upon acceptance, enabling reproducibility. Q5: Terminology, CLIP attribute anchors, methodology, and dataset definition (R2) A5: (1) Terminology: “Domain-independent” refers to data-source independence; e.g., shape/margin remain center/device-invariant. (2) Methodology: a. ChatGPT generates task-discriminative attributes; b. CLIP extracts initial attribute embeddings offline; c. An FC layer maps embeddings to visual space; d. Cosine similarity between visual features and embeddings generates attribute heatmaps; e. Final predictions are derived via weighted averaging of heatmaps, which are supervised by category-specific attribute labels mapped from category labels. (3) CLIP adaptation: CLIP is applicable because basic features, such as edges and shapes, are universal. Beyond these, our supervised optimization in step e refines all initial semantic embeddings—covering universal and specialized medical attributes—to bridge domain gaps and calibrate them to clinical nuances. (4) Dataset: Seven fetal planes: three-vessel; aortic arch; fetal bladder; transcerebellar plane; thorax; ductal arch; fetal orbits.

title: CardiacPULSE: Frequency-Aware Self-supervised Cardiac Phase Detection in Echocardiography
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper presents a new algorithm for phase detection in echocardiography that is self-supervised and uses a small number of trainable parameters. The algorithm performs equally well regardless of the specific ultrasound view. The results reported on public benchmarks are good.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: There are no significant weaknesses identified.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: A notable strength of this work is that the proposed method is able to learn cardiac periodicity without relying on any manual annotations. The design also takes practical motion characteristics into account. For instance, when extrema alone cannot reliably distinguish ES from ED, the method further introduces phase-specific frequency cues to separate the two key frames. Moreover, the use of a spatial mask to filter out irrelevant background noise while preserving rhythmically active regions is a thoughtful and effective design choice.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The inference stage appears to rely on a full input video sequence rather than a short partial clip, since motion-energy analysis and harmonic reconstruction are both performed on the extracted temporal signal. It would be helpful if the authors could clarify whether the method can operate reliably on partial clips containing only limited cardiac cycles, and how sensitive it is to input length.
reviewer_2_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_3_strengths: efficient and accurate phase detection in echocardiography leveraging Fourier analysis per pixel and a lightweight CNN learned on prior cardiac motion consequences in the frequency domain.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: This reader does not understand the clinical import: an edge device can now quickly label ED/ES candidates, but no downstream processing would take place on the edge device anyway. Also, the dominant cardiac frequency may be a weak indicator in pathologic conditions, or as noted non-ideal acquisition.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank reviewers and AC. R1 raised no major concerns. R2: input length/partial clips. R3: clinical value, weak/pathological cues, EchoNet label noise, cavity comparison, sparse candidates. AC: clinical utility, full-video reliance, pathological cues. A. Clinical role and cavity-based methods (AC, R3). CardiacPULSE is a lightweight temporal-indexing front-end, not an anatomical measurement method. It returns sparse ED/ES candidates to initialize LV-volume/EF/SV pipelines, reduce search from all frames to a few frames, and provide acquisition QC when ECG/cloud are unavailable. Even if final quantification is off-device, it can verify a usable cycle and pass the right frames to later analysis, useful for handheld/POCUS and emergency/rural workflows. We agree cavity extrema are clinically meaningful. Our claim is not to avoid cavity estimation, but to perform a different stage. A local maximum of predicted cavity volume is not available for all baselines: R3D-50 is an event classifier, not a volume estimator; MAEF uses frame-wise LV segmentation, where contour noise can make extrema unstable; and UVT is optimized for EF/volume rather than sparse ED/ES indexing. Stronger supervision does not remove per-frame speckle, contrast, or contour noise. CardiacPULSE instead imposes periodicity and harmonic consistency, trading per-frame anatomical precision for stable phase timing. B. Weak/pathological signals and label noise (AC, R3). We do not claim pathology-specific robustness without stratified labels. Our narrower claim is that the method does not rely on one raw cavity-amplitude cue: the mask is estimated over the whole frame, the band covers 0.5-4.0 Hz (30-240 bpm), and motion energy is mask-normalized. Ablations support this redundancy: Mcnn alone gives 34.8 ms vs. 34.0 ms full, Mfft alone 42.2 ms, and Fourier-only candidates 70.8 ms. EchoNet-Dynamic spans a wide EF range, including severely reduced function, so the test set is not restricted to ideal cases; severe arrhythmia, view drift, probe motion, or non-cardiac artifacts remain limitations. For EchoNet label noise, including ES preceding ED or ED/ES marked on different beats, we follow the established EchoNet/CardiacPhase protocol. Since our output is a sparse candidate set across visible cycles and MAE uses the closest prediction, evaluation does not require a fixed ED-before-ES order within one beat; it asks whether a plausible ED/ES candidate exists near the expert label. CAMEO over nine views reduces concern that the gains are EchoNet-specific. C. Input length and partial clips (AC, R2). Training uses 64-frame clips downsampled by 2, about 2.5 s and usually 2-3 cycles, for stable self-supervised spectra. At inference, EchoNet numbers use full benchmark videos at native rate for fair comparison. The method is window-based: reliable frequency estimation and harmonic anchoring need at least one stable cycle, preferably two. With very short clips, 1/T frequency resolution degrades, and rolling-window or multi-clip aggregation would be needed. Thus CardiacPULSE is not frame-instantaneous, but can operate on short cine windows. D. Sparse candidates (R3). The predictions are sparse, deduplicated candidate sets, not dense per-frame labels. Sec. 2.3 fuses motion-energy extrema with ED/ES harmonic anchors and removes near duplicates, so candidates are tied to cycle extrema rather than flooding the video. By construction, phase-specific anchors provide one ED and one ES candidate per detected cycle, followed by deduplication; the motion-energy pool is merged rather than sampled densely, so count scales with visible cycles, not video length. We use CardiacPhase closest-prediction MAE only for comparability. In the same submitted runs, our count after fusion/deduplication is close to CardiacPhase, so the gain is not from proposing more frames; counting uses existing outputs, not a new run. We will make these clarifications in the camera-ready.

title: Compass: Prostate Cancer Detection Needs Multi-view Context
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper identifies a meaningful gap between clinical practice (interpreting full 3D sweeps) and existing AI methods (single-frame analysis), and addresses it with a dual-branch architecture. The roll-angle sinusoidal PE is physically grounded, and the ablation study (Table 2) convincingly isolates each component’s contribution. 2.Compass achieves a patient-level AUROC of 87.5% and Sen@60 of 92.9%, substantially outperforming the strongest baseline (ProstNFound+, 78.8%) and expert PRI-MUS (79.6%). The comparison spans frame-level, MIL, and video baselines, providing a thorough evaluation landscape. 3.The observation that Compass excels at patient-level triage while PRI-MUS remains stronger at core-level characterization (Figure 2) is practically valuable, framing the method as complementary to expert judgment rather than a replacement. 4.The authors provide an anonymous code repository, supporting reproducibility and enabling verification of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The 5-fold CV results report only mean metrics without standard deviations or confidence intervals. With 118 patients, fold-level variance could be substantial, making it unclear whether the reported improvements are statistically significant. 2.The 118-patient cohort from 2 centers is relatively small, and no external validation is provided. Moreover, the Conclusion does not discuss any limitations, including dataset size, the biopsy-level performance gap (71.0 vs 76.7), dependence on a frozen backbone, and the requirement for IMU roll angles. This is a notable omission for a clinical application paper. 3.Sinusoidal PE, cross-attention, and [CLS] token-based transformer fusion are all well-established techniques. The paper should more clearly distinguish what is architecturally new from what is a thoughtful combination of existing methods applied to the µUS domain. Duplicated “multi-view multi-view framework,” “Mulit-view” typo in keywords, “Pca” instead of “PCa,” grammatical error in “we define to csPCa,” and undefined abbreviations (MIL, mpMRI).
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) The paper addresses an important gap between how current AI systems often analyze isolated µUS frames and how clinicians actually interpret complete µUS studies with sweep context. (2) The use of sweep frames, biopsy-time frames, roll-angle encoding, and mixed-token transformer fusion is technically sensible for this acquisition setting. (3) The reported patient-level AUROC and sensitivity are strong, and the ablation study suggests that sweep information and cross-branch fusion both contribute meaningfully. (4) The paper is readable, the figures are helpful, and the clinical motivation is easy to follow.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The manuscript’s own related work already includes cine-loop modeling, temporal/spatio-temporal ultrasound modeling, heuristic slice-level aggregation, and strong µUS foundation-model approaches. Therefore, the main novelty here is the specific sweep+biopsy fusion design, rather than the broader idea of moving beyond isolated single-frame analysis. (2) The paper reports 5-fold patient-level cross-validation results, but only aggregate point estimates are shown. Given the small cohort (118 patients) and the two-center setting with different biopsy routes, the paper should report fold-wise mean±std or confidence intervals for all main metrics. Ideally, the authors should also provide per-center results or a leave-one-center-out analysis. (3) The manuscript states that results are reported at the epoch with the best mean patient AUROC across folds, but it is unclear how this epoch was selected and whether a separate validation split or nested cross-validation was used. The thresholding protocol for balanced accuracy and Sen@60 should also be described explicitly. As written, this raises concern about optimistic model selection. (4) Table 1 shows that Compass is strongest on patient-level AUROC and Sen@60, but it is not the best method on patient-level balanced accuracy, and it underperforms expert PRI-MUS at the biopsy/core level. The abstract, results, and conclusion should therefore avoid implying uniform superiority. Similarly, the conclusion mentions targeted biopsy planning, but since the model uses biopsy-time frames, the most immediate use case appears closer to intra-procedural decision support than true pre-biopsy planning. (5) Compass appears to use richer inputs than several baselines (sweeps, biopsy frames, roll-angle information, and metadata), so the paper should clearly specify which inputs and metadata each baseline receives, whether all methods share the same splits/training budget/model-selection protocol, and how the patient-level PRI-MUS comparator is derived. As written, some of the comparisons do not appear fully apples-to-apples. In fact, the no-sweeps ablation may be the fairest internal comparison and should be emphasized more strongly. (6) Some methodological descriptions are inconsistent. The text says the biopsy prompts use Age and PSA, Figure 1 also shows PSA density, and the dataset description additionally mentions family history. The paper should provide a precise and consistent description of which clinical variables are used in each experiment.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper tackles a clinically meaningful and well-motivated problem, aligning closely with real diagnostic workflows. Rather than treating µUS as isolated 2D frames, it models a study as a continuous stream of multi-view observations, better reflecting how clinicians interpret prostate sweeps. A second strength is the integration of complementary data sources, including rotational sweep frames, biopsy frames, and clinical metadata. The method also incorporates acquisition geometry through rotation-aware encoding, preserving spatial structure across frames. Empirically, the paper demonstrates strong and consistent performance gains, including improvements in patient-level AUROC and sensitivity over a wide range of baselines (frame-based, MIL, video models, and expert scoring).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Limited novelty in core modeling components. While the paper positions Compass as a novel framework, many of its building blocks are incremental combinations of existing ideas. The use of transformers for aggregating multiple instances (frames, slices, or views) is already well explored in medical imaging. The use of foundation model backbones (ProstNFound+) with prompt conditioning is directly inherited from prior work. 2.The method is evaluated on only 118 patients from two centers , which is relatively small. No external validation set beyond the two centers are provided. This is particularly important since prior work (e.g., ProstNFound+, Cinepro) emphasizes robust training and domain generalization. 3.There are also limited demonstrations of clinical feasibility and workflow integration. Although the paper motivates alignment with clinical workflow, actual clinical usability is not rigorously evaluated. There is no study on reader-AI collaboration, or time efficiency or workflow integration. 4.Compass explicitly incorporates biopsy frames as input. This raises concerns for applicability for pre-biopsy decision-making and potential information leakage, since biopsy targets are already clinician-selected suspicious regions 5.There is no failure case analysis. It would be insightful to know performance across prostate sizes, lesion locations or patient subgroups.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. Reviewers have recognized our strong clinical motivation (R1, R2, R3), “strong and consistent performance gains” over a “thorough evaluation landscape” (R1, R2, R3); and the “practical value” of Compass (R1, R2) as a “complementary tool to expert judgment” (R1). We address major concerns below. NOVELTY (R2, R3): No prior µUS work jointly models rotational sweeps, biopsy frames, and roll-angle geometry, acquired during a biopsy study, in a single framework. Therefore, our problem formulation, model design, and empirical findings (that study-level reasoning substantially outperforms every available baseline), all constitute novel contributions. While sinusoidal encodings, cross-attention, and transformer fusion are used in other literature, their combination in this specific formulation and problem setting is novel. We will clarify this in revisions. STATISTICAL UNCERTAINTY (R1, R2, R3): We agree that uncertainty reporting would improve the paper. We have this information and will amend the tables to include the std. dev. of the reported metrics. METRICS & MODEL SELECTION (R2): The same selection protocol was applied to all methods: we selected the epoch with the highest mean validation AUROC across folds. Sen@60 is the sensitivity at the first operating point where specificity exceeds 60%. Balanced Acc. is derived from a single point estimate of Sens. and Spec., and is sensitive to the choice of threshold. At deployment, the threshold would be calibrated to the clinical setting. AUROC is more robust as it summarizes performance across thresholds. We will clarify these points in revisions. COMPARISON FAIRNESS (R2): We clarify that integrating richer inputs (sweeps and roll angles alongside still frames) is part of our contribution. These inputs are easy to obtain during a µUS study, but no prior work proposes a framework to leverage them effectively. This gap motivated Compass, whose multi-stage architecture (i) exploits these rich inputs for the first time, (ii) exploits them better than baseline alternatives at each stage (frame-level, MIL, video), and (iii) is strongly supported by ablations. For the PRI-MUS comparison, we use the maximum PRI-MUS per patient, consistent with the landmark OPTIMUM clinical trial on µUS. The comparisons are thus fair: each baseline receives the inputs it was designed for. CORE-LEVEL PERFORMANCE (R1, R2): The reviewers observe that Compass does not outperform PRI-MUS on cores. We emphasize that Compass is not intended to replace PRI-MUS, but complement it. Matching the study’s PRI-MUS raters (experts with years of experience) would be remarkable for an AI system. Even when PRI-MUS experts are available, our system complements them with stronger patient-level performance. Further, PRI-MUS scoring relies on specialized expertise unavailable in many clinical settings outside large urban centers; in these cases, Compass may provide a viable alternative. We will amend the manuscript to make these explicit and temper claims. CLINICAL FEASIBILITY (R2, R3): We only require labelled biopsy-time frames to train and test the model. At deployment, frames can be obtained by capturing images from typical biopsy locations before the procedure, so the model can be used in routine clinical workflows and pre-biopsy screening. Our use of five-fold cross-validation and data from two geographically distant centers improves the strength of our results within the constraints of dataset size. We also note that 118 patients is consistent with other published µUS AI studies used for model development (e.g. MicroSegNet, ProMUS-NET). The cohort is therefore sufficient to demonstrate feasibility, but we will state the limitation and need for prospective validation in future work in revisions. title: Defining Robust Ultrasound Quality Metrics via an Ultrasound Foundation Model
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear clinical relevance. Strong use of domain-specific foundation model features, comprehensive evaluation (task-based, cross-organ, clinician study), and practical no-reference metric.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Limited comparison with recent learned IQA methods and reliance on a specific foundation model. Insufficient ablations and limited detail on clinical study and computational cost. The tests were done at very low quality values (PSNR range 20-25).
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Methodological Novelty: The core innovation lies in leveraging the feature space of an ultrasound-specific foundation model (as opposed to natural-image models) to define quality metrics. This directly addresses the fundamental issue of domain mismatch. 2.Comprehensive and Convincing Evaluation: The validation is exceptionally thorough, demonstrating value from multiple complementary angles. Task-Linked Quality: Using the drop in segmentation Dice score as a “ground truth” to prove the proposed metrics better reflect semantic damage than VGG-LPIPS. Clinical Alignment: The blinded clinician study increases the accuracy of predicting expert preference from 47.2% to 72.8%. While inherent to foundation model-based approaches, this should be acknowledged as a limitation. 2.Limitation in Evaluation Scope: Experiments focus primarily on static images. Ultrasound is often used dynamically (e.g., echocardiography, fetal screening). The paper does not explore the metric’s capability to assess dynamic quality factors like temporal consistency or motion artifacts. reviewer_3_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs for their careful reading, constructive comments, and positive assessment of our work. We are grateful that the reviewers recognized the significance of addressing the disconnect between conventional algorithmic image-quality metrics and clinical utility in ultrasound imaging, as well as the novelty of using an ultrasound foundation model to define both full-reference and no-reference quality metrics. The reviewers’ comments provided useful guidance on how to make the paper clearer and more balanced. In the camera-ready version, we will more explicitly discuss the limitations of relying on a TinyUSFM backbone, including potential issues related to foundation-model bias, rare pathologies, unseen devices, and domain shift. meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers recommend Acceptance. The consensus is on the significance and novelty of this work, which addresses the critical disconnect between algorithmic metrics and clinical utility in ultrasound imaging. The paper presents the first unified quality assessment framework built upon an ultrasound foundation model, introducing two well-motivated metrics tailored to ultrasound physics that cover both full-reference and no-reference scenarios. The evaluation is comprehensive and convincing, spanning numerical simulations, downstream task performance, cross-domain generalization, and blinded clinician studies, forming a complete evidence chain that strongly supports the claims. For all these reasons, recommendation is towards Acceptance.

title: DeformTTA: Morphology-Aware Controllable Deformation for Test-Time Adaptation in Fetal Cardiac Ultrasound Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) Utilizes the BR coefficient as a morphological constraint to maintain the topological integrity of the ventricles and atria, mitigating the boundary collapse issues often observed in standard entropy minimization methods. (2) Isolates high-frequency speckle noise from deformation calculations by employing one-hot Gaussian-smoothed fields to guide displacement field generation. (3) Implements an effective “deform-then-generate” strategy. By using a fine-tuned ControlNet, it converts geometric deformations into realistic ultrasound images for adaptive optimization. (4) Demonstrates strong quantitative performance on a 650-case multi-center dataset. The method performs favorably against established domain generalization algorithms and recent TTA frameworks (including TEGDA), achieving a Mean Dice of 76.38% and reducing HD95 to 4.888 mm.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) High Inference Latency: The generative diffusion pipeline (which generates 4 augmented samples and performs 2 gradient steps per test image) adds approximately 3 to 5 seconds of processing time per case. This limits its feasibility for real-time intraoperative clinical applications, restricting its use primarily to offline analysis. (2) Cold-Start Dependency: The TTA process relies heavily on the accuracy of the initial segmentation prediction from the pre-trained baseline model (nnU-Net). In scenarios with severe domain shifts (drastic probe angle changes or heavy acoustic shadowing), the initial mask may fail entirely. The framework currently lacks an explicit rejection sampling or self-correction mechanism to prevent subsequent error propagation. (3) Underutilization of Temporal Dynamics: The current approach performs independent adaptation based on 2D static images, treating end-diastolic and end-systolic frames as isolated instances. Despite having a deformation module that simulates motion, the framework does not leverage the inherent temporal consistency present in continuous ultrasound video frames.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: THe problem is important and well motivated, where the different aspect of fetal cardiac ultrasound may affect the i.i.d assumption. The method is domain-informed rather than generic. Using a boundary-regularity shape descriptor, Gaussian-smoothed structural fields, controllable deformation, and motion-conditioned synthesis is more tailored to fetal heart dynamics than plain entropy minimization The ablation is directionally useful and suggests the deformation module is important, the qualitative figure on page 7 is focused on clinically relevant abnormal cases rather than only easy examples.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I find the dataset is a bit confusing, the dataset contains scans from two hospitals and also with normal/pathological. THis makes it really hard to tell where the performance gain actually come from. The ablation text states ControlNet removal changes HD95 from 24.31 to 59.61 mm, but Table 2 reports 4.888 to 11.92 mm. Those cannot both be correct. “MedSAM [7]” is mentioned, but reference [7] is the LoRA paper, not MedSAM. That is a concrete reference error. The table 2 shows w/o shape prior regularization, but the objective function doesn’t have any term for this one.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The integration of explicit physiological cardiac dynamics into the TTA process is innovative. Moving away from traditional domain-agnostic generic augmentations or purely entropy-based TTA methods, this work elegantly uses biological priors to prevent catastrophic failure under complex deformations. 2.The introduction of the Boundary Regularity coefficient provides a specific, quantifiable morphological constraint. Formulated as a radial coefficient of variation, it establishes a standardized shape prior that explicitly prevents the adaptation process from yielding biologically implausible shapes. 3.The framework integrates a ControlNet-based generative model into the TTA pipeline to resolve interpolation artifacts common in traditional geometric warping. Conditioned on the deformed masks, the generative model synthesizes artifact-free, target-style images.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.As acknowledged by the authors in the conclusion, the generative TTA process is computationally expensive, adding 3-5 seconds of processing time per case. In the context of ultrasound, which is inherently a real-time imaging modality, this computational bottleneck severely limits immediate clinical deployment. 2.The framework relies on an initial mask to generate structural fields. If the initial model prediction is flawed, the morphology-aware shape prior and the subsequent deformations will be misguided. The paper lacks a fallback or self-correction mechanism to recover from catastrophic initial failures. 3.The methodology does not provide sufficient detail on the pre-training or fine-tuning process of the ControlNet and the Deformation Network. 4.The comparison method is somewhat outdated, with only one from 2025.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback, and address the concerns below. 1.[R1-W1/R3-W1] Inference latency The computational overhead of our TTA process comes from two parts: 1) Image generation, which is the most time-consuming part. In practice, we can optimize this part by using xFormers + DDIM 2-step + fp16 + torch.compile, reducing time from 1172.7 ms to 451.8 ms per image (2.60x). For 4 representative frames, the runtime drops from about 4.8 s to 1.8 s, with negligible accuracy change (Delta = -0.01%). 2) Model parameter updating, which requires 142 ms for our 2 optimization steps. Furthermore, we can also adapt our method to new domain under per-domain TTA setting. Precisely, we can collect a set of images from the new domain without annotation, and adopt our DeformTTA once offline before online usage on the new domain. This helps to improve the performance on new domain without extra online cost. 2.[R1-W2/R3-W2] Cold-Start Dependency We further statistically analyze the results by stratifying the initial masks into three categories based on Dice score: Low (<50%), Medium (50%-75%), High (>75%). Our DeformTTA improves the performance for all tiers, even with more gains on the Low tier. This is probably because of two reasons about the generation part in our DeformTTA: 1) The deformation network has chance to make the pseudo-labels closer to optimal segmentation; 2) The diffusion model with ControlNet can generate samples with similar intensity distribution with the new domain, improving the generalization ability of the segmentation network. This explains why our DeformTTA is also effective when initial pseudo-labels are relatively poor. 3.[R1-W3] Temporal dynamics We agree video-level temporal consistency is important. The current 2D design is constrained by available labels (annotated ED/ES frames without dense temporal correspondence). We will explicitly state this limitation and discuss optical-flow-guided video adaptation as future work. 4.[R2-W1] Dataset design clarity Our split is intentionally challenging clinical and two-axis shifted: source training set = 200 normal 4CH scans from Hospital-1 (screening center); test set = 450 CHD 4CH scans from Hospital-2 (referral center). Shift comes from both center (scanner/protocol) and pathology (unseen structural abnormality). 5.[R2-W2] HD95 inconsistency: 24.31->59.61 vs 4.888->11.92 We apologize for this mistake. The in-text values were pixel-space HD95 before physical calibration; Table 2 reports clinical HD95 in mm. We will correct this inconsistency and report HD95 consistently in mm. 6.[R2-W3] Citation error (MedSAM vs LoRA) You are correct. The citation for “fine-tuned MedSAM” should be MedSAM (Ma et al., 2024); LoRA should be cited separately for the fine-tuning strategy. We will correct this into “fine-tuned MedSAM [Ma et al., 2024] with LoRA [7]”, and review the remaining references. 7.[R2-W4] Table 2 vs method naming mismatch The row “w/o Shape Prior Regularization” actually means removing the smooth loss in Eq. (3) that implements the BR-coefficient-based shape prior. We will rename it to “w/o Smooth Loss (Shape Prior Reg.)” and align wording in the method section for better clarity. 8.[R3-W3] Missing training details The details of pre-training the deformation network and fine-tuning ControlNet are as follows: Deformation network: lightweight U-Net (3 encoder/decoder stages, 32 base channels), predicts displacement (u_x, u_y) from Gaussian-smoothed one-hot distance fields, 100 epochs, Adam lr=3e-4, weight decay 1e-4.- ControlNet: SD1.5 initialization, 5,000 steps, source-domain image-mask pairs (200 cases), batch 4, AdamW lr=1e-5, 256x256, RGB-encoded 7-class mask condition. We will incorporate these details in the revision. 9.[R3-W4] Comparison with more methods Excellent suggestion. We have compared to the most related TEGDA [31]. Per rebuttal policy, we cannot provide more comparative results in this response.
