title: Discriminative Directional Projection for Reverse Distillation in Breast Ultrasound Anomaly Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses a limitation of prior reverse distillation methods at the objective level, rather than only reporting empirical improvements. The idea of replacing global cosine alignment with directional pixel-wise consistency is intuitive and methodologically interesting. The alternating optimization strategy for mining hard directions is meaningful, as it reduces reliance on overly easy alignment directions. The method shows competitive overall performance, and the ablation results reasonably support the contribution of each component. The gains are achieved without substantial architectural changes, which is a practical advantage.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Validation is limited to only two breast ultrasound datasets, so the generalizability of the method remains unclear. If the paper primarily targets breast ultrasound anomaly detection, comparisons with stronger non-RD baselines, such as diffusion-based UAD methods (e. g. , REFLECT [1], AnoDDPM [2]), would strengthen the study. [1] Beizaee, F. , Hajimiri, S. , Ben Ayed, I. , Lodygensky, G. , Desrosiers, C. , & Dolz, J. (2025, September). Reflect: Re ctified Fl ows for E fficient Brain Anomaly C orrection T ransport. In International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (pp. 456-466). Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. [2] Wyatt, J. , Leach, A. , Schmon, S. M. , & Willcocks, C. G. (2022). Anoddpm: Anomaly detection with denoising diffusion probabilistic models using simplex noise. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition (pp. 650-656). If the main claim is an improvement to the RD framework itself, additional validation on other domains and datasets is needed. It is currently unclear why RD is particularly the most suitable formulation for ultrasound anomaly detection, or whether the proposed loss generalizes broadly across RD settings. Regarding Figure 3, the qualitative examples appear relatively easy; showing improvements on more challenging or ambiguous cases would make the evidence more convincing.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The inclusion of FPR@TPR95 and consistent improvements on this metric provide meaningful clinical grounding beyond standard AUC reporting. 2.The stepwise ablation shows monotonic improvements from each component, reasonably supporting the design choices.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Class definitions and splits for BUSI-WHU are never stated, i.e., what constitutes “normal” vs. “anomaly” is ambiguous, undermining result interpretability. 2.SCRD4AD achieves near-chance AUC (~63%) but high ACC, and Skip-TS shows high AUC but ~53% ACC, suggesting reproduction or evaluation protocol issues that weaken the claimed improvements. 3.key parameters (λ_orth, update frequency) are unreported.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Traditional Reverse Distillation methods impose global cosine consistency constraints on flattened features during training, yet rely on pixel-wise discrepancies during testing, leading to a significant objective mismatch. The proposed directional subspace projection mechanism maps features into a directional subspace to perform pixel-wise consistency distillation, effectively bridging this gap. 2.Directly optimizing cosine similarity is prone to falling into poor local optima. The authors designed an alternating optimization hard direction mining strategy, which actively identifies the directions with the greatest discrepancy between the teacher and student models. This prevents the optimization process from stalling on easily aligned directions. 3.Experimental results on the BUS-UCLM and BUSI-WHU datasets demonstrate consistent improvements across key metrics, including AUC, F1-score and Accuracy. Notably, the proposed method achieves the lowest False Positive Rate, while maintaining a True Positive Rate of 0.95.This is of significant clinical value for reducing unnecessary follow-ups in breast cancer screening.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Inadequate Analysis of Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Setting the number of projection directions to K=4096 is a critical design choice,yet the paper lacks corresponding ablation studies.It remains unclear how this specific hyperparameter impacts model performance (e.g., assuming it conforms to the channel dimensions, would K=512 or K=1024 yield similar or better results?). The authors need to provide a comprehensive sensitivity analysis for K. 2.Significant VRAM Consumption and Computational Overhead: Although the sampler is described as “lightweight”, projecting features into a high-dimensional space (4096 H W) to compute pixel-wise cosine similarity will inevitably lead to massive VRAM consumption during both training and inference. This is particularly concerning for high-resolution medical ultrasound images and is highly prone to causing CUDA Out-Of-Memory errors in practical deployments. The authors should provide detailed empirical data on VRAM usage and computational complexity (e.g., FLOPs) to justify the clinical deployability of this method on standard hardware. 3.Reproducibility Concerns Regarding Noise Initialization: The sampler utilizes Gaussian noise to generate channel directions. Because anomaly detection tasks are highly sensitive to subtle feature deviations, the stability of this random initialization is questionable. While orthogonal regularization helps prevent direction collapse, the authors must provide variance,standard deviation metrics across multiple runs with different random seeds to prove that the hard-direction mining strategy is genuinely effective and stable, rather than a result of lucky initialization. 4.Mathematical Paradox in Orthogonal Regularization: The paper sets the number of projection directions to K=4096 and introduces an orthogonal regularization term to encourage the Gram matrix of normalized directions to approach the identity matrix I. However, there is a fundamental mathematical contradiction here: the multi-scale feature channel counts are only 256, 512, and 1024.In a linear space with a maximum dimensionality of 1024, it is mathematically impossible to sustain 4096 mutually orthogonal vectors. Since the rank of the Gram matrix is upper-bounded by the channel dimension, it can never truly approximate a rank-4096 identity matrix. The authors must address this theoretical inconsistency.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and the meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. Following the meta-review, we organize our response around theoretical consistency, experimental clarity, baseline reliability, and other remaining points. 1.For the theoretical consistency of the orthogonality regularization, (R3.4) we agree that when K>C, the Gram matrix of normalized directions has rank at most C, and therefore it cannot exactly approximate a full-rank K×K identity matrix. The phrase approach the identity in Eq. (6) was imprecise and may incorrectly suggest an unrealizable strict orthogonality constraint. In fact, because each direction vector is L2-normalized, the diagonal entries of the Gram matrix are already fixed to one. Thus, Eq. (6) mainly penalizes the off-diagonal correlations between projection directions, making R_orth a soft inter-direction decorrelation constraint that reduces redundancy and alleviates direction collapse, rather than enforcing K strictly orthogonal directions. The rank limitation only implies that this regularizer cannot reach zero when K>C, but it does not invalidate its role in promoting directional diversity. (R3.1) K controls the number of candidate projection directions explored during hard-direction mining, rather than the dimension of an orthogonal basis. We use K=4096 to provide denser directional coverage for discovering discriminative teacher-student (TS) discrepancies, reflecting a trade-off between coverage and computational cost. We will clarify this design choice in the revision. (R3.3) The Gaussian noise is only the input to a learnable sampler, rather than fixed random directions. The final directions are learned through hard-direction mining, so the method is not designed to rely on lucky initialization. Moreover, using a large candidate direction set reduces dependence on any single initialized direction. 2.For the clarity of the experimental setup and dataset definitions, (R2.1) in our setting, normal breast ultrasound images are treated as the normal class, while all lesion-containing images, including benign and malignant cases, are treated as anomalies. We will explicitly report the class mapping, sample counts, and train/test splits. (R2.3) We used λ_orth=0.1 and an alternating schedule of 10 student updates followed by 1 sampler update. We will add these omitted implementation details in the revision. (R3.2) Projection-based scoring adds computation, but profiling under our test-time setting shows manageable overhead: the sampler has only 4.1M parameters, about 2.5% of the 165M full model, while full inference requires 108G FLOPs and 1.1 GB peak CUDA memory. 3.For the reliability of the baseline comparisons, (R2.2) AUC evaluates score ranking across thresholds, whereas ACC and F1 reflect threshold-based classification, so they need not vary consistently. We followed the evaluation protocol of prior UAD works and rechecked the code and data splits. Skip-TS and SCRD4AD show consistent trends on both datasets, suggesting that these differences arise from their score distributions rather than evaluation errors. 4.For other remaining issues, (R1.1/R1.3/R1.5) we agree that broader validation across anatomical regions, modalities, datasets, and more challenging qualitative cases would strengthen the evidence of generalizability. However, MICCAI rebuttal guidelines do not allow additional experiments or substantial experimental changes. Our current study therefore focuses on breast ultrasound anomaly detection, a clinically meaningful and annotation-scarce setting, to examine whether DDP Loss improves the RD paradigm. (R1.2/R1.4) Diffusion-based methods are valuable, but they belong to a different generative paradigm. Since our contribution is a loss-level improvement for RD, we compare mainly with representative RD-based methods. RD is suitable here because normal-only TS distillation matches scarce abnormal annotations and yields interpretable multi-scale discrepancy cues.

title: Disentangling Clinic-Specific Acquisition Variability from Motion Dynamics in Intrapartum Ultrasound
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The work correctly identifies that multi-clinic variability in intrapartum ultrasound mainly distorts temporal trajectories rather than static appearance, a gap overlooked by traditional harmonization methods (e. g. , ComBat, DANN). This insight is clinically important because fetal head progression is a dynamic process, and preserving motion dynamics directly supports obstetric decision-making. 2.The paper proposes an original self-supervised framework that explicitly disentangles clinic-invariant physiological motion from clinic-specific acquisition artifacts by integrating three complementary components: temporal regularization (scale and spectral) to stabilize latent dynamics, adversarial dual-stream encoding to separate invariant and specific representations, and hierarchical cross‑attention (HCA) for multi-scale temporal modeling. This design is novel because it unifies disentanglement and temporal modeling for ultrasound video, whereas prior work either addressed static domain shift or modeled time without disentanglement. 3.The evaluation is thorough and convincing: it uses temporal order prediction (TOP) to validate temporal structure preservation, leave‑one‑center‑out cross‑validation to test multi-center generalization, ablation studies to verify each component’s contribution, and cross‑domain transfer to the HC18 benchmark to demonstrate anatomical generalizability. Quantitative results are strong (99.70% TOP accuracy, 87.23% Dice score) and statistically significant. 4.The authors contribute a new multi-center intrapartum ultrasound video dataset from three clinics with heterogeneous protocols, addressing the data scarcity issue in this field. The dataset supports reproducible research on temporal dynamics and multi-center harmonization.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper conducts its most critical cross-domain generalization evaluation on HC18, which is antenatal (prenatal) fetal head ultrasound data, not true intrapartum ultrasound. Although HC18 is a standard benchmark, it lacks the severe motion artifacts, probe instability, and in vivo labor dynamics of real intrapartum imaging. As a result, the reported 87.23% Dice score does not fully validate clinical performance for the target task, and the claimed clinical translational value is not sufficiently verified on the actual target data distribution. 2.The paper compares mainly with traditional static harmonization methods (ComBat, DANN) and a simple temporal autoencoder, but does not benchmark against state-of-the-art temporal self-supervised or video disentanglement models tailored for medical imaging, making it difficult to assess the absolute advancement of the HCA framework. 3.While the model quantitatively disentangles clinic-invariant and clinic-specific representations, the paper does not provide clinically interpretable analysis, leaving unclear how the representations support real obstetric decision-making. 4.The paper does not report inference speed, model complexity, or practical deployment feasibility for real-time intrapartum monitoring, which is essential for clinical translation in busy labor ward environments.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper attempts to solve an important problem, which is the disentanglement of the latent space based on some confounding factors, and specifically on the latent space of a temporal sequence. The author’s careful approach to data splitting is commendable, which is evident from the subject-level and center-level split.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: These are the major issues with the paper in my opinion: clinical relevance: this paper is motivated by the observation that “current practice rely predominantly on single-frame analysis, but fetal head progression is inherently dynamic”. while i agree with the notion where “meaningful clinical info is encoded in motion patterns across time”, i believe this should refer to multiple timepoints across the labor process. the dataset used in this paper, however, appears to be short video clip at a single timepoint during the labor process, likely acquired with some sweep-like protocol, which is really an attempt to capture wider anatomical region instead of motion pattern. I would suggest rephrasing the motivation to explain how such video is beneficial over single-frame approach, as well as to provide more details about the acquisition protocol. basic pre-processing steps: based on Fig.1D, it appears that videos collected from center A and B follow a protocol where the video recording starts either before the probe was placed on the patient, or the initial position of the probe is away from any visible tissue, resulting in the near-zero intensity of the first ~10 frames (and a similar pattern close to the end of the videos). It is intuitive to pre-process these videos such that the initial/final dark frames are cropped away, followed by interpolating the remaining frames to a constant total number of frames (i.e. 100) if necessary. doing so would also make the comparison between center in Fig.1E more meaningful and interpretable. better ablation study design: based on table 3, the ablation study was performed by adding one loss component at a time. it would be more thorough to explore more combination of the loss components. L_scale and L_spec, for example, attempt to tackle very similar issue (both trying to minimize fluctuation, with L_scale doing it at a more global scale while L_spec focus at neighboring points at various distance apart). however, i also understand that this may be out of the scope of the paper. better explanation on evaluation strategy: as far as I understand, the goal of this paper is to disentangle the latent factor based on the acquisition site. the temporal order prediction (TOP) task, however, is designed to evaluate the temporal continuity and consistency of the latent factors. I can see that somewhere down the line the author has also make use of the ASW metric as part of the evaluation process, which presumably is related to the disentanglement aspect. The paper would benefit significantly from an explanation of how this works. Furthermore, circling back to the main motivation of the paper, it would also be interesting to connect this to some clinically relevant downstream task and to provide an evaluation on how the single-frame, temporal (vanilla), and temporal (ours) approaches compare to each other, although again this might be out of scope of the paper.

author_feedback: We thank the editor and reviewers for their time and evaluations. R1/R2/R3 = Reviewer 1/2/3, M = Meta-Reviewer, W = Weakness. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE Our paper addresses a fundamental clinical challenge: robust multi-center assessment of labor progression across heterogeneous clinical sites. The partograph — tracking cervical dilation and fetal head station — relies on manual assessment introducing operator subjectivity; intrapartum ultrasound faces similar challenges. A critical barrier for AI-driven labor monitoring is acquisition variability across centers, distorting temporal representations and hindering generalization. Our work represents a principled first step by learning center-invariant temporal representations that generalize across unseen centers (Table 2) and encode anatomically transferable structure (Table 5), establishing a foundation for future clinically robust multi-center AI systems. [M.1/R1.W1] HC18 RATIONALE R1 questions the validity of HC18 as cross-domain evidence. HC18 is used as a representation quality probe, not a clinical performance claim. Both datasets involve 2D B-mode fetal head ultrasound imaging with notable variability (Voluson E8/730, 6-fold pixel range, all trimesters). The domain gap strengthens our interpretation: an encoder trained on intrapartum video achieves 87.23% Dice on antenatal images, surpassing an in-domain autoencoder (83.12%) and random initialization (80.64%), suggesting anatomically transferable representations. HC18 provides pixel-level masks, making it a suitable benchmark. [M.2/R1.W2] SOTA COMPARISON R1 notes absence of CPC/MoCo comparison. We acknowledge this would strengthen the evaluation; however, HCA already achieves 99.70% TOP (CI [99.10, 100.0]), approaching the practical ceiling. Moreover, CPC and MoCo target single-domain SSL and are not designed for multi-center temporal variability. Table 4: raw 47.3%, DANN 92.3%, HCA 99.3%. [M.3+M.4/R1.W3/R2.W1/R2.W4] CLINICAL MEANING AND EVALUATION R2 questions whether clips are single-timepoint sweeps; R1 and R2 question the clinical relevance of evaluation metrics. Regarding R2.W1: each subject contributes multiple clips at distinct timepoints throughout labor, capturing longitudinal physiological variation rather than isolated sweeps. Regarding R1.W3 and R2.W4: ASW measures center-label separability in FE latent space — lower values confirm disentanglement. FE ASW 0.24 vs. RE 0.725 shows center-specific variability isolated in RE while FE captures acquisition-invariant structure; Table 3 shows ASW improves from 0.41 to 0.24 as components are added. TOP evaluates temporal coherence by distinguishing ordered from shuffled sequences. Together these validate temporally structured, center-invariant representations. HC18 transfer (87.23% Dice) provides anatomical evidence. [R1.W4] INFERENCE SPEED R1 notes absence of inference speed data. Deployment uses only the encoder (~2.8M params., ~5.7 GMACs/seq.); Tesla T4 latency is ~2.9s/sequence. Clips are acquired periodically, making periodic inference clinically feasible. [R2.W2] DARK FRAMES R2 suggests trimming boundary frames. Figure 1D shows center-specific variability persists in valid frames (15–80): Center A rises from ~60 to >100 while Center C remains ~60, reflecting protocol-driven variability. Such frames occur in realistic deployment scenarios; robustness is therefore desirable. [R2.W3] ABLATION R2 notes that L_scale and L_spec may overlap. Table 3 shows complementary effects: L_scale provides the largest gain (+33.1pp, 52.8%→85.9%), while L_spec adds further improvement (→91.4%). This suggests distinct roles: L_scale regularizes transition magnitude, whereas L_spec suppresses high-frequency instability. [R3.W1+W2] COMPLEXITY AND ABBREVIATIONS We appreciate R3’s positive assessment of the work. All architectures share an identical backbone; complexity is incremental. Code available in anonymized repository. Thank you for your consideration.

title: Distilling Temporal Coherence Into 2D Networks for Transrectal Ultrasound Prostate Video Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: This work proposes a self-supervised temporal consistency framework by using knowledge distillation and contrastive learning. It distills temporal knowledge into a 2D network during training, enabling pure single-frame inference without runtime overhead. This elegantly resolves the trade-off between 2D flickering and 3D high latency. The authors introduce a multi-view transrectal ultrasound prostate video benchmark with 2679 annotated frames, which can be an important contribution in public datasets for this clinical task. The authors claim code and dataset will be open-sourced to support reproducibility. Experiments on SUN-SEG and TRUS-V validate the method. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results with an ultra-fast inference speed of 127.97 FPS, showing strong clinical potential.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Although the method achieves competitive results on SUN-SEG, the Dice on SUN-SEG-Easy is still lower than DALA. It would strengthen the empirical study if more recent and relevant baselines on SUN-SEG were included. Besides, there have been some other methods you didn’t compare with have even higher dice on SUN-SEG like LGRNet. Maybe you should compare more new methods on SUN-SEG, such as SAM2-based and SAM3-based to verify your excellent performance. 2.The paper should clarify the exact training protocol on SUN-SEG. Since the method is described as a self-supervised Student-Teacher framework trained on unlabeled videos, it is currently unclear whether the SUN-SEG annotations are used only for evaluation, or also for teacher pretraining / supervision. 3.The ablation study is only conduct on SUN-SEG (Easy) dataset. I think the ablation study on your own dataset is also important as you propose your method in the specific scene of prostate ultrasound video segmentation. In addition, the current ablation does not clearly explain the “partial usage” setting of the prototype module; a brief clarification, or a simple comparison between single-scale and dual-scale usage, would make the design choice more convincing. 4.TRUS-V is a useful contribution, but its current scale is still limited to 10 patients from a relatively narrow acquisition setting. It would be helpful to discuss this limitation more explicitly and clarify whether future extensions with more patients or acquisition diversity are planned. 5.Although the method does not use optical flow at inference, its temporal supervision is still derived from flow-based alignment during training. Therefore, the learned 2D model may implicitly encode scene-specific temporal regularities of the current TRUS setting. Since TRUS-V mainly contains paired axial/sagittal views from the same acquisition scenario, it would be helpful to clarify whether the learned temporal prior generalizes across views or acquisition settings, rather than being tied to a specific motion pattern.

author_feedback: To AC and Reviewers: We thank the AC and reviewers for their comments. We have addressed the concerns regarding annotation, baselines, and clinical rigor below. All revisions will be fully incorporated into the final manuscript. ﻿Clarification on Labeling Protocol (R1-R3) To clarify our protocol, we emphasize that our framework does not require any frame-wise annotations. The training follows a two-stage process: (1) Static Pre-training: An initial 2D teacher model is trained using only 10-15% random sparse image-level labels. (2) Label-free Adaptation: No additional annotations are used during the subsequent video adaptation process. Instead, we leverage self-supervised equivariance and distillation to empower the 2D model with temporal robustness. This approach effectively elevates static 2D models into robust video architectures without the prohibitive cost of video-domain labeling. Asymmetric Comparison with Baselines (R1, R2) ﻿In our preliminary evaluations, representative baselines (SALI, HilbertMamba, LGRNet, SAM 2/3) showed comparable performance. Although these baselines were omitted from the original manuscript due to strict page constraints, we emphasize that such direct comparisons are fundamentally unfair, as these methods rely on extra temporal labels and heavy interaction modules. While such models may offer marginal gains via extra temporal supervision, they operate at a much lower throughput of 10 to 40 FPS. In contrast, our method achieves 127.97 FPS, satisfying the high-speed requirements of TRUS-guided surgery. Acknowledging the reviewers’ feedback, we will incorporate these additional comparisons and an extended related work section in the final manuscript. Pioneering the TRUS-V Temporal Benchmark (R1, R3) ﻿Prior to our work, a dedicated temporal benchmark for TRUS-guided surgery was non-existent. To address this critical gap, TRUS-V uses a strict patient-level split (9 train / 1 test), yielding 2,405/274 frames across 20 axial/sagittal videos. Although limited to 10 patients, every single frame was exhaustively manually refined by an experienced radiology professor. To ensure diversity, the dataset covers major anatomical variations across both axial and sagittal planes. This rigorous clinical validation establishes TRUS-V as a highly reliable initial benchmark for evaluating real-time temporal consistency. Prototype Ablation (R1, R2) The single-scale alignment, denoted as △, is suboptimal because local prototypes are noise-sensitive, while global prototypes lack boundary precision. Our dual-scale design combines global semantic stability with local boundary refinement via area-adaptive weighting, improving both structural consistency and mask overlap, as reflected by Sα (+0.08) and Dice (+0.025) in Table 3.To ensure fair generalization evaluation, we conducted these ablations on the public SUN-SEG benchmark rather than our private TRUS dataset. Temporal Prior (R1) We utilize optical flow to acquire inter-frame temporal information without requiring any additional temporal supervision. Rather than inducing overfitting to specific probe trajectories, this mechanism serves as a training regularizer to distill artifact-invariant and anatomically stable representations. Our robust performance across both the TRUS-V and SUN-SEG datasets empirically demonstrates that our framework captures fundamental structural consistency rather than memorizing specific motion biases. Implementation Details & Visualization (R3) We will revise Sec. 3 to detail the workflow, hyperparameters (AdamW, 1e-6, batch 8, 1 epoch), and explicit loss weights (1.0, 1.0, 0.25, 1.0) in Eq. (5). In Fig. 4, all rows display raw confidence maps rather than binarized masks. DALA’s grayscale appearance reflects uncertain predictions, whereas our model produces distinctly sharper activations. Crucially, all metrics were computed using an identical thresholding protocol to ensure strict fairness.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Across the reviews, there is a consistent appreciation for the practical motivation of the work. The idea of transferring temporal coherence into a lightweight 2D model is seen as a sensible way to balance stability and efficiency, and the dataset contribution is viewed as a useful addition, especially given the limited availability of TRUS video data. That said, the main concerns are less about the core idea and more about how convincingly it is validated. Reviewers repeatedly point out gaps in benchmarking particularly the absence of stronger or more recent video segmentation baselines and some ambiguity around the training protocol (e.g., the role of annotations and fairness of comparisons). The relatively small dataset and limited diversity also raise questions about generalizability. In addition, parts of the method and ablation analysis would benefit from clearer explanations and more thorough justification. My reading is largely in line with these points. The direction is interesting and practically relevant, but the current version leaves some uncertainty around how strong the empirical support really is. Addressing the evaluation gaps and clarifying the setup would make the contribution more convincing. | The paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem: achieving temporally stable TRUS video segmentation while maintaining real-time inference efficiency. Reviewers generally agreed on the practical value of the proposed temporal distillation framework and the usefulness of the newly introduced TRUS-V dataset. The rebuttal successfully clarified several key concerns, including the annotation protocol, training procedure, dataset split, implementation details, and the rationale behind the dual-scale prototype alignment. These clarifications strengthen the validity of the proposed approach and make the experimental setup substantially clearer. Two reviewers maintained or strengthened their positive assessments following the rebuttal. One reviewer remained concerned about the completeness of the related work discussion and the absence of direct comparisons with several recent video segmentation methods. While these concerns are reasonable, they do not appear sufficient to outweigh the overall contribution, particularly given the method’s emphasis on achieving temporal consistency with lightweight 2D inference and its demonstrated efficiency advantages. Overall, I find the contribution technically sound, practically relevant, and supported by adequate empirical evidence. The paper presents a meaningful methodological contribution and introduces a valuable benchmark resource for the community Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses a practical clinical challenge in real-time TRUS prostate video segmentation by balancing the trade-off between the inter-frame inconsistencies of lightweight 2D networks and the high computational latency of 3D networks. I agree with the reviewers’ consensus regarding the method’s practical significance and the valuable contribution of the newly released, expert-annotated TRUS-V dataset. In the rebuttal, the authors resolved primary concerns regarding comparison baselines, evaluation dataset scale, labeling protocols, and general clarity issues. Regarding the absence of certain recent benchmarking baselines, I agree with the author’s rebuttal that the proposed method is emphasizing more on the high throughput (>120 fps) while maintaining a competitive performance against heavier video models. Overall, I think the practical soundness and open-source data contributions place this work in a strong position, and thus, I recommend accept. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend rejection. The paper addresses an important clinical problem, but the contribution appears limited. The method mainly combines existing ideas, including teacher-student distillation, equivariance-based pseudo-labeling, optical-flow temporal consistency, and prototype alignment, without clearly establishing sufficient novelty. The experimental comparison is also not convincing. Although some video baselines are included, the comparison with strong recent SOTA video segmentation methods is still limited. More importantly, the paper claims temporally consistent video segmentation, but the evaluation relies mostly on frame-wise segmentation metrics. Direct temporal stability metrics are needed to support this claim. Finally, the core assumption is unclear. If the model uses temporal information only during training but performs single-frame 2D inference, the paper should justify under what conditions such a model can reliably produce temporally consistent results. Without this clarification, the main claim is not fully convincing. Overall, due to limited novelty, insufficient validation, and unclear presentation, I suggest reject.

title: DK-Net: Semi-supervised Wavelet-KAN Landmark Localization for Angle of Progression Measurement in Intrapartum Transperineal Ultrasound
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed blocks make sense for high-throughput architectures and could be interesting for other researchers working on real-time deployments. Semi-supervised training is well described, even if it is not the main innovation of the paper.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The IUGC 2025 report has now been published, and this makes both the paper’s bilbliography and quantitative evaluation very weak: there is no point in implementing baselines when the results from previous challenge participants are available. reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Clinically meaningful problem: The paper addresses a well-defined and practically important task (AoP estimation), with clear relevance to labor monitoring and decision support. The motivation is strong and aligned with current clinical needs. 2.Realistic evaluation setup: The use of the IUGC multi-center benchmark, with strict separation between training and test sets, strengthens the credibility of the results. The inclusion of both labeled and unlabeled data reflects realistic clinical scenarios. 3.Appropriate metrics: Reporting AoP error (in degrees) in addition to landmark localization error is a significant strength, as it directly reflects clinical utility rather than relying solely on pixel-based metrics. 4.Consistent empirical improvements: The proposed method shows improvements over multiple semi-supervised baselines, and ablation studies indicate that both KCA and WKG contribute to performance gains. 5.Robustness in challenging cases: The qualitative examples suggest that the method is more stable under severe speckle noise and acoustic shadowing, which are common failure modes in ultrasound.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Limited methodological novelty: While the overall design is well-motivated, the framework combines several existing components (Mean Teacher, wavelet-based processing, channel recalibration) in a relatively straightforward manner. The novelty mainly lies in the integration rather than in fundamentally new formulations. 2.Unclear role of KAN: The use of Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KAN) is interesting, but its advantage over simpler alternatives (e.g., MLP-based recalibration) is not strongly justified. The reported improvement over MLP is relatively modest, and it is unclear whether the gains stem from KAN specifically or from general nonlinear modeling capacity. 3.Limited mechanism-level validation: Although ablation studies are provided, the paper does not thoroughly verify whether the proposed modules address the intended challenges. For example, it would be helpful to explicitly demonstrate robustness under controlled contrast shifts or varying levels of speckle noise. 4.Weak analysis of AoP geometry: The observation that AoP error is not directly correlated with landmark localization error is insightful, but this aspect is not explored in depth. Additional analysis could strengthen the clinical interpretation of the results. 5.Potential over-complexity: The framework introduces multiple components (KCA, WKG, phase-guided interaction), which may raise concerns about complexity versus benefit, especially given the relatively incremental performance gains.

reviewer_3_strengths: This paper presents a semi-supervised framework, DK-Net, for automatic landmark localization and Angle of Progression (AoP) measurement in intrapartum transperineal ultrasound. The method combines a Mean Teacher style training strategy with two ultrasound-oriented modules, namely a KAN-based domain-adaptive channel recalibration module and a wavelet-domain feature refinement module, with the goal of improving robustness to speckle noise, acoustic shadowing, and limited annotations. According to the manuscript, the method is evaluated on the public IUGC benchmark and shows improved performance over several generic baseline models.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Although the manuscript reports comparisons with several generic landmark detection and semi-supervised baselines, it does not compare against, cite, or discuss the dedicated methods reported in the IUGC 2025 challenge benchmark, which is the most relevant evaluation setting for this work. In particular, the IUGC benchmark report explicitly documents the top-performing challenge methods and their associated technical papers, including the winning T2 entry. The authors should therefore cite the IUGC benchmark report [1] and include a direct comparison with the winning method [2]. According to that paper, the winning approach is based on a modified TransUNet with a TinyViT backbone, together with MAE-assisted knowledge distillation from an ultrasound foundation model, label perturbation, and semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, and it reports 11.6749 px mean radial error and 3.8061° mean absolute AoP error on the IUGC2025 challenge test set. Since the current manuscript reports 12.83 px MRE and 4.30° AoP MAE on the same benchmark, the omission of this direct comparison makes it difficult to assess the real state-of-the-art competitiveness of DK-Net. At minimum, the authors should explicitly cite these two works and discuss why DK-Net should be preferred over, or considered complementary to, the current challenge-winning solution. 2.The practical value of the semi-supervised setting is not fully characterized. The method is trained with 1,580 labeled images and 5,497 unlabeled images from the same benchmark protocol, but the manuscript does not show how performance changes as the amount of unlabeled data varies, nor whether the benefit remains meaningful when only a smaller in-domain unlabeled pool is available. This matters because the usefulness of a semi-supervised approach in practice depends not only on the final test accuracy, but also on its data-efficiency and deployment assumptions. A simple sensitivity analysis or label-efficiency curve would make the paper much stronger and would clarify whether the observed gain is robust or mainly dependent on access to a relatively large amount of benchmark-matched unlabeled data. author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive comments. We respond to the main concerns on IUGC 2025, KAN, and the semi-supervised setting. Comparison with IUGC 2025 and positioning (R2,R4,AC): We thank R2, R4, and the AC for pointing out that the comparison with IUGC 2025 methods was not sufficiently discussed. We also thank R2 for questioning the strength of our baselines. We clarify that these baselines remain useful because they were re-trained under the same input, data split, and semi-supervised protocol as DK-Net, allowing a controlled assessment of the proposed KCA/WKG modules rather than a comparison confounded by different training recipes. After revisiting our work in the context of the IUGC benchmark (Bai et al., 2026) and related challenge methods (Ma et al., 2025), we would like to clarify the practical advantage of DK-Net. Compared with top-ranked IUGC methods, DK-Net uses a single-model inference pipeline, without relying on multi-model ensembles or complex post-processing, while still keeping competitive AoP measurement performance. We believe this simpler design is useful for real-time assisted recognition in intrapartum ultrasound, where timely feedback and deployment cost matter. The IUGC report also notes the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency, and the need to consider latency and model complexity in practical deployment. Therefore, we view DK-Net as a lightweight real-time complement to high-performance IUGC methods, and as a step toward more deployable and methodologically grounded AoP measurement systems. Methodological contribution and KAN effectiveness (R3,AC): We thank R3 and the AC for raising concerns about novelty and mechanistic validation. We agree that the role of KAN should be explained more clearly. Our intention is not to present KAN as a generic replacement for CNNs or Transformers. Instead, we use KAN in two small but task-motivated calibration modules. Specifically, KCA uses simple channel statistics to adapt feature responses under contrast and acquisition variations. WKG uses local high-frequency statistics in wavelet subbands to learn data-dependent soft-thresholding, suppressing speckle- and shadow-related perturbations while preserving structured landmark edges. In both modules, KAN is used as a nonlinear statistics-to-calibration function learner. Its spline-like form provides local adaptivity, which is useful because ultrasound responses can be non-monotonic: strong responses may correspond to true PS/FH boundaries, but may also come from noise or shadows. Fig. 3 further shows that KAN learns more dynamic calibration/gating curves than the MLP counterpart, supporting that the gain is not merely from adding parameters. Together with the ablation results, this supports that KCA/WKG address the intended ultrasound degradations rather than acting as generic add-ons. In addition, AoP depends on the geometry between the PS axis and the FH tangent point, rather than on independent landmark errors linearly. For example, correlated shifts of the two PS endpoints along the PS axis may increase MRE but cause little angular change, whereas a small FH displacement perpendicular to the PS axis can noticeably change AoP. DK-Net uses PS structural information to guide FH localization, encouraging the model to focus on geometry directly relevant to AoP. This helps explain why MRE and AoP MAE are not strictly linearly correlated. Semi-supervised setting and annotation-ratio analysis (R4): We thank R4 for the helpful suggestion. We agree that varying labeled/unlabeled ratios would better characterize data efficiency. Here, we focus on a controlled comparison: DK-Net, KCA/WKG, and all baselines are evaluated under the same semi-supervised protocol. The results suggest improved AoP measurement over representative methods and the no-KCA/WKG variant while retaining real-time inference. We regard annotation-ratio analysis as important future work.

title: DreamReg: Belief-Driven World Model for 2D–3D Ultrasound Registration
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Framing registration as a partially observable sequential decision problem, where the agent accumulates belief about the alignment over time, is a novel formulation over the frame-independent regression paradigm. 2.The imagination rollout during inference is practically significant. It means the model can continue refining its estimate even when observations are partially occluded or unavailable. This aligns with real intraoperative constraints. 3.Evaluation on both CAMUS (cardiac) and μ-RegPro (prostate) provides cross-anatomy evidence for the approach. 4.The paper correctly contextualizes the speed/accuracy tradeoff relative to baseline, demonstrating that the additional computational cost of iterative belief rollout is clinically acceptable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Training and testing rely entirely on rendered 2D slices, no real intraoperative data. The core training pipeline renders 2D slices from 3D volumes using a differentiable physics-based renderer. Real intraoperative 2D US images might exhibit substantially different noise characteristics that a volume-slicing renderer cannot fully simulate. The domain gap between rendered and real acquisitions is neither discussed nor quantified. This is a critical gap between the paper’s clinical motivation (surgical navigation) and its experimental validation. 2.The paper’s most novel claim at inference time is that pose refinement through imagination is effective. Yet Table 2 ablates supervision signals (reward, reconstruction) but does not include a variant that uses real rendered observations at inference time (as during training). Such an “observe rollout at inference” baseline would directly quantify how much the imagination mechanism contributes versus the action-conditioned world model learned during training. 3.During inference, the model initializes from T_0 = 0 (zero pose) and h_0 = 0.In realistic surgical navigation, the initial probe pose is unknown and may deviate substantially from zero. The perturbation range used during training may not cover all clinically realistic initialization errors. No analysis of performance as a function of initial misalignment magnitude is provided. 4.The paper claims it follows dreamer-style world modeling. Equation (3) also uses “RNN” notation, but the paper cites a recurrent transformer (Bulatov et al. , NeurIPS 2022) as the actual implementation! This is a significant architectural choice, a recurrent transformer has very different inductive biases, memory capacity, and computational cost compared to a GRU. The choice is not ablated, and the description in the paper is insufficient to reproduce this component. 5.The paper motivates the stochastic latent variable as representing pose uncertainty under partial observability. However, no analysis of whether the learned posterior uncertainty correlates with registration error is provided.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper formulates the 2D–3D ultrasound registration problem as a sequential decision problem under partially observable conditions. Starting from an initial pose, the system predicts incremental motion at each step and updates the probe pose estimate accordingly, thereby continuously refining the transformation and allowing it to couple probe motion and observation transitions in latent space. 2.During inference, the model can directly generate pose increments through a policy network combined with prior dynamics, avoiding the high cost of physical rendering during inference and achieving fast closed-loop optimization based on imagination. 3.The comparison experiments and ablation study results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Although the method introduces a framework inspired by world models and related concepts for 2D–3D ultrasound registration, the paper does not clearly explain the clinical scenarios in which 2D–3D ultrasound registration is required. This lack of discussion makes it difficult to assess the practical clinical relevance of the proposed approach. 2.In the experiments, the 2D slices are resampled from 3D volumes, which does not reflect real clinical conditions. In practice, live intraoperative 2D ultrasound images can differ significantly from preoperative 3D volumes. Variations in probe force or orientation may further alter the acquired slices. This discrepancy should be considered when evaluating the potential translation of the proposed method to real clinical settings. 3.During the training phase, the pose trajectory T is synthesized by injecting Gaussian noise onto an ideal linear path. Real-world clinical probe fine-tuning is often non-linear and exhibits specific anatomical biases, such as avoiding rib shadows. Can this simple synthesized noise adequately represent the dynamics of a real clinical scan? 4.Compared with EUReg, which achieves 189 FPS, the proposed method runs at 40 FPS. It is therefore unclear whether the proposed approach may face computational bottlenecks when deployed on resource-constrained ultrasound devices.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is clearly written and easy to follow. The authors developed a novel method that utilizes the concept of a world model for 2D-3D US registration. The evaluation in this paper is also thorough. I appreciate that the authors perform a detailed comparison of their method with previous work and provide multiple metrics to quantify the improvement of their model better. They also perform a detailed ablation study to evaluate each component of their model and show that all contribute to the improvement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Currently, the model only addresses rigid transformation. In real clinical applications, the intraoperative 2D US may be deformed by the pressure of the US probe. It will be interesting to see how the model will perform in 2D US with deformation. The authors could have simulated deformed 2D US slices to evaluate the model’s performance. There are also some unclear details of the implementation (please see additional comments below).
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for raising these important concerns regarding clinical realism, inference-time observations, and surgical navigation trajectories. We agree that our current experiments should not be interpreted as a complete validation of real intra-operative deployment. Instead, our study follows prior 2D–3D ultrasound registration works such as EUReg and CUReg, where 2D slices are resampled from 3D ultrasound volumes to provide known ground-truth transformations and enable controlled, reproducible, and fair comparison. This setting allows us to systematically evaluate local pose refinement, but it cannot fully reproduce real intra-operative ultrasound variability, including probe-dependent noise, acoustic shadowing, probe-pressure-induced deformation, orientation changes, and pre-/intra-operative domain shifts. We will revise the manuscript to explicitly state this limitation. As ongoing work, we have built a robotic ultrasound platform and collected preoperative MRI, 3D ultrasound, and tracked 2D intra-operative ultrasound data for further validation under more realistic scanning conditions. Regarding why we do not use “observe rollout” or resliced ultrasound during inference, our design intentionally evaluates a stricter observation-free refinement setting. Since the 3D ultrasound volume is available, one could reslice the volume using the predicted pose at each iteration and feed the resliced image back to the belief update. However, this would change the inference problem from imagination-based world-model rollout to observation-conditioned closed-loop refinement or visual servoing. Such a setting provides additional information and may improve accuracy, but it also requires repeated observation acquisition or renderer queries at every refinement step, increasing computation and changing the intended evaluation protocol. In contrast, DreamReg asks whether a learned world model can refine the pose through internal belief evolution and action-conditioned prior dynamics. During training, the observation-conditioned posterior branch serves as a teacher, and the KL regularization encourages the observation-free prior used at inference to approximate the posterior belief that has access to observations. For surgical navigation, we also agree that real probe trajectories are often non-linear and anatomy-dependent, for example due to rib shadow avoidance, probe contact constraints, and tissue deformation. Therefore, the synthesized trajectory with Gaussian perturbations is not intended to model a full clinical scanning policy. Rather, it provides reproducible intermediate supervision for learning action-conditioned local refinement from an initial misalignment toward a target imaging plane. Similarly, the initial pose in our implementation denotes a canonical pose in a normalized scanning coordinate frame, not a zero pose in the global physical coordinate system. In realistic robotic ultrasound navigation, DreamReg should be used after a coarse initialization stage, which may be obtained from robot kinematics, optical tracking, surface landmarks, calibrated patient/scanning coordinates, or a standardized anatomical scanning plane. Thus, the DreamReg is best interpreted as a fine pose refinement module within a future coarse-to-fine robotic ultrasound navigation pipeline, rather than a global localization method from an arbitrary unknown probe pose. We will clarify this assumption and explicitly discuss the limitation that the current perturbation range and synthetic trajectories may not cover all clinically realistic initialization errors and scanning dynamics.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All reviewers agree on the merit of the submission. It is an interesting attempt to solve 2D–3D registration using a world model. However, its impact is limited by the strong assumption of rigid registration and the lack of intraoperative data for evaluation, where images from the same location can still exhibit significant variation. Some analysis in this regard will further strengthen the paper.

title: Dual Agreement Consistency Learning for Semi-supervised Fetal Ultrasound Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: The framework is designed to output a highly efficient lightweight convolutional neural network that requires only 1.47 million parameters and 7.03 GFLOPs. This makes the resulting model highly practical for deployment on portable or low-cost ultrasound devices. The implementation of the dual-agreement consistency loss is a skillful approach. By enforcing both probabilistic alignment and confidence-aware agreement at the pixel level, the framework elegantly suppresses the unreliable pseudo-labels that often plague semi-supervised learning in low-data regimes.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The massive gap in capacity between the 1.47M parameter UNeXt student and the 27.15M parameter Swin-Unet teacher might establish a rigid ceiling on what the student can actually learn. Additionally, the very small labeled batch size needs more justification to fully ensure the reproducibility of the training process.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.It focuses on semi-supervised fetal ultrasound segmentation when labeled data is limited. 2 The main strength is the dual-agreement consistency loss, which does more than standard CPS by encouraging the CNN and Transformer to agree not only on predictions but also on confidence. 3.The ablation results also suggest that this part of the method improving the performance.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1 The overall framework is still built on several existing ideas. It combines known components like CPS, CNN–Transformer co-training, EMA teacher supervision, and mixup-based consistency. So the novelty feels more like an incremental improvement than a really new framework. 2 Also, it is not very clear what the main focus of the method is. Is it mainly about improving accuracy, making the model lightweight, or increasing speed? At the moment, it seems to cover all of these, and they are all presented as strengths. I think the paper would be stronger if the authors picked one main theme and made that the central message, while discussing the other benefits, like lightweight design or faster inference, in the discussion section.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) This paper addresses a challenge: pixel-level annotation scarcity in fetal ultrasound, while maintaining practical deployability. 2) Using a heterogeneous teacher-student (CNN + Transformer) architecture leverages complementary representations, which is a reasonable strategy for semi-supervised segmentation. 3) Promises open-source code, enhancing reproducibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) The core novelty is ambiguous. It remains unclear whether the two agreements refer to (a) CNN vs. Transformer predictions, (b) two terms inside the loss, or (c) CPS plus interpolation consistency. This risks being an overstated claim. 2) Comparisons are made only against LMCT and a few others. Recent SOTA methods are missing. The claimed improvement may not hold against true state-of-the-art. 3) The entropy-guided confidence alignment is described vaguely. How are unreliable pseudo-labels suppressed? No thresholding, weighting, or filtering scheme is specified. 4) The 1.47M parameter claim applies only to inference. Training cost (memory/time) is not reported. 5) All improvements/losses are presented as point estimates without p-values or confidence intervals, making it impossible to judge whether differences are meaningful.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: R2-Q1, R3-Q1, R3-Q3: We thank the reviewers for highlighting the need to better clarify the core novelty and the role of the proposed dual-agreement mechanism. The core novelty of this work is the proposed Dual-Agreement Consistency (DAC) loss, which introduces two complementary cross-architecture agreement constraints for semi-supervised segmentation: (1) probabilistic agreement via KL divergence and (2) uncertainty-aware confidence agreement via entropy regularization. Unlike standard CPS-style supervision that mainly enforces hard pseudo-label agreement, DAC jointly regularizes both prediction distributions and prediction uncertainty across heterogeneous CNN/Transformer architectures. Rather than explicit confidence thresholding, the entropy-guided agreement term penalizes inconsistent high-entropy predictions while favoring mutually confident low-entropy agreement. The heterogeneous CNN/Transformer pairing further provides complementary local/global inductive biases, making agreement regularization more informative than homogeneous supervision. Consequently, DAC improves pseudo-label stability under extreme annotation scarcity, particularly for lightweight models. This is supported by the ablation study (Table 3), where adding L_dac produces the largest gains in boundary-sensitive metrics, especially on the challenging F-Abd dataset. We agree these mechanisms can be clarified further and will revise the manuscript accordingly. R1-Q1, R2-Q2, R3-Q4: We appreciate the reviewers’ comments regarding lightweight deployment. The primary goal of this work is to develop a robust semi-supervised framework for lightweight fetal ultrasound segmentation suitable for low-resource clinical deployment. Swin-Unet is used only during training as a high-capacity teacher to guide the lightweight UNeXt model (1.47M parameters, 7.03 GFLOPs). During inference, only UNeXt is deployed, while the teacher is discarded and introduces no inference overhead. The large teacher–student capacity gap is therefore intentional and clinically motivated. Existing SSL frameworks still struggle to effectively train lightweight models under limited annotations, whereas DACL consistently improves both overlap and boundary accuracy. R2-Q1, R3-Q2: We thank the reviewers for raising concerns regarding fair comparison. All cross-supervision methods were implemented using the same Swin-Unet/UNeXt pair, while mean-teacher methods used UNeXt/UNeXt. All methods were trained using identical data splits, augmentations, optimization settings, and evaluation protocols. Therefore, the observed improvements are attributable to DACL rather than stronger backbones. We additionally included several recent SSL methods, including PCPCS (2024), DSTCT (2024), and LMCT (2025). DACL achieves the best overall HC18 performance and the strongest boundary accuracy on the challenging F-Abd dataset. R1-Q1, R2-Q2: We appreciate the reviewers’ concerns regarding reproducibility and training stability. The labeled batch size of 1 follows common SSL medical image segmentation practice under extreme low-label settings. Stability is further improved through EMA guidance, interpolation consistency, and DAC regularization. We will release the complete training configuration, hyperparameters, implementation details, and data split settings to ensure reproducibility. R1-Q1, R3-Q5: We thank the reviewers for these valuable suggestions. In the camera-ready version, we will report mean±std across repeated runs together with statistical significance testing for the primary quantitative comparisons. Fig. 2 samples were selected as representative examples reflecting overall metric trends rather than best-case outliers, and we will clarify this explicitly in the manuscript. We additionally agree that future validation across additional datasets and lightweight backbones would further strengthen the generality of the framework.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviews are mixed. The other reviewer did not fully explain his/her motivation for rejecting the paper, mentioning only that concerns (presumably, the lack of p-value measuring the significance of improvements) where not resolved. Therefore, the AC recommends acceptance but strongly urges authors to update their paper accordingly, Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the rebuttal and the post-rebuttal reviewer comments, my recommendation is to accept the paper. The paper addresses a clinically relevant and practical problem: semi-supervised fetal ultrasound segmentation with a deployment-oriented lightweight model. The proposed dual-agreement consistency learning framework is technically sound, and the use of a lightweight CNN student with a stronger Transformer-based teacher is well motivated for low-resource clinical deployment. The rebuttal adequately addressed most of the major concerns, including the motivation of the lightweight design, training stability under limited labeled data, the representativeness of qualitative examples, and the need for repeated runs and statistical significance testing. Although one reviewer still maintained concerns about the need for major revisions, the majority of post-rebuttal opinions support acceptance, and the authors provided concrete commitments to improve the final manuscript. Therefore, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that the authors will clarify the novelty, report statistical significance and mean/std results, and better explain the training/inference cost distinction in the final version.

title: Dual-Domain Meta Conditioning Network for Fetal Head and Pubic Symphysis Segmentation in Ultrasound Images Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: High clinical relevance: The work targets a critical clinical task for labor progression assessment and delivery mode decision, solving the subjectivity and high variability of conventional vaginal examinations. Strong methodological novelty: DMC-Net breaks through single spatial-domain modeling and uses a structural–frequency dual-domain paradigm well-matched to ultrasound imaging characteristics. The DMCM, FCAM, and PSRD are well-motivated and technically distinct from standard U-Net or Transformer variants. Rigorous and complete evaluation: Experiments are conducted on the standard PSFHS2023 challenge dataset with comprehensive comparisons and ablation studies. Quantitative metrics (DSC, HD, ASD, ΔAoP) and visual results consistently support the effectiveness. Clear and reproducible pipeline: The network architecture, module formulations, training settings (optimizer, lr, batch size, GPU), and implementation details are well-described. Robust performance in challenging conditions: The model maintains stable segmentation under severe speckle noise, acoustic shadowing, and fetal motion, showing strong potential for clinical translation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Lack of efficiency analysis: The paper does not report model parameters, FLOPs, or inference speed, which are essential for real-time clinical ultrasound deployment. Insufficient generalization validation: Experiments are limited to the PSFHS2023 dataset; no cross-device, cross-center, or external dataset validation is provided. Partial novelty clarification: While the integrated pipeline is novel, frequency-domain attention and spectral reconstruction have been explored in prior medical image segmentation works. The paper could better highlight its unique design choices. Limited clinical case analysis: The paper does not analyze typical failure cases (e. g. , severe head rotation, strong acoustic shadowing) from a clinical perspective. Minor presentation issues: Some mathematical symbols lack clear definitions, and ablation studies lack corresponding visual comparisons.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1) This study focuses on the segmentation of the fetal head and pubic symphysis in intrapartum ultrasound, which has clear practical clinical significance. (2) The method targets typical challenges in ultrasound images, including speckle noise, weak boundaries, and anatomical variations, with a complete and logical overall framework. (3) The proposed method achieves competitive results on the public PSFHS2023 dataset, with improvements in both segmentation accuracy and AoP estimation.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) The proposed method represents an incremental improvement upon the U-Net architecture. However, the added components: including the meta-information-based cross-attention-style design (DMCM), multi-scale fusion-style mechanism (FCAM), and frequency-domain processing-style module (PSRD), are all widely adopted in existing literature [1,2]. As such, the work essentially constitutes a straightforward combination of established architectural designs, rather than introducing fundamentally novel mechanisms. (2) It remains unclear what specific input constitutes the “meta-info” in the DMCM. Is it a random learnable parameter, or a structured anatomical prior derived from the data? This critical design detail is insufficiently clarified. (3) While the ultimate goal of the work is AoP estimation, the model itself is fundamentally a segmentation network. The lack of validation on multiple independent datasets makes it difficult to substantiate the claimed competitive improvements in clinical utility. Furthermore, given that the authors have stacked multiple complex modules, it is also unclear whether such a sophisticated model is suitable for real-world clinical deployment. reviewer_3_strengths: The main novelty is a dual-domain meta-conditioning framework that explicitly combines structural/anatomical cues with frequency-domain priors at different stages of the network, rather than relying only on standard spatial CNN features. This is interesting because ultrasound quality is strongly affected by both structural ambiguity and speckle/high-frequency artifacts, so modeling both domains is well motivated.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The choice of scale factors s \in {4, 2} in the FCAM module is not well justified. Please explain why these values were selected and provide an ablation study to demonstrate their effectiveness for PS and FH segmentation. 2.There is an inconsistency in the dataset description. The PSFHS2023 dataset [4] (Zenodo) reports 1,358 images from 1,124 pregnant women, while this study uses 4,000 training, 400 validation, and 700 test images. This discrepancy should be clearly explained, and the correct reference should be verified. 3.The details of the initial convolution block \phi_0(I) are unclear to show how it extracts meta-information. What are the details of the convolution layers? 4.Important experimental details are missing, such as the number of training epochs, data augmentation strategies, and model complexity (e.g., number of parameters and FLOPs). These should be included for reproducibility. 5.The proposed architecture integrates multiple specialized modules, which increases model complexity. This may affect robustness, computational cost, and memory usage, especially in real-time clinical settings such as labor wards. 6.How about the runtime performance or parameter efficiency? There is no such clear info to claim the practical deployability and real-time applicability. 7.Although the paper focuses on segmentation, the clinical motivation is AoP measurement and labor outcome assessment. In Table 1, the improvement in AoP (0.02) appears marginal. In Fig. 2, the predicted masks do not show clear improvement over U-KAN. reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers (Meta, R1–R3) for their constructive and insightful feedback. We are encouraged by the reviewers’ recognition of the clinical significance (Meta, R1, R2), novelty (R1, R3), well-motivated methodology (R1, R3), and technical contributions (R1, R2) of our work. Below, we address the main concerns. 1.Novelty and “Meta-Info” Clarification (Meta, R1, R2, R3): Our framework introduces a task-oriented dual-domain collaborative design. The core novelty lies in a progressive dual-domain meta-conditioning paradigm, where complementary structural and frequency priors are hierarchically injected at different optimization stages for intrapartum ultrasound segmentation, rather than relying solely on feature fusion or self-attention. Specifically, “meta-info” in DMCM refers to task-specific prior features extracted from different domains. In the encoder stage, shallow structural features are injected into the decoding process through the first DMCM to improve anatomical consistency. In the decoder stage, FCAM models spatial-frequency interactions to generate frequency-aware priors, which are injected into a second DMCM to refine reconstruction and recover fine-grained boundaries. PSRD further refines amplitude and phase components using enhanced frequency-aware priors, recovering high-frequency details while suppressing low-frequency artifacts. The ablation experiments in Table 2 also demonstrate the performance improvement brought about by the utilization of prior information and module design. We will further clarify the design motivation and distinctions from existing methods. 2.Experimental Details and Reproducibility (Meta, R3): To ensure reproducibility, we will release details such as the source code, training configuration, and hyperparameter settings upon publication. 3.Dataset Description (Meta, R3): The dataset follows the PSFHS Challenge introduced in MICCAI 2023 [4], which consists of the PSFHS and JNU-IFM datasets. The Zenodo page reports statistics only for the PSFHS datasets, whereas our study uses the complete challenge dataset containing 5,100 ultrasound images. 4.AoP Measurement (Meta, R3): Although AoP improvement over U-KAN appears small, AoP is highly sensitive to boundary localization accuracy of both fetal head and pubic symphysis. Even minor segmentation improvements can enhance measurement stability and reduce clinically relevant localization errors. Moreover, our method achieves better DSC, HD, ASD, and Score metrics than U-KAN, indicating more reliable segmentation performance. 5.Computational Efficiency (R1, R3): The proposed model contains 44.405M parameters and requires 95.692 GFLOPs. It achieves real-time performance at 52.78 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU, with an average inference time of 18.946 ms per image. 6.Insufficient Generalization Validation (R1, R2): Our data come from two independent datasets involving multiple hospitals and clinical environments. This introduces variability in imaging quality, patient distribution, and acquisition conditions, providing a certain degree of generalization evaluation. 7.Failure Cases (R1): Failure cases mainly occur when fetal head boundaries are severely blurred or affected by strong acoustic shadowing. These cases highlight the importance of structural and frequency priors for robust ultrasound segmentation. We will present the failed cases in the qualitative results. 8.FCAM Scale Factor (R3): The scale factors balance global context and local detail. Larger downsampling captures global anatomical structure, while smaller scales preserve fine-grained boundary details. 9.Details of \phi_0(I) (R3): The initial block \phi_0(I) uses lightweight convolutional layers to extract low-level structural features from ultrasound images. Such features better preserve anatomical topology and edge information. We will further provide architectural details including kernel sizes and channel dimensions in the revised manuscript.

title: Echo-SCAR: Temporal Feature Learning for Myocardial Scar Detection from Routine Echocardiography
reviewer_1_strengths: Up to my knowledge this is the first demonstration of the ability of machine learning methods applied to echocardiography to reproduce LGE results in a dataset of this size. The methodology is sound and the validation is well performed. The results, showing an advantage of nnuNet embeddings over radiomics, and of both over clinical baselines, are interesting. The paper is well written and clear.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The methods used are well established; the novelty relies on the application. It could be argued that the methods are not optimal for the task either. While the radiomics methodology is appropriate, the nnUNet is not an optimal way to obtain embeddings for capturing image content. Other approaches are standard in the literature and could have been used here. While the paper includes, to some extent, temporal characteristics, these are also included using simple methods (values at ED/ES, root mean square, spectral entropy), which are likely to miss interesting temporal features. There are several methods in the literature to encode spatio-temporal representations that could have been used here. I am unsure of the relevance of reference [12].

reviewer_2_strengths: Clinically, the major contribution is using echocardiographic images to detect myocardial scars. Most work in myocardial scar detection are focused on CMR. The universal availability and lower cost of echocardiography makes it a scalable application.
