Lack of enough details about CMR and echocardiography data acquistion and curation. Technical: Potential data leak: In section 4.1, authors mention 5-fold CV applied to 1921 patients which is the entire dataset. Hyperparameter tuning is to be done on training data (train plus val) only. Test set needs to be separated out before any model training or tuning. This needs to be addressed. Bull’s eye plot in figure 2 shows AUC of 0.86 for apex (segment 17). But the authors mentioned in section 2 that this segment was excluded “because reliable feature extraction from this region is compromised by near-field clutter artifact and apical foreshortening inherent to transthoracic imaging”. This needs to be addressed. The paper, after addressing concerns above, is adequate for a conference presentation.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The major strength of the paper is in its application to a private large dataset, coupled by a clever combination of established ‘state-of-the-art’ tools (temporal encoders, image radiomics). It provides ‘strong’ evidence that echo is a viable imaging modality to ‘more precisely’ refer to LGE CMR. While often the Fusion combination is better, the difference is not significantly better. Why do you think that is? Is there an anatomical or signal acquisition (noise) reason for this? Methods are easy to follow, uncomplicated, rational, and explainable from a clinical / physiological point of view.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Please define LGE earlier. Wording, drop second ‘a dataset’ from ‘Using an in-house dataset at a large medical center…’ (Abstract) Did anything change clinically during that year you gave yourselves for the LGE referral? What do you mean by ‘approximately 412 radiomic’? (just before Section 4) In terms of clinical workflow, are there instances where these echo-informed referrals would provide less value because the MRI referral would happen anyway?
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback and careful reading. We group the major concerns below. 1.Cross-validation is nested, not leaky (R2). We apologize for the abbreviated wording in Sec. 4.1.The procedure is in fact nested patient-stratified CV: an outer 5-fold StratifiedGroupKFold for performance estimation, with an inner 3-fold StratifiedGroupKFold inside GridSearchCV for hyperparameter selection within each outer training fold. Patient grouping by MRN keeps all videos from a patient in the same fold, eliminating train/test leakage. 2.Choice of radiomics and nnU-Net encoder (R1). Thank you. Segment-level scar prediction from echocardiography is, to our knowledge, a novel direction, and the methods were chosen to match the localized nature of the task: scarring is a localized process, radiomics is a localized feature extractor, and segmentation is a localizing task. The reported performance was achieved without scar-specific supervision, which we view as one of the more interesting observations of the study. Alternative encoders (DINOv2/MAE with echo fine-tuning, video transformers) are reasonable next steps and will be flagged. The temporal summaries capture tissue state at key moments of the cardiac cycle (ES and ED at peak-contraction and peak-relaxation) and the temporal dynamics across the full cycle (RMS for signal magnitude, spectral entropy for variation). 3.Echo to CMR timing (R2, R3). Thank you, this is an important point, and we appreciate R2’s example of the post-MI patient whose echo precedes mature scar formation. The pairing in our institution follows the typical clinical sequence: echo as the first-line study, then CMR when findings warrant tissue characterization, with the closest pair per patient selected. We accepted pairs within the window described in Section 2 because scar positives at any specific AHA segment are lower prevalence, and tighter windowing would have left too few positives for stable per-segment estimates. Some positive labels likely correspond to scar that matured between studies, which we will note in the limitations. 4.Segment 17 in bullseye (R2). Correct, and thank you for the catch. Segment 17 is excluded from the per-segment analysis and should not appear colored; the figure will be corrected. 5.CMR label provenance (R2). Labels were derived from clinical CMR-LGE reads at a large academic medical center as part of routine clinical reporting, with hyperenhancement scored per AHA segment on the 0 to 5 ordinal transmural extent scale. For this work we binarized scar-present (≥1) versus absent (0); ordinal transmurality and external validation are part of future work. AHA conventions align between CMR and apical echo views. 6.Minor items (R3). Thank you for the careful reading. LGE will be defined on first mention, the duplicated “a dataset” will be corrected, and “approximately 412 radiomic features per segment” will be clarified as 103 raw PyRadiomics features times 4 temporal summaries. On workflow value: while patients with overt indications are referred regardless, many echocardiograms are performed for non-specific indications (dyspnea, atypical chest pain, screening), where the framework may help surface patients who fall through current pathways. Reference [12] (R1) is ComBat (originally microarray); we will cite an imaging-specific adaptation. 7.Fusion view-dependence (R3). Thank you. Radiomic and encoder features carry partially overlapping and partially complementary information about the same region. Properties of the acquisition view likely contribute to the observed view-dependence, and further investigation remains to disentangle the underlying factors. Extending toward RWMA scores is a natural follow-on we plan to pursue. These edits will be made in the final manuscript. We thank the reviewers for their time and consideration
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The manuscript presents a clinically important and well-executed application study showing that routine echocardiography can predict CMR-defined myocardial scar at segment and view level. The reviewers agree that the dataset size, clinical relevance, clear presentation, and comparison of radiomics with segmentation-derived encoder features make the contribution valuable, despite the use of established methods. The remaining minor concerns are mainly clarifications about the validation protocol, echo–CMR time interval, CMR label generation, and the segment-17 figure inconsistency.

title: Echo4DIR: 4D Implicit Heart Reconstruction from 2D Echocardiography Videos
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is very well written, well motivated and included a comprehensive summary of prior work and challenges. The paper introduced a few methodological innovations into the 4D cardiac anatomy reconstruction problem, including the addition of conditional SDFs regularized by SSM priors, DR to bridge the domain gap, and RSA to ensure temporal smoothness. The paper demonstrated the advantages of each components with convincing metrics and appropriate statistics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The proposed method involves a SDF and test time optimization, both can be computationally expensive. A runtime analysis will be helpful to understand the computational cost of this approach. The results would benefit from a more detailed analysis of regional accuracy, particularly in clinically important areas such as the mitral annulus and the aorta. Those regions are also important the digital twin implementation listed in the future work.
reviewer_1_rating: (6) Strong Accept — must be accepted due to excellence
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The framework demonstrates a significant quantitative leap in performance on the synthetic SSM dataset. Echo4DIR substantially outperforms the latest baselines (such as the mesh-based MIA’25). 2.The experimental design is exceptionally thorough, validating the framework across two distinct domains. The authors utilize a 10k-mesh synthetic dataset to rigorously assess 3D geometric precision against a strict ground truth, while concurrently evaluating a 144-subject real clinical dataset to prove practical clinical utility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The framework’s evaluation on the real-world clinical dataset (the Control Cohort) relies entirely on 2D projection overlap metrics, specifically 2D Dice and IoU. However, 2D projection overlap does not equate to 3D geometric accuracy, particularly in the “blind spots” between the sparse ultrasound probe views. Without evaluating the method against paired 3D clinical ground truth (such as corresponding patient-specific Cardiac CT or MRI scans), it is impossible to definitively prove that the method does not suffer from anatomical hallucinations in unobserved regions. 2.The assumption of a purely rigid, affine transformation to map the 2D image plane to the 3D spatial coordinates ignores non-linear distortions, beam thickness artifacts, and refraction that occur when sound waves pass through varying tissue densities. This simplified probe model may limit the ultimate precision of the spatial mapping in highly complex clinical cases
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a clinically meaningful problem: reconstructing patient-specific 4D cardiac geometry from sparse multi-view 2D echocardiography. This is an existing task. 2.The method is technically coherent, combining SSM priors, conditional SDFs, differentiable rendering, and temporal modeling, with solid quantitative results and ablations.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The real-data validation is still indirect, since the main clinical evaluation is based on 2D projection overlap rather than true 3D/4D ground truth. 2.The paper’s framing is somewhat broader than its actual setting, as the experiments focus on LV reconstruction from segmented masks rather than full-heart reconstruction directly from raw echo videos.

title: EchoFID: A Multi-teacher Distilled Evaluation Network for Cardiac Ultrasound Image Generation
reviewer_1_strengths: The decodability-based formulation is a well-motivated alternative to strict feature matching when distilling from multiple heterogeneous teachers. Requiring that teacher features be recoverable through narrow-bottleneck converters, rather than identical to the student embedding, is a reasonable way to combine supervisory signals with differing inductive biases. The asymmetric gradient routing via stop-gradient is a sensible design for decoupling the forward and reverse flows. The Symmetric Gradient Routing ablation in Table 2 shows this choice has a large measurable effect. The controlled-degradation protocol varies three structurally independent axes (training epochs, data quota, model capacity) and multiple generator families. Triangulating across axes is a reasonable substitute for the absent ground-truth quality ordering in generative-model evaluation. The ablation table isolates the contribution of decodability cleanly.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper provides no statistical reporting. All entries in Tables 1 and 2 are single point estimates, with no bootstrap confidence intervals or seed variation. The central claim that EchoFID is smoother than baselines is not testable without per-cell variance, and the red monotonicity violations in Table 1 have no defined tolerance threshold. Bootstrap CIs over the held-out test set, plus a formal violation definition, would fix this. Reproducibility is insufficient for a paper claiming to define a new metric. Section 4.3 does not specify the converter MLP width, depth, or bottleneck, the value of lambda, which teacher layer h_k is used, the Frechet sample size per computation, the private-dataset size, or whether the Inception-V3 student is ImageNet-initialized or trained from scratch. The last point matters because ImageNet initialization would mean part of the effect is domain-adaptive fine-tuning of Inception-V3 rather than multi-teacher distillation per se. No code release is mentioned. The delta_real construction is under-specified. The partitioning scheme (J), and sample counts per R_j are not stated. The metric also admits negative values when DIS(T,G) is smaller than delta_real. This case is not discussed and a reader using EchoFID operationally will encounter it. The tone of several claims exceeds the evidence. Describing EchoFID as clinically grounded and a principled benchmark is stronger than the experiments support. Scoping to what is actually measured (anchored to echo-specialist models, smoother under three controlled-degradation axes) would not weaken the contribution.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The critique of standard natural image generative metrics is convincing in the echocardiography setting. Anatomy, motion-related morphology, texture, and measurement of relevant cues are heterogeneous, so a single generic encoder is plausibly insufficient. This is a worthwhile evaluation problem. The decodability formulation is more interesting than a simple ensemble or feature concatenation. The asymmetric gradient routing is also a meaningful design choice rather than a cosmetic modification. The manuscript does more than report one off metric values. Authors consider training epochs, data quota, and model capacity to test whether the metrics behave monotonically under controlled degradation. This is kind of a good protocol for evaluation. The ablation study is good and useful. They have used different kinds of model variants such as removing teacher-to-student alignment, using symmetric routing, direct feature matching, naïve averaging, and restricting teachers to one task family all worsen separation. This shows that that the proposed formulation, not just the presence of more teachers, matters.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The experiment scope is too narrow for a manuscript about a general evaluation metric. Manuscripts says “a mixture of private echocardiography studies and the public EchoNet-Dynamic dataset” with only cardiac ultrasound domain. This would be fine for a manuscript but then claim must be narrower. Specially, it is unclear that EchoFID generalizes across views, institutions, ultrasound vendors..etc. Since this is a benchmark like evaluator, broader stress testing would strengthen the contribution. The student is distilled from 15 pretrained expert models (“6 state-of-the-art segmentation networks trained for chamber delineation” and “9 networks for regression models for ejection fraction and structural measurements”). But some of the important details are missing such as “1.Were all teachers trained on exactly the same data distribution? 2.How sensitive is EchoFID to the exact teacher pool? 3.How expensive is teacher preparation in practice?” Table 1 compares against different metrics but the manuscript needs to fully explain some baselines or why each is appropriate in this exact setting. Specially, there is limited analysis of why certain baselines fail. For example, “Why are LPIPS/ASW negative or erratic in some conditions?”, “Are these metrics computed in their standard intended usage?”. Several implementation choices are too vague for full reproducibility. Such as “which intermediate teacher features are used”, “how teacher features are normalized”, “converter bottleneck size”, “λ selection”, “training schedule” and “whether EchoFID inherits all assumptions of Gaussian feature modeling as in FID”. Authors do not share the code for reproducibility. The related works could be sharper. For example, the manuscript cites task-based medical AI evaluation [11] and RadImageNet [16], but does not clearly articulate where EchoFID is complementary versus superior.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper is clearly written and easy to follow in terms of both the problem formulation and the proposed solution. 2.The experiments are diverse and thorough, including analyses across training epochs, architectures, and dataset usage percentages, as well as demonstrating the expected ranking behavior of the proposed metric relative to baselines. 3.The paper includes ablation studies that help clarify the contribution of each component of the proposed method. 4.The problem addressed is interesting from multiple perspectives, and the proposed idea has the potential to be extended to other imaging modalities. 5.Once the student model is trained, the method appears more efficient for metric computation, since it avoids evaluating multiple separate backbones and instead provides an all-in-one model.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Some explanations are missing, which can cause confusion. For example, in Section 3.3, in the first equation, (\tau) and (R_j) are not clearly defined. It seems they may refer to two selected images from the dataset, but this should be stated explicitly. 2.In Figure 1, for instance in the first row, the third image from the left appears to have worse quality than the second image, yet it receives a lower EchoFID score. This is confusing. The paper would benefit from more explanation of how image quality is being judged and why that image is considered better than the previous one. Also, from my perspective, evaluating with a single image is not fully convincing, since FID-based metrics are usually computed over the entire test set rather than at the individual-image level. I understand there may not be enough space to include many examples, but some clarification would be helpful. 3.It is also unclear whether the traditional FID baseline uses a medically pretrained backbone or not. The details of the backbone used for the baseline metrics are missing, and this makes the comparison harder to interpret. 4.Several metrics are not properly cited, and some of them, such as CMMD, RS, and MAID, are not explained in the paper. This leaves the reader uncertain about what exactly these metrics are measuring and how they were implemented. 5.In Table 1, when increasing the model size, some metrics violate the expected monotonic behavior around the 676M model. Could this be due to overfitting on a relatively small dataset? With limited data, increasing model size does not always improve performance and may even reduce it. The paper should explain how this possibility was considered and ruled out, because if overfitting is a factor, then monotonic behavior should not necessarily be expected.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

title: EchoPilot: Training-Free Ultrasound Video Segmentation via Scale-Space Semantic Prompting and Reliability-Gated Memory
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses training-free, sparse-interactive ultrasound video segmentation requiring only a single point click and a category label, which is significantly more practical than prior approaches relying on dense annotations or task-specific fine-tuning. 2.The work clearly identifies two fundamental failure modes initialization ambiguity and temporal drift and proposes targeted solutions for each. 3.The method leverages frozen VLM and VFM priors in a complementary way (semantic grounding + spatial refinement), showcasing a nice way of using pretrained models rather than modifying or retraining them. 4.The generation of auxiliary point prompts from dense foundation features (without additional user input) is an effective way that improves segmentation robustness while maintaining minimal interaction. 5.The proposed Reliability-Gated Memory update is a plug-and-play modification to existing segmentors that avoids error accumulation without additional training or significant computational overhead.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The method relies on multiple pretrained foundation models (VLM, VFM, and a video segmentor), which increases system complexity and may limit practicality in resource-constrained clinical settings where deploying and maintaining multiple large models could be challenging. 2.Although the approach is training-free, it implicitly depends on the quality and domain alignment of pretrained models (e. g. , BioMedCLIP, DINO), and the paper does not thoroughly analyze how performance degrades under domain shifts 3.A component ablation isolating Stage II on all datasets is missing. The paper ablates the reliability-gated memory mainly on Breast Lesion, but a broader analysis across CAMUS and Placenta would better establish that the gain is consistent rather than dataset-specific. 4.A comparison against simpler scale-selection heuristics is missing. Since S. E. E. D. is presented as a key novelty, it would be helpful to compare it against alternatives such as fixed crop size, best semantic score only, random scale, or largest/smallest crop. This would show whether the proposed energy-entropy formulation is truly necessary.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This work addresses an important and clinically relevant use case for ultrasound video segmentation. The sparse-interactive, training-free setting is well motivated, particularly because dense video annotations are expensive to obtain and the common assumption of a full first-frame mask is often unrealistic in practice. A further strength is that the method is organized around two concrete failure modes in this setting: Stage I addresses the ambiguity of determining what and where to segment from sparse initialization, while Stage II targets temporal drift by reducing contamination of the memory bank from unreliable predictions. This high-level decomposition makes the pipeline easy to follow, and Fig. 2 communicates the design particularly clearly. The empirical evaluation is also a strength. Table 1 indicates consistently stronger Dice and ASD performance across CAMUS, Breast Lesion, and Placenta relative to the compared training-free baselines, and the qualitative examples in Fig. 3 are consistent with the claim that the proposed approach reduces drift over time. Finally, the introduction of a dynamic placenta ultrasound VOS dataset adds potential value beyond the method itself and could be useful to the community, provided that sufficient documentation and access details are made available.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty appears somewhat limited, and the key scale-selection criterion remains only partially justified. The overall framework is well designed and practically motivated, but it mainly combines existing frozen priors in a careful way rather than introducing a clearly new segmentation principle. In addition, although the proposed S.E.E.D. criterion is intuitive, the manuscript does not yet fully justify why a more spatially dispersed attribution pattern should reliably indicate a better contextual scale in ultrasound, where such dispersion may also reflect uncertainty. 2.The reliability-gating mechanism seems to rely on a rather restrictive notion of correctness. The write decision is based on the similarity between the current prediction feature and an anchor derived from the first frame. This design is elegant and computationally efficient, but it implicitly assumes that correct predictions should remain close to the initial appearance. In ultrasound videos, however, substantial deformation, probe motion, shadowing, and out-of-plane variation are common, and a semantically correct target may legitimately deviate from its first-frame representation. As a result, the proposed gate currently reads more as a conservative stabilization heuristic than as a general reliability estimator. 3.The experimental design does not fully disentangle the source of the reported gains. The quantitative improvements are encouraging, but the comparison protocol makes it difficult to determine how much of the gain should be attributed to the proposed orchestration itself and how much comes from the richer prompting setup. In the main comparison, EchoPilot is evaluated with both point and text inputs, whereas most SAM2/MedSAM2 baselines are evaluated with point prompts only. This does not invalidate the comparison, since the target setting indeed includes a category name, but it does weaken the causal interpretation of the results. The ablation study is helpful, yet the respective effects of text conditioning, auxiliary prompt refinement, and memory gating remain only partially separated. 4.The practical scope of the method would benefit from clearer discussion. The framework depends strongly on the first frame providing a sufficiently informative anchor, since both prompt refinement and memory gating are tied to initialization. However, the manuscript does not clearly discuss what happens when the target is only partially visible at the beginning, is poorly localized in the annotated frame, disappears temporarily, or reappears later in the sequence. These cases seem important for understanding the realistic operating range of the method in clinical ultrasound videos. 5.There also appears to be a bibliographic inconsistency in the current manuscript. The same MedSAM3 work seems to be listed twice in the reference list under two different reference numbers, while the main text uses those indices as if they referred to different papers. This should be corrected for clarity and accuracy.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The training-free setting with minimal interaction is practical and clinically relevant, especially for ultrasound where annotations are costly and limited. The integration of VLM and VFM for semantic guidance and spatial refinement is well-motivated and effectively leverages pretrained priors. The method is evaluated across multiple datasets and backbones, showing consistent improvements over SAM-based baselines.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The reliability-gated memory relies on a fixed first-frame anchor and a cosine similarity threshold. While the ablation shows overall effectiveness and stability to the threshold, it does not evaluate robustness under significant appearance changes, occlusions, or initialization errors, where this design may still lead to incorrect acceptance or rejection decisions. The comparison with baselines may not be entirely fair, as most baselines rely solely on point prompts, while the proposed method additionally leverages textual input, which introduces additional semantic information. The prompt refinement step selects up to three auxiliary points via cosine similarity and NMS, but the choice of the number of prompts is not well justified. The method relies on a single category name as the text prompt, but it is unclear how sensitive performance is to prompt phrasing or whether richer textual descriptions could improve or destabilize the results.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents EchoPilot, a training-free framework for ultrasound video object segmentation that requires only a single point click and an anatomical category name on the first frame. The method addresses initialization ambiguity and temporal drift via Scale-Space Semantic Prompting (S.E.E.D.) and a Reliability-Gated memory mechanism. Additionally, it introduces a new placenta US video dataset. Reviewers agree that the problem formulation is clinically relevant and that the training-free, low-interaction setting is well motivated. The framework is coherent, well presented and shows consistent improvements over training-free baselines. The raised concerns relate to limited methodological novelty (R#2), justification of design choices (R#2, R#4), and incomplete evaluation (missing ablations) (R#1, R#2, R#4). Overall, considering the practical relevance of the work, the empirical performance and its presentation, I support early acceptance.

title: EchoTracker2: Enhancing Myocardial Point Tracking by Modeling Local Motion
reviewer_1_strengths: *A strength is the domain-motivated design, where the method uses the locally constrained and temporally smooth nature of cardiac motion. While the individual components are not entirely novel, their combination results in consistent performance improvements. *Another strength is the comprehensive experimental evaluation. The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, including a large in-house dataset, an ODD setting, and a public dataset, which provides some evidence of generalization. The comparison includes both domain-specific and general-purpose tracking methods, and improvements are consistently observed across datasets. *The paper demonstrates clinical relevance by evaluating downstream (beyond standard tracking) metrics including agreement with expert measurements and reproducibility.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: *First, the method description lacks clarity and is difficult to follow. Key components of the pipeline are described using heavy notation with limited intuitive explanation. As a result, it is challenging to form a clear understanding of how the method operates in practice. Even though Fig. 2 aims to summarize the approach, it combines multiple stages in a single diagram, which reduces readability. *Second, the central claim that coarse/global motion modeling is unnecessary is not fully supported by the experimental evidence. While Table 3 suggests that removing the initialization stage from prior methods has limited impact, this does not constitute a controlled ablation of the proposed method. Since EchoTracker2 differs from prior work in multiple aspects, it remains unclear to what extent the reported improvements are specifically due to the local-only design, as opposed to other architectural changes. *Third, the ablation studies do not fully isolate the contributions of key components. In Table 2(b), all variants include some form of temporal feature enrichment, and there is no baseline without temporal modeling at the feature level. Similarly, in Table 2(c), all variants incorporate some form of joint reasoning across points, making it difficult to assess the actual contribution of inter-point interactions. *Fourth, the paper somewhat overstates the level of domain-specific modeling. The method is framed as modeling physiologically constrained myocardial motion (e. g. “We design EchoTracker2 to model the locally constrained deformation that characterizes myocardial motion. ”), but in practice this is implemented through architectural design choices such as restricting correspondence to a local spatial neighborhood and removing the coarse stage. While this inductive bias is reasonable, it does not constitute an explicit model, and the framing may therefore be somewhat misleading. *Fifth, the clinical motivation is not clearly articulated. Although the paper mentions downstream applications, it does not clearly explain why accurate myocardial point tracking is critical for clinical decision-making. This makes it harder for readers outside the immediate subfield to appreciate the importance of the problem. *Finally, while the evaluation includes a public dataset (CAMUS), the generalization claims are somewhat limited, as this dataset relies on automatically generated trajectories rather than real-world ground truth. Additional evaluation on more diverse real-world data (e. g. , from different vendors or acquisition settings) would strengthen the conclusions.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a tracking approach focused only on local motion, which is well suited to the characteristics of echocardiography, and achieves SoTA tracking performance. 2.The paper includes strong comparisons with existing SoTA methods, and the evaluation is well designed for the medical domain, including GLS agreement, test–retest reproducibility, and OOD evaluation. 3.It is particularly interesting that the paper directly shows, through experimental results on existing studies, that the initialization stage provides little performance gain in this domain.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Major 1.The ground-truth generation process is not described in enough detail. The paper does not specify which semi-supervised tracking algorithm was used, nor how many clinical experts were involved in the manual verification process. 2.The methodological novelty is somewhat limited, since most of the main components are adapted from existing methods. 3.In Table 3, the AIT for LocoTrack without initialization is reported as N/A, but no explanation is provided. Minor 1.More details on ethical approval, such as the IRB number or institution, would improve transparency, although I understand that these details may have been omitted at this stage for anonymization purposes.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper challenges the assumption that coarse initialization is needed in most motion tracking problems by identifying the unique latent constraints in myocardial motion, and subsequently explicitly showed that coarse initialization is indeed not necessary. Methods are generally well-defined and explained The result section included multiple proprietary and public datasets and mutliple similar motion tracking models, and demonstrated that the proposed model generally performed the best across almost all datasets. This makes a strong argument in favor of the proposed approach. The inclusion of both in-distribution and out-of-distribution results showed good generalizability
reviewer_3_weaknesses: This is a rather minor point but I wish the authors could have published an anonymized link to their source code. A github link that’s partially masked is present and I believe that the authors have made the attempt to open source it. It might be good to offer more explanation on how exactly are the ground truth landmarks placed, as it seems that the landmark points are spatially very dense given the relatively low resolution of ultrasound images in general. For example, are they interpolated between a few anatomically important landmarks (such as the apex of the left ventricle, the mitral valve root etc).
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their time and feedback. We have carefully addressed the major weaknesses as noted below. Reviewer#1 R1.1 We aim to improve the clarity of the method description and Figure 2 in the camera-ready version. R1.2 By explicitly removing the global initialization stage from SOTA methods and observing minimal performance impact, we believe our results provide sufficient support that global motion modeling has limited benefit in echocardiography. R1.3 For Table 2(b), the benefit of temporal features is well-established, so we focus on comparing different enrichment strategies. For Table 2(c), the advantage of joint reasoning over none is demonstrated in the main results; Table 2(c) specifically compares forms of joint reasoning, showing KNP-Joint is most effective for anatomical deformation. R1.4 We respectfully note that incorporating domain knowledge through architectural design is well-established in deep learning. Our design choices exploit the local constraints of myocardial motion, though not through explicit cardiac motion priors. R1.5 We agree that the clinical motivation can be better emphasised and will strengthen this in the camera-ready version. R1.6 To our knowledge, no public dataset with real-world ground-truth myocardial tracking annotations exists. Our private dataset represents real-world clinical scenarios with high-quality annotations, and we believe our evaluation across both datasets provides sufficient validation within the scope of a MICCAI paper. Reviewer#2 R2.1 The tracking algorithm is a proprietary GE HealthCare speckle tracking system, so specific details are unavailable. Several cardiologists — including co-authors with many years of experience — were involved in manual verification. We will clarify this in the camera-ready version. R2.2 While components are adapted from existing methods, our contribution lies in their principled selection and problem-specific modification — a process involving extensive experimentation whose effectiveness is reflected in the results. R2.3 Although we deactivated the global stage of LocoTrack, the associated computation still ran internally, making it impossible to report a meaningful AIT. A clarifying note will be added in the camera-ready version. Regardless, removing the global stage is expected to reduce computation time. R2.4 We thank the reviewer for suggesting EchoNet-LVH. While landmark annotations are sparse, they could potentially be adapted to our setting — we will keep this in mind for future work. Reviewer#4 R4.1 We will ensure a proper public code release is included in the camera-ready version and will keep the anonymized link suggestion in mind for future submissions. R4.2 As described in the dataset section, ground-truth trajectories are obtained by tracking sparse points along the left and right ventricular walls using a semi-automatic proprietary method, verified by clinical experts. We will ensure this is clearly presented in the camera-ready version. We thank all reviewers once more for their time and constructive engagement. We are confident the camera-ready version will address the raised concerns and further strengthen the paper.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): The paper’s core value lies in its domain-inspired simplification of an established paradigm, which is effectively supported by its insightful ablation and comprehensive evaluation. While the method’s description and component-level novelty could be improved, the strength of the central idea and the robustness of the validation are sufficient.

title: Expert-like Bone Ultrasound Segmentation through Expert-in-the-loop Mask-conditioned Progressive Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a real clinical bottleneck, namely the time-consuming manual annotation of bone surfaces in ultrasound, rather than being framed mainly as a benchmark-driven segmentation study. 2.It proposes a reasonable simulation strategy to turn the practical expert workflow into a learnable training setup, which is an important step in connecting the clinical use case to the model design. 3.The method is evaluated from a clinically relevant application perspective, and the results support its practical effectiveness.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty is limited, as the framework is built on a simple U-Net and mainly focuses on adapting the workflow to the application. 2.The training setup relies heavily on synthetic brush-based annotation simulation, and it is unclear how well these intermediate states reflect real expert behavior. 3.Although the study focuses on assisting manual annotation, the efficiency evaluation is based on only a single expert annotator. 4.The paper lacks comparison with other strong methods for interactive annotation.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Problem formulation:- Strong problem formulation, well aligned with the practical annotation workflows and addresses a real clinical need of efficient annotation tools. 2.Hence, the core novelty is the workflow modeling: brush-like mask trajectory simulation + expert-approved online updates, applied to US bone segmentation and measured via time-to-acceptance. 3.Improvement of 66.7% in the annotation time.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The validation is a bit ambiguous. The abstracts and discussion sections state that the evaluation is performed on data sets of three cadavers, but the validation section states that the data is for three real patients creating uncertainty about the test data set composition. 2.The fact that the validation was performed using a single expert annotator may limit the generalization of the claims about annotation robustness and efficiency across users. 3.It is not clear how realistic the simulator is when compared to real expert behavior. 4.The novelty claims should be tightened. While there is novelty in exploring the brush-based annotation workflow, a progress aware adaptive refinement network for boundary completion and iterative improvement is not entirely novel. This novelty claim would be stronger with clearer positioning relative to prior ultrasound interactive editing work such as Shahin et al. (MICCAI’23, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11041 ) which already formulates sequential user edits and explicitly optimizes for incorporating edits locally while preserving the segmentation away from the interaction (via an editing-specific loss/metric). 5.Online learning details insufficient for reproducibility The “expert mode” update is conceptually described, but specifics parameters: update frequency, number of gradient steps, learning rate during adaptation, regularization to avoid forgetting, and safeguards against drift are not disclosed.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The idea of introducing an expert-in-the-loop framework with progressive learning for bone surface annotation in B-mode ultrasound is novel. The method is well motivated by the characteristics of real annotation workflows, particularly the brush-like behavior commonly used by experts. 2.The expert-imitating annotation synthesis is well designed. By simulating annotations at different coverage levels, the mask-conditioned network is able to progressively learn how to generate high-quality bone labels. 3.Expert-in-the-loop deployment. The network is trained on synthetic annotation data. To close the gap between synthetic data and real data, the authors update and refine the model’s performance with expert knowledge. 4.Well designed experiments and ablation studies. I look forward to seeing the generalizability of the method to new anatomies in future work.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Overall, I have a positive view of this work. My main concern is reproducibility. I understand that MICCAI imposes a strict page limit and that the authors have chosen to focus on the most important aspects. However, based on the current manuscript, it remains challenging to reproduce the proposed method. Although expert knowledge is incorporated during deployment for further refinement, the quality of the synthetic data remains highly important. More realistic simulated annotations could improve the network’s initial performance before expert involvement and thereby reduce the number of refinement iterations required. At present, the description of the synthetic data generation process is not detailed enough to fully reproduce the results. For example, statements such as “Brush-like masks are produced with stochastic stroke trajectories, where starting points are sampled inside the mask and paths evolve through temporally smoothed random motion” remain too vague for reproducibility. I would suggest releasing the code with sample data.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the Meta-Reviewer (MR) and reviewers for their constructive comments. MR, R1–3: Implementation details: We agree the paper under-specifies the expert-mode update procedure and brush simulator, and provide the full details below, all to be incorporated in the final version. For expert-mode details: The encoder is frozen in deployment, preserving the generalizable features learnt during pretraining. Decoder weights are updated online, which bounds the adaptation and serves as the primary mechanism against representation drift. The model is updated immediately after each expert-approved mask, with 5 gradient steps at a learning rate of 1e-4 consistent with pretraining. Fig 5b in the paper confirms that this scheme produces monotonic Dice improvement across sequential frames with no observed degradation, supporting the stability of the chosen configuration. For brush simulator: The simulator generates synthetic brush masks from ground-truth annotations using the following fixed configuration. A spatial bias field is produced by applying Gaussian smoothing with 5 px to random noise, creating uneven inward painting patterns. Stroke trajectories evolve through temporally smoothed random motion with a direction momentum of 0.2, a step size of 2 px, and a randomized thickness sampled uniformly from 3–5 px per stroke. Coverage ratios are drawn from three predefined ranges 10–30%, 40–60%, and 70–90%. Starting points are sampled uniformly inside the ground-truth mask. MR, R2: Relevance to Shahin et al While our work and Shahin et al’s explore sequential interactive refinement, they differ in objective and interaction modality. That work focused on locally refining model-generated masks via geometric point prompts. In contrast, ExiL learns from user inputs iteratively to improve the model’s context awareness over time in clinical practice. Additionally, our MSK application targets thin structures where patch-based prompts are unsuitable and may cause Dice drift as SAM-style models propagate them away from expert-prompted keyframes. Finally, ExiL is designed to complete missing anatomical structure from partial expert intent, a fundamentally different task from mask correction. MR, R1, R2: Reliance on single annotator results We acknowledge this as a limitation of this proof-of-concept study. The readers shall interpret our reported 66.7% time-to-completion reduction as a controlled within-annotator feasibility result rather than a universal estimate across users. Our objective was to evaluate if ExiL can reduce repetitive manual interaction during bone segmentation of US via adapting to sparse re-annotations. MR, R2: Ambiguity between patient vs cadaver datasets We apologize for the confusion. Two separate datasets were used for the two evaluation objectives: Quantitative segmentation metrics (Dice, boundary error) were evaluated on the publicly available UltraBones100k (“cadaver dataset”), which provides expert ground-truth but contains no annotation timing. Annotation time (Table 2) was measured on a prospective dataset of three volunteer patients, 6 US sequences per patient × 20 frames per sequence = 360 annotated frames in total (“patient dataset”). This study was conducted under IRB approval (number withheld for double-blind) and demographic details will be disclosed in the final manuscript. R1.4 Table 1 already includes a SAM-style interactive baseline evaluated under the same limited-data setting. R1.2 and R2.3 While perfect simulator fidelity is unattainable, we believed progressive Dice improvement observed in expert-mode (Fig. 5b) confirms that synthetic pretraining provides a strong initialization that real expert corrections can efficiently refine, “empirically” validating the simulation’s practical utility. R2.4: We will revise the novelty claims in the final manuscript brush-based interaction modeling, progress-aware trajectory learning, and online expert adaptation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The reviewers are positive overall about the practical contribution: a brush-based annotation pipeline aligned with real expert workflows for bone-surface labeling in ultrasound, an SDF-driven brush simulator with coverage-stratified synthetic states, and a substantial −66.7% annotation-time reduction on cadaver sequences. Nevertheless, three substantive concerns raised by the negative reviewer warrant a rebuttal phase: the trajectory-aware framing needs explicit differentiation from Shahin et al. (MICCAI 2023); the efficiency study is limited to a single annotator; and key implementation details are insufficiently specified for reproduction. For the rebuttal, the most pressing items are the disclosure of implementation details — the online expert-mode update mechanics and the simulator specification — to enable reproduction, and the differentiation from Shahin et al. (MICCAI 2023) on iterative editing. Further items that would strengthen the response include reconciling the “three cadaver datasets” vs “three real patients” inconsistency, and either supplying a small multi-annotator efficiency check or explicitly scoping the time-saving claim to a single-expert feasibility study. | The paper contributes a brush-based annotation pipeline aligned with real expert workflows for bone-surface labeling in ultrasound, supported by an SDF-driven brush simulator with coverage-stratified synthetic states and a substantial −66.7% reduction in annotation time demonstrated in a feasibility study with a real expert. The authors’ rebuttal satisfactorily addressed concerns regarding the presentation of methodological details, comparison with prior work, and evaluation scope. The reviewers subsequently reached consensus to accept, and I concur with this recommendation. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After rebuttal, all reviewers are in favor of acceptance, and I do not see a reason to disagree with them. In particular, I believe that the two main concerns highlighted by the meta reviewer have been adequately answered in the rebuttal. I do want to echo the reviewers’ statement that making the implementation open source would be appreciated. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers have now agreed on acceptance of the paper.

title: Exploring Efficient Weakly Supervised Ultrasound Video Object Segmentation with VLM-Guided Structure Advantage Learning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The proposed VLM-driven weak supervision framework substantially alleviates the labor-intensive burden of manual labeling in medical video segmentation. By leveraging frozen VLMs (Qwen3-VL-8B) to generate coarse bounding boxes with confidence scores, the method reduces manual annotation workload by approximately 60% compared to conventional box-supervised approaches. 2.The paper introduces an innovative combination of the GCDS and Structure Advantage Learning, which effectively addresses boundary ambiguity in weakly supervised settings. The Dirichlet-based adaptive weighting mechanism and RL-inspired relative quality quantification enable autonomous exploration of optimal lesion structures without requiring complex reinforcement learning pipelines.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The method section is difficult to follow, with insufficient intuitive explanations of key components like GCDS and Structure Advantage Learning. Figure 1 is cluttered with excessive information and lacks clear visual hierarchy, making it challenging to understand the workflow and interactions between modules. 2.The approach heavily depends on Qwen3-VL-8B’s zero-shot capability for pseudo-box generation; however, this model is primarily trained on natural datasets, raising concerns about its reliability in ultrasound-specific scenarios with blurred boundaries and artifacts. Furthermore, the VLM operates frame-independently without explicit temporal modeling. Incorporating video-aware trackers like SAM 2 [1] could significantly enhance spatiotemporal consistency of pseudo-labels across frames, which is critical for video segmentation yet completely overlooked. [1] Sam 2: Segment anything in images and videos, 2024.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.New dataset. A 433-video breast lesion ultrasound dataset is a meaningful contribution. Ultrasound video segmentation datasets are scarce, and this fills a real gap. The promise to release the dataset and code adds value. 2.Evaluation is solid. Three datasets (ULBV400+, ERUS-10K, DPSTT), all with standard deviations reported. This is a good statistical practice to prove it’s not a chance. Consistent improvements across all three datasets strengthen the claims. 3.Practical annotation reduction. Table 5 shows the method saves ~60–70% of manual annotation effort compared to existing methods that require 100% manual bounding boxes. This is a concrete, measurable practical benefit. 4.Interesting core idea. Using a VLM as both an annotation generator and a quality evaluator for candidate predictions is a creative approach. The idea of sampling multiple candidate strategies and letting the VLM rank them to guide learning is genuinely different from standard pseudo-label or consistency-based methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The RL framing is misleading. The paper repeatedly draws connections to reinforcement learning, but what’s actually happening is just score normalization of quality scores across candidate predictions (Eq. 9). There’s no policy, no environment, no reward signal in the RL sense. The advantage weight A^n is a static score normalization, not a learned advantage function. Calling this “Structure Advantage Learning” and framing it as RL-inspired overstates what the method actually does. The contribution is still valid, it’s just candidate ranking with VLM feedback, but the framing should be more honest. 2.Computational cost of VLM-in-the-loop training is not addressed. The temporal semantic score (Eq. 8) requires prompting Qwen3-VL-8B to compare N candidate predictions per frame, across T frames, during training. This is only a training-time cost; inference doesn’t need the VLM; but it still seems expensive and no training time or cost comparison with baselines is reported. For a paper that emphasizes “efficiency” in its title, this should be quantified. 3.The method is very complex with many moving parts. Diffusion backbone + wavelet features + BioMedCLIP embeddings + Dirichlet distribution sampling + spatial quality scoring + VLM temporal semantic scoring + advantage-weighted loss. It’s hard to tell what’s actually necessary. The ablation (Table 4) adds components progressively (M1→M2→M3→M4→Ours) which is helpful, but doesn’t test whether simpler alternatives to individual components (e.g., learned attention instead of GCDS) could achieve comparable results. A simpler method might get most of the gains. 4.No comparison with fully supervised methods. The paper only compares against other weakly supervised methods. A fully supervised upper bound using the same backbone and full pixel-level annotations would help contextualize how much performance is being left on the table. Without this, it’s hard to judge whether the remaining gap justifies the complexity of the approach. Minor Weaknesses 5.The paper claims compatibility with “different diffusion models and vision language models” (Section 3.1, italicized in the paper) but only tests one of each. This claim is unsupported without experiments. 6.Dataset details (ethical review, hospital information) are deferred to after review. While understandable for anonymity, this makes it harder to assess data quality, patient diversity, and annotation protocol. Clarity and Presentation The paper is reasonably well-written but the method section is dense. Figure 1 tries to show the entire pipeline in one diagram and ends up being hard to parse, the text in the figure is too small to read at print resolution. The math is mostly clear, though the notation gets heavy with the Dirichlet formulation. The RL terminology adds confusion rather than clarity, as discussed in 1.The experimental section is clean and the tables are easy to read.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Adapting the concept of relative advantage comparison (conceptually from RL/GRPO) into a weakly supervised segmentation pipeline is a innovative strategy. 2.The application of the Mixed Dirichlet distribution aligns well with the adaptive fusion of combinatorial guidance cues. 3.The framework achieves a substantial and practically valuable reduction in the manual annotation burden for ultrasound video segmentation. Experimental validation is extensive across multiple diverse datasets.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Figure 1 is overly dense and hard to map to formulas. Several variables are undefined or inconsistent (e.g., $n$ in Eq. 2, $\epsilon$ in Eq. 9). The extraction process for the three Guidance Cues ($F, F^W, F^{VLM}$) lacks technical detail. 2.Table 5 raises concerns regarding its practical significance. To my knowledge, methods like BBTP, FSRM, and MonoBox are purely weakly supervised segmentation algorithms. I would be much more interested to see how these baseline models perform when fed the exact same annotations generated by VLM (partially manual refined). Additionally, the authors may consider exploring how performance fluctuates as the volume of manual annotation (dictated by the required annotation threshold) varies. 3.Were the weakly supervised baseline methods trained using the original ground-truth annotations provided by the dataset or the coarse annotations generated by the VLM? If the former, does the proposed ULBV400+ dataset also contain 100% dense manual annotations to support this? This may need be confirmed.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal

meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received mixed review scores of weak reject and weak accept. The major strengths summarized by reviewers include the dataset contribution, the annotation cost reduction by using frozen VLMs, two module designs based on RL and mixed Dirichlet distribution. The critical concerns raised by reviewers include unclear method description, the over-reliance and sensitivity on VLM, complex method without full justification for each module, incomplete validation and comparisons, along with other comments detailed in individual reviews. | After the rebuttal, three reviewers gave the acceptance decision. The AC concurs with this recommendation and the final submission should be revised based on the reviews and rebuttal accordingly. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): I recommend rejection. The main weakness is that the paper does not convincingly justify why a language or vision-language model is necessary for this problem. The proposed VLM is mainly used to generate bounding boxes/confidence scores and to rank candidate masks, but these are essentially visual localization and mask-quality estimation tasks. The paper does not establish that language reasoning provides a principled advantage over simpler vision-only alternatives, such as a detector/segmenter teacher, SAM/MedSAM-style promptable model, temporal tracking, visual foundation features, or conventional boundary/temporal consistency scores. The experimental evidence also does not isolate the contribution of language. The ablation only shows incremental gains from adding VLM-related features and the proposed loss, but lacks key controls: an image-only foundation encoder, a non-language pseudo-box generator, a learned visual quality scorer, prompt-free VLM features, different prompts/models, or expert-validated mask ranking. Therefore, the reported improvement may come from using a strong black-box pseudo-labeler rather than from any necessary language-based reasoning. The VLM-based temporal semantic score is particularly under-validated. The paper asks the VLM to compare candidate masks and provide scores/reasoning, but does not show that these scores are calibrated, reproducible, robust to prompt variation, or consistently correlated with expert mask quality. In a medical segmentation setting, using such unverified language-generated scores as training supervision is not sufficiently reliable. Overall, while the dataset and empirical results are potentially useful, the core methodological claim is not adequately supported. A stronger paper would need to clearly demonstrate why language/VLM supervision is needed for ultrasound video segmentation and provide rigorous comparisons against simpler visual or geometric supervision mechanisms. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I have read the manuscript, review comments, rebuttal letter. All three reviewers recommend acceptance (after rebuttal). The responses addressed the concerns about method description.

title: FARSIGHT: A Dynamic Multi Modal Medical Image Analysis Framework Powered by a Prior Knowledge Guided Vision Language Model
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Clinically Motivated Problem with Broad Relevance The paper targets universal bottlenecks in real-world retrospective archives — “lack of fine-grained annotations, unreliable metadata” and studies with “variable image counts, redundant or noisy frames, and missing modalities” — a challenge highly representative of large-scale clinical practice. 2.Magos: Zero Fine-Tuning Curation with Auditable, Privacy-Preserving Design Magos achieves “privacy-preserving on-prem deployment” without any annotated training samples by decoupling VLM perception from deterministic rule mapping and enforcing “JSON-Schema-constrained decoding” for structured, verifiable outputs. This design is both practically innovative and deployable under strict institutional constraints. 3.Convincing Large-Scale Empirical Validation Deployed on 40,000+ uncurated images, Magos achieves “99.98% routing accuracy” with “complete parsing success rate without a single pipeline crash,” substantially outperforming a supervised ResNet18 baseline (66.7% on Power Doppler) in a zero-shot setting. 4.HMMIL Design Aligns with Clinical Acquisition Logic The two-level hierarchy — intra-modality attention followed by inter-modality Transformer fusion — explicitly mirrors clinical workflows where “instances are first filtered within modality before any cross-modality interaction,” yielding robustness under variable-length and incomplete studies, with each component validated through ablation. 5.Top-K Hard Negative Loss Addresses a Known MIL Weakness Standard MIL tends to “assign high attention to non-diagnostic frames, especially in negative patients. “ The proposed auxiliary loss directly targets this failure mode and is shown to improve both prediction performance and instance-level saliency reliability. 6.Strong Clinical Translation Potential The system “requires no changes to physician workflows” and is compatible with existing PACS infrastructure, offering a practical path to automating retrospective cohort construction at scale.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The framework is validated exclusively on one private hospital dataset for CAI assessment, with no external multi-center validation or public benchmark testing. The generalizability of Magos’s spatially tuned heuristic rules to different device manufacturers or acquisition protocols remains unconfirmed. 2.The reported B-mode mIoU of 62% falls well below the paper’s self-defined acceptance criterion of 0.80, yet this is rationalized as “sufficient for patient-level prediction tasks” without rigorous ablation evidence. Given that B-mode is identified as “the most informative single modality,” the downstream impact of this coarse extraction warrants more careful quantitative analysis. 3.Table 2 does not clearly specify whether modality ablation and module ablation share a consistent baseline configuration, creating ambiguity in the conclusions. Notably, B+C+S (Test AUC 0.808) outperforms other modality combinations in the modality ablation, yet the final HMMIL model uses only B+C and reports AUC 0.816.This improvement likely reflects the contribution of the full module configuration rather than the modality choice itself. Critically, the paper never reports B+C+S with full modules, making the final modality selection decision experimentally unjustified. 4.All baselines in Table 1 are single-modality, general-purpose MIL methods. No multimodal MIL or multimodal fusion baselines are included, making it difficult to determine whether HMMIL’s gains stem from the hierarchical design or simply from incorporating multiple modalities. A more comprehensive comparison with relevant prior multimodal MIL works would be needed to substantiate the claimed contributions. 5.All performance metrics are reported as point estimates without confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Given the modest absolute improvements (e. g. , AUC 0.777 → 0.816), it remains unclear whether the differences are statistically significant, which does not meet the MICCAI reviewer guideline requirement for “performance measures reported with measures of uncertainty or confidence. “ 6.Hard negative mining in MIL is not new — MHIM-MIL (Tang et al. , ICCV 2023, ref. 11) already proposes masked hard instance mining for WSI classification. The paper should more clearly articulate how its asymmetric treatment of positive and negative bags differs from existing approaches to substantiate its novelty claim.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper integrates clinical archive data governance with patient-level prediction, effectively addressing key challenges in retrospective clinical archives, including missing fine-grained annotations, irregular numbers of images per patient, noisy frames, and missing or misaligned modalities. 2.Magos combines VLM perception with prior-knowledge rules, JSON-schema-constrained decoding, a fallback parser, and deterministic ROI extraction. The strategy makes the pipeline more auditable, privacy-compatible, and robust. 3.The proposed HMMIL is well aligned with the characteristics of archival multimodal data, effectively addressing the challenges of variable-length studies and missing modalities.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The description of MAGOS in the Method section is not sufficiently clear. For example, the definition of the clinical prior knowledge and the specific procedure used to obtain modality labels are not described in enough detail, and these implementation steps are not clearly illustrated in Fig. 1.The presentation could be strengthened by adding a more explicit formulation, for example with a few representative equations. 2.The evidence for clinical generalization is limited, all predictive results come from a single retrospective cohort from one hospital. In addition, the manuscript does not specify whether the dataset is public or private. If it is a public dataset, the source should be clearly stated. If it is a private dataset, the data collection process should be described in detail. 3.The authors describe the dataset only in Section 2.1, but the final classification task remains insufficiently clear. For example, it is not explicitly stated whether the goal is to distinguish patients with chronic allograft injury from normal controls. The manuscript should provide a clearer definition of the final prediction task and report performance metrics for each class. 4.Fig. 1 is too small and lacks sufficient clarity. 5.The best results in the table should be highlighted, and the table should be formatted to avoid spanning multiple pages.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Handling of real-world-data: The proposed framework, applied here to ultrasound data, handles classic real work noisy data, namely missing modalities and varying number of frames. The authors also mentioned that it has been designed to be compatible with PACS workflows. While only evaluated on data collected from one hospital, the authors outline this limitation and discuss their intention to extend to multiple centers and open source data in the future. 2.Archive-to-prediction: Though “archive” here can be slightly misleading, this paper handles an end-to-end workflow, including data curation to prepare the data for model as well as model prediction, which can save significant time in clinical workflows. Moreover, the data-curation part is designed without requiring any model training so could be applied to other cases.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Clarity: The evaluation of the individual parts of the framework and the ways in which the data is split for evaluating these is rather confusing, e.g. authors state 686 samples in test set (section 2.1) for evaluating model, 200 images, Independent test set A, randomly sampled for modality routing and region extraction (section 3.2), 400 images, internal development set A for rule refinement and pipeline verification (section 2.2). Generalizability: Though this work is presented as a general framework it is only applied to the task of renal transplant. It would have been nice to see it’s applicability to other tasks and modalities.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair and Reviewers #1–#3 for their evaluation and comments. We appreciate their recognition of the novelty of our framework and its close alignment with real-world clinical practice, including archive-to-prediction workflow, handling of variable frame counts/missing modalities. Generalization/data validation. Although single-center, our cohort spans 2008–2025 and includes 4,576 patients/41,203 images from varied US devices and heterogeneous UIs. Meanwhile, external cohorts are being collected, and FARSIGHT is also used in echocardiography/breast imaging. Per MICCAI rules, we do not report these studies, but will conduct external validation and broader evaluation in future journal work. Task, dataset, and splits. We clarify that the private cohort consists of post-transplant US exams from Hospital A, with CAI status from clinical records. The task is patient-level classification of CAI vs. non-CAI patients; the latter were termed “normal controls” in Sec. 2.1.The 3,204/686/686 split is the main patient-level train/val/test split for HMMIL, with no patient overlap. Independent Sets A/B were only for MAGOS validation: A (400 images) for routing and B (200 images) for ROI extraction. They were not used to optimize MAGOS or train/test HMMIL. MAGOS/Fig.1.Fig.1 was compressed to retain content, reducing readability. Four modalities were found during data cleaning via VLM-assisted inspection of distinct US patterns; Sec. 2.1 gives counts. “Clinical prior knowledge” in Sec. 2.2 refers to radiologists’ visual knowledge for modality recognition, e.g., waveform panels (S), grayscale fields (B), red/blue overlays (C), and power-flow overlays (P), encoded as visual states/rules.
