title: From Point Estimates to Distributions: GMM Pooling for MIL in Preterm Birth Prediction
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed pooling mechanism is well motivated and addresses an important theoretical limitation of other pooling methods. Min/mean/max pooling reduce instances to a single point estimate, which lacks expressiveness. Other attempts at representing a distribution over instances usually consider only marginals for each feature dimension. To my knowledge, this is the first attempt to explicitly formulate a trainable neural network architecture that captures a multidimensional distribution over instances. It seems reasonable to suppose that this would be important in solving certain types of pooling tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Despite its potential theoretical advantages, the results are not especially compelling. On the preterm birth task, the task used to motivate the paper, the GMM pooling performs worse than much simpler baselines (max pooling, attention pooling), depending on the metric. Slight improvements are seen on the lymph node dataset classification task (but not the more challenging regression task), though this dataset is treated like an afterthought in the paper. Though I appreciate the general technical motivation for more advanced pooling mechanisms, it is not really clear to me why this is important in the PTB application. My understanding is that in clinical practice, cervical measurements are taken and this is used to predict the risk of pre-term birth. The authors do not adequately justify why automating the cervical measurement process would be insufficient and a more sophisticated (but less interpretable) classifier is necessary, and the vital comparison to using cervical measurements to predict risk (current practice) is not evaluated experimentally. The paper is also muddied by the inclusion of the segmentation part of the model, which is quite tangential to the main methodological contribution. The use of the features from the center of a UNet is rather unconventional, and is not the natural choice for evaluating the pooling methodology. I don’t understand why the choice of pooling mechanism for the intermediate features would have any effect on the segmentation branch, so it’s not clear to me what I can draw from the “Segmentation Dice” column of Table 1.Generally, the segmentation part of the paper is discussed little and does not add much to the paper.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: This paper formulates PTB as a MIL problem, which better conforms to clinical practice and has strong clinical utility. The study is conducted on a cohort of clinically defined high-risk pregnant women, making the task more challenging and better reflecting the potential value of the model in real clinical settings. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the generality and robustness of the proposed distribution-based pooling strategy.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1) This paper clarifies that density-based pooling does not explicitly model cross-dimensional dependencies in the feature space. Given that the authors propose GMM pooling to address this issue, how exactly does GMM pooling explicitly capture such dependencies? (2) The study uses a small PTB dataset and therefore applies 5-fold cross-validation. However, it is unclear whether the data splitting was performed randomly and whether an independent test set was used. (3) The differences in PR-AUC between GMM pooling, max pooling, and attention pooling are very small (below 0.01). Although the authors claim that GMM pooling is more stable, the paired t-test yields a p-value of 0.873, indicating no statistically significant difference. Thus, the observed lower standard deviation might merely reflect random fluctuation. Furthermore, GMM pooling involves two sets of attention weights: instance importance weights and soft instance-to-component responsibilities. Without clear performance gains, is attention pooling not simpler to implement and more suitable for real-world deployment? (4) This paper lacks comprehensive ablation studies to verify the contribution of key components, such as the instance importance weights, soft instance-to-component responsibilities, and learnable probes. (5) This study employs U-Net to segmentation, but what is the role of segmentation in the PTB task?
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposal of aggregating MIL features with GMM pooling is interesting. Conventional approaches aggregate feature of the instances in a bag into a single point. According to the author, this “create an information bottleneck by collapsing within-bag variability that may be informative for bag-level prediction”, to which I agree. Distribution-based MIL pooling aims at resolving this issue, but doesn’t capture inter-feature dependencies, which is addressed by the author in this work.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: the author noted that “all patients were prospectively classified as high-risk for PTB by the treating clinicians”, even though only 44 out of the 182 cases were eventually PTB. It would be nice to evaluate the method also on the low-risk cases, and I am concerned about whether there’s a sample selection bias here. the author noted that “the comparison between GMM and max pooling showed no significant difference” on the preterm birth dataset, and did not report similar comparison on the lymph node dataset. i am curious about the advantage of using GMM pooling over the simpler methods.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank reviewers for their comments and suggestions. We appreciate that R1 highlighted the novelty and strong theoretical motivation of GMM pooling, particularly its ability to capture feature distributions and inter-feature relationships compared with standard pooling approaches. We also appreciate that R2 noted the methodological contribution and clinical relevance, highlighting that the formulation aligns with practice and shows consistent behavior across datasets. We also note that R4 found the approach interesting and valuable, especially for mitigating information loss in conventional MIL pooling and its potential applicability to broader problems. Lack of performance advantage R1,R2,R4: We agree that GMM’s performance gains are marginal. However, GMM pooling addresses a representation limitation rather than optimizing only for predictive performance. Standard pooling collapses a bag to a single point, discarding intra-bag heterogeneity, while GMM models the instance distribution via multiple components. This is important in medical imaging, where variability is intrinsic. We observe consistently lower variance across runs, which may indicate improved robustness despite similar average performance. Weak clinical motivation R1: Yes, cervical length is a standard metric in clinical practice, but it is a rudimentary, subjective, and has limited predictive power [AJOG 2015, PMCID: PMC4675685]. Our goal is to assess whether full-image information can improve risk prediction by capturing clinically relevant imaging patterns beyond a single measure (e.g., cervical funneling and shape variations). Our model implicitly learns cervix characteristics through segmentation, resulting in a more comprehensive and consistent PTB risk assessment. Segmentation motivation unclear R1,R2: The segmentation branch is not a primary contribution; rather, it serves as an auxiliary task that encourages the model to learn anatomically meaningful features. This acts as an inductive bias, guiding the feature representation used for pooling and classification. The reported Dice scores are included for completeness, but the paper’s main focus is the pooling mechanism. We will revise the manuscript to better clarify the role of the segmentation branch as an auxiliary inductive bias. Dataset & evaluation R2,R4: The dataset size is limited, but the fetal application is unique. To ensure a rigorous evaluation, we perform 5-fold cross-validation with patient-level splits to prevent data leakage, repeated across 3 random seeds (15 runs), and report aggregated results. Given the cohort size, an independent held-out test set is not available, and cross-validation is standard practice in this setting. Regarding cohort composition, all patients were prospectively identified as high risk, reflecting the real-world clinical use of transvaginal ultrasound, where screening is not performed in the general population. This also makes the prediction task more challenging due to reduced class separability. We agree that evaluating on a broader population, including low-risk cases, would be valuable, and consider this an important direction for future work. We will clarify patient-level splitting in the revision. How GMM captures feature dependencies R2: GMM pooling represents a bag as a mixture of Gaussian components, where each component models feature relationships through its covariance structure. This allows dependencies between features to be captured. In contrast, density-based pooling treats each feature dimension independently, ignoring such relationships. Ablation analysis R2: While additional ablations could add detail, we emphasize that the paper already includes the most critical analyses (e.g., temperature and probes), which capture the core behavior of the method. Further ablations will be included in future work. Typo R1: Fig3: “K” → “P” thanks. We will revise the manuscript to clarify these points and incorporate the suggested improvements.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper received mixed reviews, including two weak accepts and one weak reject. The authors are invited to submit a rebuttal. The paper proposes a GMM-based pooling strategy for MIL, which reviewers considered an interesting attempt to address a limitation of conventional pooling methods: collapsing instance embeddings into a single point estimate. By modeling the distribution of instance embeddings, the method has potential value for capturing richer within-bag information. However, the reviewers raised several important concerns, including the lack of clear improvement over simpler baselines, insufficient clinical motivation for the preterm birth application, small dataset size, missing ablation studies, unclear role of the segmentation branch, and limited evidence of statistical significance. Overall, the method is potentially useful, but its practical advantage and empirical support require further clarification; therefore, the authors are invited to submit a rebuttal before a final decision is made. | After rebuttal, this paper receives three accept recommendations and one rejection. The AC acknowledges that the proposed GMM pooling strategy addresses an important limitation of conventional MIL pooling by modeling within-bag instance distributions rather than collapsing them into a single point estimate. Although the empirical gains on the preterm birth task are modest and the segmentation branch remains somewhat tangential, the rebuttal reasonably clarifies the methodological motivation, the role of segmentation as an auxiliary inductive bias, the patient-level cross-validation protocol, and how GMM pooling captures feature dependencies through mixture covariance. The majority of reviewers view the approach as technically interesting, generally well motivated, and potentially applicable beyond the presented tasks. Therefore, despite remaining concerns about limited clinical comparison, small dataset size, and marginal performance improvement over simpler baselines, the AC believes that the paper makes a useful methodological contribution to MIL and recommends acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This paper received two accept and one reject after rebuttal. I recommend rejection of this paper. The main reason is that this paper formulate a MIL problem, without comparing to sota instance aggretators in the MIL field. The MIL techniques, especially the instance feature aggregators, have developed very fast in recent years. These techniques are mostly used for pathology image analysis, which is also a task used for evaluation in this paper. There are too many aggregators that are more powerful than the simple baselines used in this paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): GMM Pooling sounds technically interesting regardless of its limitations.

title: From Scanning Guidelines to Action: A Robotic Ultrasound Agent with LLM-Based Reasoning
reviewer_1_strengths: Novel and Compelling Framework: The idea of translating scanning guidelines into dynamic tool use via an LLM-based agent is highly compelling and timely. Unified System: The framework successfully integrates reasoning, planning, perception, and robot execution within a single agentic pipeline. Generalizability: The contribution is highly meaningful because it does not rely on heavily hand-crafted, task-specific pipelines, which is an important step toward more general robotic ultrasound systems. Clinical Feasibility: The real-world demonstrations on multiple anatomical targets (gallbladder, spine, and kidney) significantly strengthen the practical value and clinical relevance of the work.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Guideline Construction & Retrieval: It would be helpful to clarify how the scanning guidelines are constructed, formatted, and retrieved in practice. Since the guideline database is an important part of the framework, more detail on how these instructions are written and organized would improve reproducibility. RL Fine-tuning Details: The RL fine-tuning component is interesting, but the design choices in the reward function could be discussed in more depth. For example, what motivated the specific weighting terms in Eq. 1–4, and how sensitive is the final performance to these choices? Experimental Setup Clarity: For the verbal interaction experiments, it may be useful to further explain how the 20 guidelines were designed, how diverse they are, and to what extent the held-out guidelines differ from the training ones. Failure Mode Analysis: A brief discussion of failure modes—especially for the gallbladder case mentioned in the real-world experiments—would make the paper even stronger.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The introduction effectively contextualizes the problem, making the paper’s objectives and intended contributions easy to follow. The figures are well-designed, presenting the framework and pipeline clearly. The methodology pragmatically leverages existing software tools, suggesting a framework that could be highly effective in practice. The bridge between high-level LLM reasoning and low-level robotic control for specialized medical tasks like US scanning is highly relevant.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The authors claim “reasoning capability over state and observations” as a core contribution, yet the core method is unclear: (1) There is no formal definition of what constitutes a “state” or an “observation” within this framework. (2) It is unclear how raw sensory data and US images are converted into text-based tokens or descriptors that an LLM can process. Without this detail, the “reasoning” remains a “black box.” 2.The workflow for path generation and refinement lacks sufficient detail: (1) Localization of organs: While skeletal atlas registration is mentioned, the paper does not explain how soft-tissue organs (e.g., kidneys) are localized relative to the skeletal landmarks. (2) Path Definition: It is unclear if the scanning path is a simple linear interpolation between landmarks or another form that more sufficiently covers the anatomy. (3) Refinement & Segmentation: The trajectory refinement section lacks citations and technical specifics. Crucially, the authors do not specify which algorithm or model is utilized for the 3D US segmentation. 3.Experimental Validation: (1) While gallbladder scans include visual evidence, the results for spinal and kidney scans are presented only as text. Additional visual proof (e.g., reconstructed volumes or overlayed trajectories) or numerical results (e.g., success rates/reconstruction accuracy) will convince the reader better. (2) The paper does not report results from repeated trials. Without metrics on success rates or variance of trajectories across multiple runs, it is hard to assess the system’s robustness or statistical significance.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: I appreciate the direction of this research, despite its imperfections. Utilizing an agentic approach for general-purpose reasoning to guide robotic motion offers a compelling solution for several scenarios. It effectively unleashes the reasoning potential of LLMs and provides a distinct advantage over other autonomous control schemes , even though its drawbacks are also clearly evident.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The reward function design for RL fine-tuning is overly focused on syntactic correctness, specifically tool naming and JSON schema matching, rather than clinical optimality. While this approach ensures the agent produces well-formatted and executable commands, it fails to bridge the gap between logical correctness and actual medical efficacy. Consequently, the model is incentivized to mimic reference traces rather than optimize for the best possible clinical outcome in a real-world setting. The architecture reduces complex, high-stakes medical maneuvers into a simplified sequence of textual reasoning and discrete tool calls. This paradigm may work for rigid, standardized protocols, but it lacks the high-frequency haptic feedback and sub-millisecond responsiveness required for safe physical interaction, making its true clinical utility in doubt. 3.Could the authors provide the average and peak latency for a single reasoning step (from observation input to tool call generation) on the hardware used? 4.How does the system handle instances where the patient’s breathing cycle is faster than the LLM’s reasoning frequency?
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the timeliness and relevance of our work, with R1 describing the idea of translating scanning guidelines into adaptive robotic scanning decisions via an LLM-based agent as “highly compelling and timely,” and R3 noting that the agentic approach offers a “compelling solution” with a “distinct advantage over other autonomous control schemes.” We also appreciate that R1 acknowledged the unified integration of reasoning, planning, perception, and robot execution, while R2 positively highlighted the clear problem contextualization, well-designed figures, and practical use of existing software tools. Importantly, R1 recognized the generalizability of our framework beyond hand-crafted, task-specific pipelines, and both R1 and R2 emphasized the relevance of bridging high-level LLM reasoning with low-level robotic control for robotic ultrasound. Finally, we thank R1 for recognizing that our real-world demonstrations on multiple anatomical targets strengthen the practical and clinical value of the work. Our work proposes a guideline-driven agentic framework for autonomous robotic ultrasound, where the LLM serves as the high-level “brain” that retrieves scanning steps, reasons over the current state, and selects appropriate perception, planning, patient-guidance, and robot-execution tools. In contrast, the tools and low-level robot controllers act as the execution and reflex layers, handling real-time contact, force regulation, and robot motion. Therefore, the key contribution of this work is a unified hierarchical system that enables non-linear, decision-dependent scanning workflows beyond fixed rule-based pipelines, supported by RL fine-tuning and validated on held-out guidelines as well as real-world gallbladder, spine, and kidney scans In this context, we would like to clarify the role of the LLM in our system (R3Q2 and R3Q4). The LLM is not intended for high-frequency physical control; instead, similar to human motor control, it performs high-level reasoning while dedicated low-level modules handle real-time contact, force regulation, and safety-critical interaction. Similarly, our RL fine-tuning is not designed to learn an unconstrained clinically optimal policy (R3Q1), but to make the LLM a reliable guideline-grounded planner. Given the dependence of robotic ultrasound on scanning guidelines and the risk of LLM hallucination, we intentionally prioritize faithful guideline following, correct tool selection, and valid parameterization, while recognizing patient-specific clinical optimization as an important future direction. We also want to further clarify some minor implementation details regarding state representation (R2Q1) and path generation/refinement (R2Q2). Raw ultrasound and camera inputs are processed by the corresponding perception tools, whose outputs are returned to the LLM as structured text for high-level reasoning and tool selection. The current path generation is implemented as a simple trajectory connecting anatomical feature points. While more advanced path planning could be incorporated, this is not the main focus of the paper, and we will clarify this in the revision. To further improve clarity and reproducibility, we will make several minor revisions following the reviewers’ suggestions. Specifically, we will briefly clarify guideline construction and the design of training/held-out guidelines, with code and guideline examples released for further details (R1Q1, R1Q3). We will also clarify the RL reward design (R1Q2), add a short failure-mode discussion for the gallbladder case (R1Q4), and strengthen experimental validation by adding repeated-trial numerical results and releasing an online video with additional visual evidence (R2Q3).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All the reviewers recognize the proposed LLM-based agentic framework as both novel and timely, specifically the unified pipeline and the clinical feasibility demonstrated through real-world anatomical scans, including the gallbladder, spine, and kidney. In summary, the proposed work presents a significant and meaningful step in medical ultrasound robotics, and I lean towards early acceptance, However, authors should address the limitations raised by the reviewers, e.g. clarity of state/observation definition and sensor data to text conversion. More details are needed on guideline construction, segmentation algorithms and RL reward function, and consider including metrics such as success rates and latency.

title: GCM-Net: Anatomy-Aware Gaussian-Contrastive Multi-layer Fusion Network for Abdominal Ultrasound Standard Plane Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper proposes an adaptive anisotropic Gaussian refinement (AAGR) module that combines differentiable anatomical centroid regression with anisotropic Gaussian attention, which is novel for standard plane classification. Unlike generic attention, this module explicitly models anatomical geometry and conforms to the ultrasound scanning sector, effectively suppressing speckle noise and irrelevant background while focusing on diagnostically critical regions. This clinically inspired design improves both accuracy and interpretability. 2.The learnable multi-layer feature fusion (LMFF) module dynamically weights and aggregates hierarchical features from a pre-trained medical foundation model. Rather than simple concatenation or summation, it learns task-adaptive weights to combine fine-grained details and high-level semantics, which is well-suited to capturing subtle anatomical differences between similar standard planes in ultrasound. 3.The dual-head classification architecture with a memory-bank-augmented supervised contrastive loss addresses key challenges in ultrasound standard plane recognition. By using historical embeddings to enlarge negative sample diversity, it significantly improves feature compactness and separability, especially for low-quality, low-contrast, and highly similar classes. The ablation study confirms this is the most impactful component. 4.The method is validated on two distinct datasets (public fetal ultrasound FPUS23 and private abdominal AbdoSP‑9 with 9 classes) and compared against multiple strong baselines including recent foundation models. Beyond static image classification, the paper further evaluates real-time causal video inference with temporal confidence refinement (TCR) and conducts an expert clinical validation, demonstrating practical utility for autonomous robotic ultrasound and clinical workflow assistance. 5.The paper provides detailed implementation settings, complete ablation results, and an anonymous public code repository, supporting transparent reproduction. The writing is well-organized, with clear motivation, methodological details, and clinical context, making the work accessible to both technical and clinical researchers.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The overall framework combines medical foundation model fine-tuning, dynamic multi-scale feature fusion, anatomical attention, and supervised contrastive learning with memory bank. While the integration is effective, the individual components and overall pipeline lack groundbreaking methodological innovation. 2.The private AbdoSP-9 dataset is collected from a single center, with no validation on multi-center, multi-device, or pathological cases. Real abdominal ultrasound involves diseases, artifacts, and patient variations that are not represented in healthy volunteers, which weakens the evidence for real-world clinical translatio 3.The ablation only validates the presence/absence of LMFF, AAGR, and SupCon, but does not analyze critical hyperparameters (e. g. , temperature τ in contrastive loss, weight λ, memory bank size, Gaussian kernel shape). The contribution of the MED-SA adapter backbone versus other pre-trained models is also not ablated, leaving unclear whether gains come from the backbone or the proposed modules. 4.Although the AAGR module is claimed to be anatomy-aware and interpretable, the paper provides no visualizations of the Gaussian attention maps, anatomical centroids, or feature distributions to support this claim. Interpretability is asserted but not demonstrated.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.From a real clinical perspective, focusing on ultrasound standard plane classification is timely. 2.GCM-Net achieves both high accuracy and meets the real-time requirements of ultrasound scanning. 3.The authors provide a realistic scenario simulation test, which strengthens the paper.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Although the authors focus on the recognition of ultrasound standard planes, the task is narrowly formulated as a classification problem, which limits the practical applicability of the method in real clinical settings. 2.Table 1 introduces the private dataset AbdoSP-9.I note that the authors define 9 categories; however, to my knowledge, this categorization does not follow a complete clinical standard [1], and no corresponding medical justification is provided for this design. According to prior work [1], the liver alone includes 13 standard planes, suggesting that the proposed AbdoSP-9 has limited coverage. This significantly undermines the credibility of the problem setting. In addition, treating N-SP as an independent category introduces a very broad semantic space, and the manuscript does not clarify how these negative samples are constructed. These issues indicate substantial dataset-related limitations, raising concerns about the reliability of the reported metrics and their potential clinical applicability. 3.Although Table 2 reports performance on FPU23, the improvement in accuracy is marginal, and an accuracy of 99.53% may indicate severe overfitting. 4.The evaluation in Section 3.4 appears superficial. The authors should provide a more detailed description of the implementation process corresponding to Figure 2.5.The comparative analysis is insufficient. While foundation models may offer advantages during training, the authors should also report the performance of conventional frame-by-frame models on the proposed dataset to justify the necessity of GCM-Net. Furthermore, although Section 3.4 claims that GCM-Net achieves good real-time performance, quantitative metrics such as FPS are not provided for precise comparison. [1] Zhang, J., Chen, Y., Zeng, P., Liu, Y., Diao, Y., & Liu, P. (2023). Ultra-attention: automatic recognition of liver ultrasound standard sections based on visual attention perception structures. Ultrasound in Medicine & Biology, 49(4), 1007–1017.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The authors proposed a system which can adapt its focus to irregular or elongated organ shapes, which is much more flexible and allows the model to be easily adapted to different types of ultrasound scans. The proposed LMFF module that uses adjustable scalar weights to adaptively balance fine-grained spatial details with high level semantic information. Along with physical geometric constraints, such as a trapezoidal probe mask, which is effective way to filter out background noise and speckle artifacts. The use of memory-bank-based supervised contrastive learning strategy (though not new but) allows the model to better distinguish between morphologically similar anatomical planes. The system was validated using real-time clinical video streams and a readers study was also done to validate the key frames selected by the model which makes the claims of paper solid and clinically grounded.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The model lacks manual ground truth for the anatomical centroids (c_x, c_y); instead, it relies on implicit supervision from the classification task, which means the attention center is optimized for prediction accuracy rather than being strictly validated against anatomical landmarks. The size of memory bank M for contrastive loss is not provided. TCR is credited with achieving the expert-validated clinical accuracy of 81.25%, but the authors do not provide a dedicated mathematical breakdown or a TCR subsection in the Methodology section. Authors mention that the AbdoSP-9 dataset was curated by “chief physicians” , but the paper does not specify if multiple experts cross-verified the labels or provide a Kappa coefficient to measure agreement. The model is described as capable of real-time processing (~15fps), yet the paper never specifies the actual processing speed (latency) of the entire pipeline on the NVIDIA RTX 4080 hardware. For the dynamic scanning evaluation, the success rate is reported as 70.83% , but the paper does not explicitly define the mathematical threshold (e.g., a specific confidence score or time window) used to categorize a detection as a “success” vs a “failure”. Minor: There is no mention of the number of training epochs or total iterations. The authors also didn’t mention how many trainable parameter did their trainable (peft) adapters added on top of frozen encoder. The figure 1(b) should have separate boxes/outlines separating LMFF and AARG modules.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for recognizing our method’s novelty, clinical relevance and realistic applicability. Below, we address the key concerns. 1.Dataset Validity(@R1,R2,R3)： Generalization(R1): GCM-Net demonstrates generalizability across two dimensions: (1) multi-domain applicability, evidenced by 99.53% accuracy on the public fetal dataset FPUS23, in addition to the AbdoSP-9 dataset (2) temporal robustness, confirmed by video testing (Sec 3.4) on unseen clinical ultrasound scan with real-world patient motion. Clinical protocol(R2): AbdoSP-9 aims to provide fine-grained subxiphoid screening of multiple organs (liver, gallbladder, pancreas), including essential pancreatic planes (PB, PT) often omitted in single-organ studies, rather than expanding coverage through intercostal views as in [1]. Our 8 SPs were curated by chief physicians based on established clinical standards [2] to balance diagnostic depth with robotic navigation utility. For comparison, contemporary work like Cai et al. [3] utilizes only 6 SPs. The N-SP category includes transitional/blurred frames, specifically designed to enhance deployment robustness. Annotation verification(R3): A subset (30 subjects) was cross-verified by one chief physician and two physicians, yielding a Fleiss’ Kappa of 0.7114.Discrepancies were resolved via consensus. We will add these details to Sec 3.1.[1] Zhang J, et al. (2023). Ultra-attention: recognition of liver ultrasound standard sections. Ultrasound Med Biol, 49(4), 1007-17.[2] Zhang M (Ed). (2018). Atlas of Humman Body Ultrasound Scanning (Rev. ed.). Science Press. [3] Cai Q, et al. SEMC: Structure-Enhanced MoE Contrastive Learning. Proc. AAAI, 2026.2.TCR & Real-time Processing(@R2, R3): We will add the complete TCR formulation to the revision. The TCR applies a 30-frame moving average for temporal smoothing. Following a 3.0-second warmup, exceeding a validation-derived threshold triggers peak-tracking. To mitigate transient noise, the task locks if no new maximum is reached within a 60-frame (2.0 seconds) patience window. End-to-end latency is 65.25 ms/frame on an RTX 4080 (FP16/TF32), including pre-processing (1024x1024 resizing, normalization), inference, and post-processing, making it fully suitable for real-time clinical use. 3.AAGR & Visualizations (@R3, R1)： The anatomical centroid supervision does not rely on manual annotation. Nevertheless, the regressed coordinates consistently converge to meaningful anatomical structures during optimization, demonstrating that the model can reliably localize relevant landmarks without explicit ground truth. To further support the claimed anatomy awareness, we will add qualitative visualizations in the revised appendix, including Gaussian attention heatmaps overlaid on ultrasound frames, which show that the AAGR module consistently focuses on the relevant anatomical regions. 4.Implementation Details & Ablations (@R1, R3): We will add the following implementation details in the revised manuscript. Specifically, the SAM ViT encoder is frozen. The bottleneck adapters add ~7.10M trainable parameters to the backbone. Total trainable parameters (adapters, neck, classification head) are ~9.72M. We evaluate τ and λ on AbdoSP-9.Optimal performance (81.37%) occurs at τ=0.1, where low temperature facilitates hard negative mining to distinguish subtle anatomical variances. Higher τ (e.g., 76.03% at 0.5) over-smoothes the distribution. λ=0.6 yields the peak accuracy (81.37%), balancing contrastive regularization with classification (76.49% at 0.2; 78.47% at 1.0). Notably, AAGR σ_w, σ_h is adaptively predicted, not fixed. The memory bank size M is set to 512, trained for 10000 iterations. We will expand the implementation details accordingly. The bare MED-SA backbone (72.37%) underperforms MedViTv2 (73.44%), while our GCM-Net achieves 81.37% (+9%), proving the proposed LMFF, AAGR, and SupCon drive the improvement rather than the backbone. We hope these address your concerns.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Some reviewers show the interesting of this work. However, there are some concerns shown by the reviewers, including but not limited to: 1.Limited methodological novelty 2.Insufficient justification of task setting of classification and the private dataset. 3.The ablation study is incomplete。 4.Details are missing (e.g., TCR module, training details) | While concerns regarding methodological novelty remain and the contribution is best characterized as an incremental system-level innovation rather than a fundamentally new method, the reviewers generally agreed on the clinical importance of the problem, the soundness of the technical approach, and the value of the experimental validation. The work demonstrates clear practical relevance and consistent performance gains on a clinically meaningful task. Taking into account both the methodological contribution and the clinical/application impact, the paper provides sufficient merit for acceptance in my view. I therefore support acceptance. In the camera-ready version, the authors should incorporate the key clarifications from the rebuttal. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The clinical definition and coverage of the private AbdoSP-9 protocol lack rigorous justification; combining multiple distinct organ systems (liver, gallbladder, pancreas) into a arbitrary 9-class paradigm without following accepted radiological standards compromises its utility as a reliable clinical benchmark. Methodologically, the network represents an incremental assembly of established components (medical foundation model adaptation, basic scalar multi-layer feature fusion, and memory-bank supervised contrastive learning) rather than a novel paradigm. Furthermore, the validation is entirely constrained to a single-center private dataset without multi-center, multi-device, or pathological variability testing, which fails to support the claims of real-world clinical translatability or robustness against genuine patient anomalies. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper is interesting, proposing a strong method to solve an important task. The rebuttal addressed the major reviewer concerns.

title: GeoCAN: Nonlinear Causal-Geometric Learning for Echocardiography Quality Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The overall design of the CGL and NRA modules is novel, and the authors have demonstrated that the discriminability enhancement of CGL by integrating latent hyperbolic learning into causal modeling to deconfound quality factors from visual degradations, and the quality representation under complex degradation conditions improving by NRA 2.The Experiment section is solidified and the evaluation has broad coverage. Three datasets constitute a relatively comprehensive multi-distribution test. The combination of multi-granularity metrics such as KRCC, SRCC, and PLCC is also more persuasive than a single metric.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Cij, as defined in Eq. (1), is merely a conditional ratio obtained by element-wise multiplication of feature maps followed by GLM normalization; it is not equivalent to the causal effect as defined in the Pearl framework or structural causal models (SCM). It’s fundamentally an attention reweighting mechanism. Without the constraint of an external explicit causal graph, the model may learn an “asymmetric matrix that minimizes the classification loss” rather than the true causal direction. 2.No ablation on hyperbolic space: If the author believes that hyperbolic space is the core mechanism that significantly outperforms traditional Eulerian embedding in deconfound quality factors from visual degradations, they should have designed an ablation study on hyperbolic space to validate its contribution.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper identifies two specific and well-motivated pain points in EQA — spurious correlations and feature entanglement — and designs CGL and NRA respectively to address them. The logical chain from problem to solution is coherent and easy to follow. 2.The attention visualizations in Fig. 3 show the model focusing on anatomically meaningful structures such as chamber boundaries and myocardial regions rather than artifacts, consistent with the paper’s claims about causally grounded representations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper repeatedly claims that CGL achieves “causal deconfounding,” but the quantity Cij=P(F(i)∣F(j))C_{ij} = P(F^{(i)} | F^{(j)})Cij​=P(F(i)∣F(j)) in Eq. (1) is fundamentally a conditional dependency estimate, not an interventional causal effect under Pearl’s do-calculus framework. There is a conceptual gap between conditional probability and causal effect. The paper provides no interventional experiments, counterfactual analyses, or do-calculus-based justification to support genuine causal claims. This constitutes an overclaim. 2.Necessity of hyperbolic embedding not sufficiently validated. The paper embeds factor nodes into hyperbolic space and claims this preserves hierarchical causal topology, but 1) No ablation comparing hyperbolic vs. Euclidean embedding is provided; 2) No sensitivity analysis of the curvature parameter cc c is reported. 3.Eq. (2) introduces the GLM as a nonlinear aggregation operator, but no explanation is given for why GLM is preferable to standard softmax attention or other aggregation mechanisms. No ablation comparing GLM to alternatives is provided, and the learning stability of parameters α and β is not discussed. 4.The dimension-wise functional decomposition in Eq. (6) using learnable piecewise spline basis functions is formally very similar to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN) [12]. While [12] is cited, the paper does not clarify whether NRA is an instantiation of KAN, nor does it articulate the specific improvements over directly applying KAN. This leaves the contribution boundary unclear. 5.The private dataset Echo-Q lacks description of annotation protocol, acquisition equipment, and institutional source, making it impossible to assess its representativeness. 6.The retraining of baselines does not describe hyperparameter search strategies, leaving open the risk of unfair tuning. 7.Several baseline entries in the result tables are missing (“-“) without explanation — it is unclear whether the method does not support that task or simply failed to converge. 8.A “[?]” placeholder reference appears on page 1, indicating an incomplete citation at submission time. 9.Several sentences contain redundant phrasing (e.g., “To sum up the above limitations” appears more than once).

reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Bad representation: i) Reference 18 is same as Reference 19.ii) On the first page, Introduction section, line 10, there is a reference error “[10,?]”. Please check the paper carefully to avoid these problems. 2.The paper claims the nonlinear relational aggregation mechanism can explicitly disentangles relational structures from quality representations, while the final performance of the model is still black box, without any demonstration of the effectiveness of decoupling in the middle layer.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Thanks to the reviewers for your valuable comments on our work. Especially, thanks to R1 and R3 for accepting the paper directly. We appreciate your recognition of: 1.Novelty (R1: “Novel model design”; R2: “an interesting framework”; R3: “an interesting attempt”) 2.Good theoretical support (R2: “specific and well-motivated pain points”; R3: “good theoretical foundation”) 3.Experimental effectiveness (R1: “detailed experimental setup” “the experiment section is solidified” “the evaluation has broad coverage”; R2: “consistently outperform baselines” R3: “demonstrated the effectiveness of the method and supported motivation”) We will release the code, datasets, implementation details, and experimental details for reproducibility, while correcting typos/presentation issues to address all constructive comments (R1, R2, R3). Q1: Novelty of CGL (R1/R2). CGL is a novel advance in causal-disposition modeling for EQA. Inspired by multiple studies without explicit causal graphs, e.g., [1,13, DOI: 10.52202/068431-2776], it infers causal tendencies between quality factors and visual degradations from directional conditional support under limited causal supervision. CGL infers causal direction from Cij/Cji asymmetric disposition built on directed conditional dependencies and organizes it into latent hyperbolic causal topology for causal-disposition-guided deconfounding, rather than learning a free classification-driven matrix. Q2: Hyperbolic-embedding ablations (R1/R2). Hyperbolic-embedding ablations were left out due to space limitations. Euclidean replacement weakens quality-order consistency, while hyperbolic geometry yields average QA/KRCC gains of 3.94 percentage points/0.0801, supporting hierarchical asymmetric causal topology. Curvature analysis had indicated c=1.0 as a balanced hyperbolic scale for Lgeo: small c approaches Euclidean geometry, while overly large c may over-compress embeddings, causing an average 11.56% KRCC drop. Tables 3/4 further support CGL’s hyperbolic topology modeling. Removing CGL drops ranking-correlation metrics, showing its necessity for stable causal-geometric representations. Q3: Novelty of GLM (R2). GLM has two advantages over softmax attention and other aggregation mechanisms: adaptive distribution sensitivity and stable order-aware pooling. Learnable α/β shift it from min- to mean- to max-like behavior, capturing weak-to-dominant activations for conditional-dependency estimation. The learning stability of α/β is theoretically supported by [14]. GLM is bounded within the input range, reduces to arithmetic mean when α→1, and is differentiable w.r.t. α/β. Q4: Relation between NRA and KAN (R2). NRA advances KAN-style spline decomposition from generic nonlinear mapping to relation-aware aggregation, addressing feature entanglement by explicitly separating relational structures from quality representations. Q5: Clarification about “-” entries, Echo-Q, and baseline retraining (R2). “-” denotes unsupported task/output settings rather than convergence failure. Specifically, single-task IQA baselines and w/o MTL variants lack the CA output head. Echo-Q was collected from routine echocardiography using Philips systems. Three expert sonographers annotated de-identified images under rigorous quality control. Baselines followed GeoCAN’s experimental protocol, with hyperparameters selected only on the validation set to avoid unfair tuning. Q6: Clarification about disentanglement of NRA (R3). Tab. 3/4 support the disentanglement effect of NRA in stabilizing quality representations. Its removal causes drops in correlation metrics (PLCC/SRCC/KRCC), indicating weakened consistency between predicted and ground-truth quality scores. Fig. 3 supports the disentanglement effect by visualizing GeoCAN, which focuses on structured anatomical relations rather than isolated local activations or superficial degradations, consistent with key anatomical structures and quality-determining factors.

Overall, the proposed framework is innovative with decent theoretical backing but bears multiple unresolved flaws. Therefore, the recommendation is Invite for rebuttal. | After the rebuttal, two reviewers choose Accept and one reviewer vote for Reject. The pros include good novelty and the authors plan to open-source codes. The cons include core methodological issues unaddressed, bold causal claims and the lack of adequate ablation tests and comparisons etc. Considering the pros and cons, I slightly incline to Accept. Well most of them have been explained in the author’s response, an important concern raised by R2 is the overstated causal contribution. This should be tuned down to avoid misunderstanding .
