The core issues remain unresolved: the strong causal claims lack interventional or counterfactual support, key components are not sufficiently validated, and dataset transparency concerns persist.

title: HAR-MoE: Hierarchical Affinity-aware Routing Mixture-of-Experts for Unified Multi-Organ Ultrasound Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.A main strength is that the method disentangles the analysis into two aspects, task and organ, and performs routing respectively. This is novel or different from existing MoE routing mechanisms. 2.Another strength is that the paper demonstrates the technical feasibility of performing unified analysis for ultrasound images, spanning across multiple organs. The proposed method achieves promising performance for segmentation and classification for various types of ultrasound images.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The loss term L_{aux} in Eq. (7) is not clearly explained. What is this MoE load-balancing regularization term please? 2.It is worth elaborating how the baseline segmentation models are trained. For example, in Table 3, are the single-task segmentation models trained for just one organ and evaluated on one organ, or trained using images from all organs? Sometimes, with good augmentation, a simple U-net or nnU-net may perform quite well for a single organ. It would be worthwhile explaining why the proposed method HAR-MoE improves the segmentation Dice metric by 5% or more, compared to the single-task segmentation models.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The authors have some solid observations: the failure of unified MoE models is not simply due to insufficient capacity, but due to a structural misalignment, task identity and organ identity serve orthogonal inductive roles that should not be conflated in a single routing space. 2.The affinity priors are not just heuristic additions. Instead, they are derived from a factorized posterior. 3.Comprehensive and extensive experiments along with nice ablation analysis.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Image-level routing is not always optimal. The authors never highlight these limitations over token-level routing and discuss their decision. 2.Stronger statistical analysis (confidence intervals, cross-validation, or significance tests) is required to support the main claim of 16% F1 increase. 3.The temperature hyperparameter (in Eq 5) is not reported. No sensitivity analysis is also provided for it.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Methodological Improvement is significant as Hierarchical Routing incorporating both task and organ conditions to extract relevant experts to improve segmentation and classification performance which make final results more promising. It makes it more novel and robust along different organs by making approach which ensured that fine-grained diagnostic tasks are not overwhelmed by dominant segmentation gradients.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Hard Top-K routing creates discrete switches between experts, so small changes in inputs or logits can abruptly change which experts are chosen, making gradients less stable and harder to optimize. 2.As only a subset of experts receive gradients at each step, some experts may dominate (collapse) while others receive little to no training signal, leading to underutilization, training instability. 3.Sensitivity to hyperparameters such as K1,K2,τ: The number of selected experts and the Softmax temperature strongly affect routing behavior, too few experts limits capacity, too many reduces specialization, and improper temperature can make routing either too sharp or too uniform. 4.Even with load-balancing loss, certain experts may be consistently favored due to early training dynamics or affinity biases, resulting in uneven workload distribution and reduced overall efficiency.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive and encouraging comments. We address their concerns point by point below. 1.Load Balancing and Expert Use (R1, R3) For R1, we clarify that L_aux is the standard MoE load-balancing loss (Ref. [24]): L_aux = N·Σ_i f_i·p_i, where f_i is the fraction of routing assignments to expert i and p_i is its mean routing probability. Minimizing this term discourages routing collapse and promotes balanced expert use. For R3, HAR-MoE mitigates expert underuse through two complementary designs. (i) L_aux explicitly penalizes imbalanced routing, with λ=0.01 giving the best overall trade-off in Table 5.(ii) The learnable task and organ affinity priors, A^T and A^O, provide stable structured biases, so routing is not determined solely by noisy instance-level logits during early training. Fig. 3 further shows that segmentation and classification activate largely different expert subsets, while different organs exhibit distinct activation patterns, suggesting no obvious single-expert collapse. 2.Hyperparameter Sensitivity (R2, R3) For R3, Table 5 systematically ablates K1, K2, and λ. M=16 with (K1=8, K2=4) gives the best performance-efficiency trade-off, and λ=0.01 achieves the best overall results. Increasing capacity to M=64 lowers breast subtype F1, supporting our observation that simply adding experts may aggravate expert dilution under heterogeneous supervision. For R2/R3, τ was fixed to 1.0 in both routing stages, which we will add to Table 2.We use τ=1.0 as the unscaled softmax baseline to avoid overly sharp or overly uniform routing while preserving specialization. A compact τ sensitivity analysis will be added in the revision. 3.Baselines and Reliability of Gains (R1, R2) For R1, single-task baselines are trained and evaluated independently per dataset, while all multi-task methods, including HAR-MoE, are jointly trained across all datasets and evaluated per dataset. HAR-MoE benefits from shared ultrasound representations while its hierarchical routing preserves organ-specialized capacity and reduces negative transfer. For R2, we will report mean±std over multiple seeds and paired significance tests in revision. The main gain is supported by both baseline comparisons and ablations. In Table 3, HAR-MoE reaches 58.12% subtype F1, improving over the strongest competing multi-task baseline, MTANet, by 16.46 points. Table 4 further shows progressive gains from Flat Routing 19.05% to Hierarchical 35.95%, +Task Affinity 49.37%, +Organ Affinity 51.73%, and Full 58.12%, supporting the contribution of the proposed design. 4.Image-level Routing (R2) Image-level routing is a deliberate choice because both task identity and organ semantics are image-level conditions in our setting. Sharing expert selection across tokens therefore gives more semantically consistent and interpretable routing. In contrast, token-level routing may offer finer local specialization, especially for heterogeneous lesions, but it may also assign visually similar ultrasound patches from the same organ to different experts, reducing routing stability and interpretability. We will clarify this design choice and add token-level routing as a future direction. 5.Hard Top-K Stability (R3) We agree that hard Top-K routing may cause discrete expert switches. HAR-MoE mitigates this through two designs. (i) The two-stage routing constrains the final Top-K2 selection within a task-consistent candidate set, reducing unconstrained switching over the full expert pool. (ii) The task/organ affinity priors provide stable biases, reducing dependence on small perturbations in instance-level logits. Together with L_aux, these designs improve routing stability and expert use. Table 4 supports the effectiveness of this design, and we will discuss hard Top-K as a limitation.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): All three reviewers agree that the paper makes strong and novel methodological contributions by introducing hierarchical mixture of experts framework for disentangling tasks and organ specific routing. All reviewers recommend acceptance of the paper.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Video Multiple Instance Learning: AI-Interpreted Point-of-Care Ultrasound for TB Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: The study addresses TB screening using accessible handheld POCUS technology. Problem Formulation: The authors successfully frame the 14-site POCUS protocol as a multi-video multiple instance learning problem, which naturally aligns with the clinical workflow of examining multiple anatomical zones. Methodological Integration: A notable strength is the demonstration of performance gains achieved by aggregating auxiliary pathology signatures, which suggests the model is capturing relevant clinical features beyond simple global labels. Performance: The HMV-MIL approach shows superior performance over single-video baseline methods in TB classification tasks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major Comments The conceptual novelty of the Hierarchical Multi-Video Multiple Instance Learning (HMV-MIL) architecture is not sufficiently established. The proposed framework bears significant similarities to existing multi-view evaluation models, such as the view-primed vision-language systems used in echocardiography [1]. The authors should explicitly clarify what distinguishes HMV-MIL from these prior multi-view architectures. The comparison between the proposed multi-video model and single-video baselines lacks clarity. It is unclear which specific video from the 14-site protocol was provided to the single-view models, or if they were trained on all videos independently. This ambiguity makes it difficult to determine if the performance gain is due to the architecture or simply the volume of data processed. There is a concerning discrepancy regarding the reported results. The manuscript claims a 0.15 AUC improvement, yet this is not supported by the data in Table 1.Furthermore, the closest performing model, DINOv3-Bert, is notably absent from the discussion in Section 5.1 (Architecture Comparison) and the abstract. Minor Comments In Section 3.1, the authors define the video dimensions as (Ti×3×224×224). It is unclear why three channels are maintained for monochromatic ultrasound data. The description of the HMV-MIL architecture in Section 3.1 is presented as a dense block of text, making the technical workflow difficult to follow. This section would benefit from a more structured explanation and connecting the text with Fig. 1. The performance gap between the baselines and the proposed model (92M parameters) may be attributed to model capacity rather than architectural design. The authors used ResNet-18 as a baseline; comparing HMV-MIL against higher-capacity models (e. g. , ResNet-50 or ResNet-101) would provide a more rigorous evaluation. [1] Vukadinovic, M. , Chiu, IM. , Tang, X. et al. Comprehensive echocardiogram evaluation with view primed vision language AI. Nature 650, 970–977 (2026).
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: To achieve TB detection, the paper proposes a novel intra video attention and inter video aggregation which is the core novelty. The multi head MIL (multi Instance Learning) approach captures spatial heterogeneity of the dataset. The hierarchical design genuinely matches clinical practice. TB diagnosis requires synthesizing evidence across bilateral thoracic zones, and no prior system addressed this from raw video. The auxiliary pathology heads add interpretability that most end-to-end systems lack. Fine tuning of vision transformer for the task is also commendable.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Single-site evaluation (one hospital in Benin) is a serious limitation — the authors acknowledge it but the paper’s claims about decentralized, global TB screening are difficult to support without multi-country validation. The robustness and performance of the model to unseen data is not validated since the test data is held out set from the training data.There is no analysis on false positive, false negative and TB cases that the model misses. TB varies significantly with co-morbidities, malnutrition, age, demographic and geography, however, the impact of these parameters on the accuracy of the model is not analysed. The paper claims that the system is developed for “resource limited settings” however there are no discussions related the deployment of the model in real time.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clear organization and presentation The manuscript is well structured and clearly written, making it easy to follow the proposed methodology and experimental design. 2.Novel and timely application The use of lung ultrasound for TB classification is an emerging research area, with most prior work focusing on chest radiographs. The proposed patient-level classification framework, which aggregates information across multiple standardized ultrasound videos, appears to be a novel contribution in this space. 3.Thoughtful validation strategy The authors evaluate their framework across different backbone architectures and include ablation studies to assess key components of the model. This provides some insight into the behavior of the proposed approach and demonstrates an effort to systematically analyze design choices.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Unclear benefit relative to simpler approaches While the proposed framework is novel, it is not yet clear whether the added complexity is justified. Prior work on TB classification from individual ultrasound frames appears to achieve stronger performance, in some cases surpassing the WHO-reported benchmarks cited by the authors. Including a direct comparison to simpler 2D models would help clarify whether the multi-instance, multi-video framework provides a meaningful advantage. 2.Missing or incomplete citations Several methods referenced in the introduction, including qXR and CAD4TB, are not accompanied by citations. In addition, the WHO guidelines referenced in the paper should be properly cited to support the reported benchmarks and provide appropriate context. 3.Interpretation of ablation results may be overstated The conclusions drawn from the ablation study do not appear to be fully supported by the reported results. In particular: Variants using attention-based key frame selection, uniform sampling, and mean pooling show relatively small differences in performance, suggesting that the attention mechanism may not play as strong a role as claimed. Increasing the number of selected key frames appears to degrade performance, which does not clearly support the interpretation that the attention mechanism is effectively identifying the most informative frames. Mean pooling performs comparably or better than key-frame selection, which may indicate that simpler aggregation strategies are sufficient. Removing pathology supervision results in only a minimal performance drop, raising further questions about the necessity of this component. Overall, these findings suggest that some components of the proposed architecture may not contribute as substantially as implied, and the interpretation of these results could be revisited for greater balance.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank R1, R2, R3, and Meta for their careful comments; all clarifications will be incorporated in the final manuscript. Problem formulation and multi-view comparison (Meta, R1):TB caused 1.23 million deaths in 2024, and AI-POCUS offers a promising path to point-of-care detection. Yet no prior work has built a deployable TB detection system from raw, multi-site POCUS video. HMV-MIL’s novelty lies in defining this previously unformulated problem space and constructing an architecture purpose-built for it. Existing multi-view AI-systems, particularly in echocardiography, rely on standardized acquisition planes, canonical views, and structured exams. TB lung POCUS has none of these: no canonical TB views, no frame- or site-level labels, and no single sufficient ultrasound sign. Diagnostic evidence is weak, sparse, and distributed across bilateral sites. HMV-MIL is the first framework to formulate this as hierarchical multi-video MIL, intra-video attention identifies informative frames under temporal noise; inter-video gated MIL integrates anatomically distributed findings under patient-only weak supervision. This is structurally and operationally distinct from view-primed architectures. AUC discrepancy and DINOv3-BERT (Meta, R1, R2, R3): We will clarify the paper: the 0.15-0.35 AUC improvement refers exclusively to conventional spatiotemporal baselines. We will revise Section 5.1 to discuss DINOv3-BERT (418.6M parameters) achieves 0.85 AUC, 0.04 below HMV-MIL (4.5x smaller). A larger backbone does not match our purpose-built design, disproving the capacity hypothesis. Baseline protocol (Meta, R1): All baselines used full patient-level data across all 14 sites. Section 4.2 will be revised to remove ambiguity around “single-video” terminology. Comparison to prior work (R3). The prior 0.93 AUC (Suttels et al.) requires trained sonographers to curate frames before inference, selecting the clearest, most diagnostically informative images, simplifying the input distribution and presupposing the expert knowledge the system is meant to replace, making it undeployable at scale in resource-limited settings. HMV-MIL achieves 0.89 AUC end-to-end on raw, operator-acquired video, eliminating expert curation entirely. The residual gap represents the cost of removing the expert from the loop, a deliberate trade-off for a fully autonomous system. Ablation interpretation (Meta, R2, R3): Modest 0.01-0.02 AUC differences are expected near clinically relevant performance thresholds, where gains are increasingly constrained by noise and inter-patient heterogeneity, these results reflect robustness, not insensitivity to design, all ablations degraded performance, confirming each component contributes. Pathology supervision’s primary value is clinical interpretability, per-site, human-readable outputs for auditing, and we will frame it as such. Deployment and operator training (Meta, R2): “Minimally trained operator” refers to frontline workers trained over ~20 hours across 4 days. HMV-MIL has been converted to TensorFlow.js (344 MB) for consumer-grade hardware. We will add discussion of acquisition quality sensitivity and quality-control thresholds, and will temper global deployment claims pending multi-site validation. False positives/negatives (Meta, R2): At 82% sensitivity/75% specificity, the model’s FN rate (~18%) reflects the cost of removing expert curation. For screening deployment, the operating threshold can be shifted toward higher sensitivity (e.g., ≥90% sensitivity is achievable at reduced specificity, per the ROC curve). We will add a confusion matrix and per-fold FP/FN breakdown to the supplementary. References and citations (R1, R3): We recognize that reference errors undermine manuscript credibility and will have verified and addressed all concerns in the final manuscript. We will also restructure Section 3.1 for clarity. Code and full implementation details will be released upon acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents an ultrasound-based approach for TB screening in which the 14-site (as in sites on the patient anatomy) image acquisition protocol is posed as a multi-video multiple instance learning problem. The work has many strengths including the use of intra-video attention and inter-video aggregation design, which matches clinical practice. It is recommended that the authors clarify these points in order to improve the quality of the manuscript: Explicitly clarify what distinguishes the HMV-MIL architecture from existing multi-view frameworks, such as vision-language systems used in echocardiography. Address the major concerning discrepancy where the claimed 0.15 AUC improvement is not supported by Table 1, and explain why the closest performing model (DINOv3-Bert) is omitted from the discussion. Clarify the comparison with single-video baselines, specifically identifying which video from the 14-site protocol was used for single-view training. Elaborate on the meaning of “minimally trained operator” and provide discussion related to the model’s real-time deployment in “resource limited settings.” Clarify the absence of or add the analysis on false positives, false negatives on model accuracy. | The authors have answered the key questions satisfactorily. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper addresses an important and clinically relevant problem by formulating multi-site point-of-care ultrasound for tuberculosis detection as a hierarchical multi-video multiple instance learning problem. The proposed framework is well aligned with clinical practice, combining intra-video attention and inter-video aggregation to integrate evidence across multiple anatomical sites. The work is timely, particularly given the need for scalable TB screening solutions in resource-limited settings. The reviewers highlighted the novelty of the problem formulation, clinically meaningful design of the hierarchical aggregation strategy, and strong empirical performance. The rebuttal successfully clarified key concerns regarding the comparison protocol, reported performance gains, distinction from existing multi-view architectures, and intended deployment setting. Some limitations remain, including single-site validation, limited analysis of failure cases and subgroup performance, and need for stronger external validation. Overall, the paper presents a meaningful and well-executed contribution that is likely to stimulate further research in ultrasound-based TB screening. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The rebuttal clarified the novelty of the hierarchical multi-video MIL formulation, resolved questions regarding reported performance, baseline comparisons, deployment considerations, and error analysis. The remaining concerns primarily relate to presentation and scope rather than fundamental methodological flaws. Given the clinical importance of the problem, the strong empirical results, and the positive reviewer consensus after rebuttal, I recommend acceptance.

title: High-Frequency Guided Feature Refinement for Semi-supervised Ultrasound Image Segmentation
reviewer_1_strengths: A high-frequency–guided feature refinement semi-supervised segmentation framework is designed, that improves pseudo-label reliability by explicitly enhancing boundary-sensitive information during up-sampling. Results are relatively good.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Though results are good, the improvement in fact is not significant. The improvement is less than 2 points averagely. Moreover, the novelty is quite limited. It seems this work is a combination of existing techniques. Feature frequency analysis has been widely studied in computer vision, image analysis, and image segmentation. It is thus unclear if this work brings enough new contributions to this domain. Overall, the marginal performance gain and the limited novelty make this paper below the acceptance standard.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Propose a High-Frequency Component Enhancement (HFCE) module based on a 2D discrete wavelet transform to enhance boundary-aware features and inject high-frequency information into the upsampling stage for improved segmentation accuracy. 2.Adapted a frozen AnyUp upsampling module that leverages both encoder features and HFCE outputs to further refine the upsampling process and preserve structural details. 3.Developed a high-frequency–guided semi-supervised segmentation framework that effectively utilizes unlabeled data to improve model performance. 4.Validated the proposed framework on three diverse datasets.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper lacks key methodological details and justification of design choices, including augmentation strategies and feature alignment between modules. The experimental evaluation is limited, with no cross-validation, insufficient analysis of performance under low-label settings, and missing ablation studies to assess individual components. These issues reduce the clarity, reproducibility, and overall rigor of the work. These are more detailed comments. 1.The manuscript does not specify the augmentation strategies used for the weakly and strongly augmented branches. Clarification on the types and magnitudes of augmentations is necessary for reproducibility and fair comparison. 2.The output of the HFCE module is reported as 3×256×256 and is used as input to the AnyUp module for upsampling. However, this appears inconsistent with the spatial resolution and channel dimensions of the final DINOv3 encoder features. The manuscript lacks an explanation of how this mismatch in feature dimensions is addressed. 3.It is unclear why the AnyUp module is not applied to all upsampling stages within the teacher decoder. The authors should justify this design choice or provide empirical evidence supporting the selected configuration. 4.To better assess the robustness and generalizability of the proposed method, n-fold cross-validation is recommended in all test results. 5.In Table 3, competing methods show substantial performance improvements when using 3% labeled data, whereas the proposed method demonstrates comparatively smaller gains. An analysis explaining this discrepancy would strengthen the paper. 6.An ablation study isolating the contributions of DINOv3 and the HFCE module is missing. Additionally, since AnyUp is introduced to improve upsampling, it would be important to evaluate its effectiveness when applied to all upsampling stages.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Evaluation spans three distinct ultrasound datasets (CCAUI: carotid vessel wall; BUS-BRA: breast tumor; PSFHS: intrapartum fetal anatomy). These targets differ in anatomy, imaging depth, and noise characteristics. Consistent improvements across all three support a claim of generalization within the ultrasound modality. The motivation is technically grounded. Frozen VFM encoders suppress high-frequency spatial detail in favor of global semantic abstraction. Wavelet sub-bands capture exactly the boundary-related content that frozen encoders attenuate. Replacing raw-image guidance, which carries speckle noise and low tissue contrast, with frequency-filtered cues addresses a real limitation of the AnyUp architecture in noisy imaging settings. Boundary-sensitive metrics (HD95, ASD) are reported alongside DSC for all datasets and labeling ratios. For anatomical segmentation tasks where contour precision carries clinical meaning, these metrics provide more diagnostic information than DSC alone. The ablation in Table 4 isolates the contribution of DINOv3, AnyUp, and HFCE as separate components with quantitative results for each combination. This makes the role of each design choice explicit and testable.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The abstract describes HFCE as a module that “adaptively selects informative high-frequency components in the frequency domain.” Equation 2 implements this as an independent scalar gain per sub-band, g_i ~ U(g_min, g_max), sampled without reference to image content. All three sub-bands (LH, HL, HH) are retained unconditionally. Section 2.2 repeats the same framing: “selectively amplifying high-frequency information to provide structural guidance.” The word “selectively” implies content-dependent filtering. The operation is uniform random scaling. This is a factual mismatch between the described mechanism and the implemented one. The abstract and Section 2.2 should be revised to accurately characterize HFCE as stochastic gain augmentation applied uniformly to all wavelet sub-bands. The uniform distribution U(g_min, g_max) in Equation 2 defines the core HFCE operation. However, hyperparameters g_min and g_max do not appear anywhere else in the paper, making the method not fully reproducible. Statistical significance is not established. Several key improvements over UniMatch fall within one standard deviation: BUS-BRA 1% reports 78.45±4.36 vs. 75.95±4.74 (difference: 2.5%, SD overlap substantial); PSFHS 1% reports 87.69±0.93 vs. 85.87±1.47.No significance test is reported for any comparison. Table 4 compares DINOv3 alone, DINOv3 + AnyUp, and the full model (+ HFCE). No condition substitutes an alternative guidance signal for HFCE inside AnyUp (for example, gradient magnitude or Canny edges). The gain assigned to HFCE may arise from providing any structured guidance to AnyUp rather than from the frequency-domain design. An ablation against at least one non-wavelet guidance alternative would isolate this. PSFHS results (Table 3) are reported without category-wise breakdown. The paper justifies this in the caption by calling aggregated metrics “sufficient.” Fetal head and pubic symphysis differ substantially in size, shape, and imaging contrast. Aggregated DSC and HD95 do not allow the reader to determine which structure drives reported gains, or whether performance degrades on one target while improving on the other.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their insightful feedback. The main concerns and our responses are summarized below: [R1-Q1] Novelty of Paper: Existing semi-supervised segmentation (SSS) methods mainly emphasize semantic consistency while often neglecting fine-grained structural boundaries that are critical for generating high-quality pseudo-labels. Our method is not merely a combination of existing modules; its key novelty lies in demonstrating that high-frequency structural guidance, combined with pre-trained upsampling priors, can significantly improve pseudo-label quality and segmentation performance in low-label ultrasound SSS, which remains insufficiently addressed in current literature. Furthermore, our framework highlights the broader potential of integrating foundation-model priors and generic pre-trained upsampling modules into label-scarce segmentation settings. Overall, our work demonstrates a general framework that effectively leverages pre-trained priors under high-frequency guidance for SSS. [R1-Q2] Limited Performance Gain: In low-label ultrasound SSS, stable boundary recovery is more critical than coarse localization. While Dice gains appear incremental, HFCE significantly improves boundary-sensitive metrics. For instance, on CCAUI (1% labels), HD95 drops from 9.95 to 3.66 and ASD from 3.45 to 1.55.Our method achieves superior stability and boundary precision over UniMatch across all ratios. [R2-Q1] Augmentation Strategies: Weak and strong augmentations strictly follow UniMatch to ensure a fair and direct comparison. [R2-Q2] Feature Mismatch: HFCE outputs serve as high-resolution guidance for the frozen AnyUp module; they are not directly fused with DINOv3 features, thus avoiding explicit alignment issues. [R2-Q3/Q6] Selective Upsampling: AnyUp is applied only at the first upsampling stage to balance performance and efficiency. Deeper integration would significantly increase GPU memory usage and potentially amplify ultrasound speckle noise. [R2-Q4] Lack of Cross-validation: Following standard SSS protocols, we used fixed dataset splits to ensure fair and reproducible comparisons. The consistent improvements observed across multiple datasets and labeling ratios further indicate that the performance gains are not dependent on a specific split. [R2-Q5] Performance Saturation: Baselines often benefit from increased supervision at higher ratios. Our boundary-aware guidance is more effective under extremely sparse supervision, which directly aligns with our motivation for low-label medical imaging. [R2-Q6] Incomplete Ablation: Table 4 presents a progressive ablation from DINOv3 to AnyUp, then to HFCE-guided AnyUp. As HFCE is specifically designed to guide the upsampling framework, it cannot operate independently. We provided more detailed analysis on our Github page. [R3-Q1] Misleading Description: We appreciate the observation and will revise the Abstract and Section 2.2 for clarity. [R3-Q2] Missing Hyperparameters: The parameters g_min and g_max are fixed across all experiments. Optimal performance is consistently observed at g_min and g_max=5.[R3-Q3] Lack of Significance Testing: Our method consistently achieves lower HD95/ASD, indicating superior structural stability. The larger standard deviations in BUS-BRA (1% setting) are inherent to the dataset’s blurry boundaries and strong speckle noise under sparse labels. [R3-Q4] Insufficient Baseline Comparison: Additional experiments with different wavelet bases (e.g., db3 and coif3) show that our method consistently outperforms competing approaches across settings. Moreover, the compared methods were selected as representative SOTA methods widely used in recent literature. [R3-Q5] Missing Class-wise Evaluation: PSFHS category-wise results (omitted for space) show consistent gains in the 1% setting: our method leads UniMatch on both Fetal Head (84.41% vs. 82.74%) and Pubic Symphysis (90.96% vs. 88.99%). Additional details, results, and code will be released on GitHub.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Three reviews note marginal gains and limited novelty, but methodological concerns dominate. | While the integration of high-frequency features into semi-supervised segmentation is conceptually well-motivated, consensus post-rebuttal highlights that the manuscript’s core novelty remains limited, representing an incremental combination of pre-existing modules. Furthermore, critical concerns remain unresolved regarding the factual mismatch between the described adaptive mechanism and its actual stochastic formulation, the lack of ablation comparisons against non-wavelet spatial guidance baselines, and marginal empirical gains that lack statistical significance testing. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After the rebuttal, most reviewers provided positive recommendations for this work. Overall, although considering high-frequency information into semi-supervised segmentation is not new, it is reasonable and effective. By using DINO features and wavelet operations, this work achieves superior performance, particularly on shape-related metrics. It indicates a clear contribution and could benefit the relevant community. Therefore, acceptance is recommended, and the authors are suggested to improve the manuscript based on reviewers’ comments in the camera-ready version. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a semi-supervised ultrasound image segmentation framework enhanced by high-frequency component guidance. While the method is relatively straightforward, which is composed of a few established modules (e.g., the teacher-student framework, the discrete wavelet transforms, and the AnyUp upsampling module), the design motivation is sound. I am also impressed by the comprehensive evaluation settings, which include three distinct ultrasound image datasets and eight competing baselines under two label ratios (although it sacrificed some clarity regarding the methodology and implementation details). After the rebuttal, the author generally addressed the primary concerns raised by the reviewers. The unaddressed comments do not undermine the core empirical strength of the work, and thus I recommend accept. PS: I have one additional comment for the authors’ potential future revisions: the high-frequency components in the ultrasound may not fully correspond to the object boundaries as there is severe noise existing in the ultrasound image. Emphasizing the high-frequency component in the ultrasound data may also amplify the noisy level.

title: HypOProto: Hyperbolic Ordinal Prototypes for Left Ventricular Filling Pressure Classification
reviewer_1_strengths: The research addresses a high-impact clinical problem by framing LVFP classification as an ordinal task. By mapping clinical ambiguity near the hyperbolic root and severity toward the periphery, the authors provide a geometric intuition that aligns with the $E/e’$ threshold, effectively moving beyond traditional “black-box” approaches. The technical design is highly coherent, successfully integrating a frozen DINOv3 backbone with Lorentzian prototype learning. Using predicted $E/e’$ values to determine radial coordinates establishes a direct, interpretable link between the model’s geometry and established clinical metrics. The empirical validation is thorough, comparing the framework against a diverse set of baseline architectures across roughly 141K cines, providing confidence intervals. The inclusion of study-level metrics and a detailed discordance analysis adds a level of rigor often missing from prototype-based studies, providing a clear picture of failure modes. Qualitative evidence strongly reinforces the paper’s claims, with CoSNE visualizations and prototype activation maps demonstrating that the model correctly localizes features around the mitral valve. These results confirm that the hyperbolic geometry is a functional representation of physiological data rather than just a mathematical abstraction.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The work is very interesting and I really enjoyed reading it. Although there are some relevant works that have not been cited not discussed. First, HyperPAS mirrors existing hyperbolic supervised contrastive objectives, and the interpretation of radial distance representing ambiguity has already defined in [1]. The contribution should be reframed as an adaptation of these concepts to a prototype-based setting rather than a novel invention. There is a significant omission regarding Busemann-style prototype learning [2], which is a canonical approach for hyperbolic classification. The authors do not justify why they chose a geodesic formulation requiring an auxiliary regression target over the ideal boundary approach proposed in [2]. A discussion or baseline comparison is necessary to explain the trade-offs of using an externally supervised radial scalar versus the inherent geometric properties of the Busemann framework. The methodological advancement over existing works like HiProtoNet and HAPPI appears incremental. The paper lacks a direct head-to-head comparison with these very similar frameworks. The manuscript does not describe the angular initialization of the prototypes or the specific hyperparameter values for projection frequency and tolerance. Combined with missing mathematical definitions for log-maps and tangent-space similarity, significantly reduces the reproducibility of the proposed method. The statistical evidence supporting the model’s superiority is thin, as reported performance gains often fall within or near one standard deviation of the baselines. In some metrics, such as study-level balanced accuracy,the proposed method is actually outperformed by a standard MLP baseline. The absence of significance testing makes the “SOTA” claims difficult to substantiate given the high data imbalance and small number of training runs. [1] Alvaro Gonzalez-Jimenez, Simone Lionetti, Dena Bazazian, Philippe Gottfrois, Fabian Gröger, Marc Pouly, Alexander Navarini. Hyperbolic Metric Learning for Visual Outlier Detection. European Conference on Computer Vision ECCV 2024 BEW Workshop. [2] Mina Ghadimi Atigh, Martin Keller-Ressel, Pascal Mettes. Hyperbolic Busemann Learning with Ideal Prototypes. NeurIPS 2021
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper introduces a principled use of hyperbolic geometry to model ordinal LVFP labels, aligning the embedding space with the physiological ordering of the E/e′ scale. This is a meaningful innovation, as it naturally captures graded disease progression, unlike standard Euclidean approaches. 2.The model enables case-based reasoning through learned prototypes, offering transparent and clinically relevant explanations. Integrating prototype learning with ordinal structure in hyperbolic space is both original and practically valuable for clinical interpretability. 3.The proposed Hyperbolic Prototype Angular Separation loss enforces clear inter-class separation while preserving ordinal relationships. This improves prototype diversity and stability, addressing a common limitation in prototype-based models. 4.By leveraging frozen DINOv3 features, the approach reduces computational cost while maintaining high performance, improving practicality and reproducibility. 5.Prototype activation maps highlight relevant anatomical regions, and borderline cases are placed near the hyperbolic origin, reflecting diagnostic uncertainty and aligning well with clinical reasoning. 6.Detailed Ablation studies clearly show that hyperbolic ordinality and the HyperPAS loss contribute directly to improved performance and representation quality.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The paper does not adequately explain how the spatiotemporal attention module operates or how it interacts with the learned embeddings. In particular, the process by which the model identifies k salient regions of interest (ROIs) remains unclear. This lack of clarity limits interpretability and reproducibility. 2.The model employs a complex combination of five loss functions, yet the rationale behind selecting specific components, particularly L1 loss and transformation consistency loss, is not provided. If mean absolute error (MAE) is already used for predicting E/e’, the additional role and necessity of L1 loss are unclear. Similarly, the purpose and contribution of the transformation consistency loss are not explained, raising concerns about redundancy and over-parameterization. 3.The dataset is highly imbalanced (approximately 85% normal vs. 15% elevated cases), which poses a risk of model bias and overfitting. Which measures have been taken to avoid it. 4.There is a mismatch between the framework diagram and the methodological description. While the text states that five loss functions are applied, the figure does not clearly reflect this design. It is also unclear whether these losses are optimized jointly, assigned to separate heads, or combined in a specific training strategy. This inconsistency creates confusion about the actual implementation and optimization pipeline.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is clear and well-written and is thorough in their experiments. The paper proposes a novel prototype-based echocardiography framework using frozen foundation model and is the first interpretable model for LFVP classification. The proposed method HypOProto performs better than all baselines including an improvement in the elevated LVFP class which are the more challenging diagnostic boundary cases. Results also include qualitative visualizations that highlight anatomically relevant regions. The method’s ability to handle ambiguous cases near the diagnostic threshold is well-supported by both quantitative and qualitative result.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The overall novelty of the paper is more in terms of the application specific for LVFP classification in echocardiography as there have already been similar prototype-based and hyperbolic methods applied to related cardiac tasks. The dataset is heavily imbalanced, with 85% normal and only 15% elevated LVFP cases, which may affect model calibation and sensitiyvity to minority classes The lack of benchmark dataset for fair comparison makes it a bit difficult to judge generalizability as the current study relies on a private dataset from a single tertiary care center. Authors may comment on whether using frozen DINOv3 encoder for feature extraction that is not specifically fine tuned on specific LVFP classification task may limit the models ability.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank reviewers for their thoughtful and constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognized the clinical motivation and potential of our work. We agree that the manuscript can be strengthened based on reviewer comments, and we will address these in the revision. Novelty and Positioning (R1, R3): We agree that our contribution is best framed as an adaptation of hyperbolic learning to a prototype-based clinical setting rather than an entirely new objective. We acknowledge that radial distance encoding ambiguity was previously established, and that HyperPAS shares similarity with hyperbolic contrastive losses. We clarify that: (1) HyperPAS operates exclusively on learnable prototypes, not on all sample pairs, and (2) the radius is not implicitly learned but explicitly anchored to predicted E/e’, enforcing clinically meaningful ordinal structure. We will revise the manuscript to cite the papers mentioned by R1, position the method relative to prior hyperbolic contrastive methods, HiProtoNet, and HAPPI, and clarify our key contribution as the explicit physiological organization of prototypes. Busemann Prototypes and Geometry Design (R1, R4): In Busemann-style classification, prototypes are positioned at the ideal boundary and class structure emerges from unconstrained geometric properties alone. While elegant, this offers no guarantee that the learned representation aligns with clinically established measurements. Our externally supervised radius enforces fidelity to the E/e’ threshold (14), making the geometry auditable by clinicians and encoding ordinal “distance from the diagnostic boundary,” which boundary-positioned prototypes (maximally committed to a class direction) cannot capture. We will discuss this trade-off and the rationale for clinically imposed vs. purely learned geometry in the revised manuscript. Experimental Clarifications and Statistical Significance (R1, R4): We acknowledge that some gains are modest compared to reported baselines. Our goal is to balance predictive performance with interpretability and physiologically meaningful representation learning. Although EchoPrime+MLP achieves slightly higher study-level balanced accuracy, it is not explainable. We nevertheless believe the observed improvements are meaningful given the large scale of our dataset and the gains observed across metrics. To address the substantial class imbalance (85% normal / 15% elevated), we employed class-balanced sampling during training, and reported balanced accuracy and per-class F1 rather than standard accuracy. We will make this more explicit in the revised manuscript. HyperPAS Interpretation (R4): We agree that HyperPAS primarily acts as a prototype organization regularizer rather than a pure performance enhancer. We will revise the manuscript to explicitly state that HyperPAS improves prototype organization, even when classification gains are modest. Reproducibility and Methodological Clarity (R1, R2, R4): We will expand implementation details and clarify loss optimization and the spatiotemporal attention/ROI selection process. While several components follow prior work, we will explicitly reference the corresponding papers. Dataset and Foundation Encoder (R3, R4): We agree that external validation is crucial. While public echo datasets with LVFP labels have been scarce, we recognize the recent release of MIMIC-IV-ECHO as a candidate for future benchmarking. We will clarify this limitation and look forward to validating on the external dataset. We will also clarify that the frozen DINOv3 encoder was not fine-tuned on the LVFP task itself, and discuss both the benefits and limitations of relying on pretrained echo representations. Finally, we will address presentation issues noted by the reviewers, including defining “E2E,” standardizing DINO capitalization, and improving figure clarity. We believe these revisions will strengthen the manuscript and improve clarity and reproducibility.

title: InSPIRE: Multiparameter Inversion for Ultrasound Computed Tomography via Sequential Position-Based Implicit Representation
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Joint reconstruction of sound speed and acoustic impedance is an important extension of quantitative USCT, since the two parameters carry complementary information about tissue properties and interfaces. The paper is also well motivated by two well-known challenges in waveform inversion, namely cycle-skipping and parameter crosstalk. 2.The geometry-aware encoding is well aligned with the ring-array acquisition setting, and the dual-branch design is a reasonable architectural choice for separating parameters with different spatial characteristics. Likewise, the frequency-progressive strategy is consistent with standard practice in stabilizing FWI optimization.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The current submission appears highly continuous with [1] at the levels of problem formulation, methodological perspective, and empirical presentation. Both works formulate USCT reconstruction as a subject-specific unsupervised INR/FWI problem, both exploit acquisition geometry in the coordinate representation, and both follow a very similar experimental narrative including synthetic studies, in vivo visualization, ablation analysis, and convergence behavior. While the present paper extends the target from single-parameter sound-speed reconstruction to joint sound speed and acoustic impedance estimation, the manuscript does not yet make sufficiently precise which aspects constitute a substantive methodological advance beyond this prior line of work. 2.Several components are introduced simultaneously: geometry-aware radial modulation, a dual-branch formulation, frequency-adaptive coordinate attention, and sequential optimization. However, the manuscript does not fully clarify which of these should be viewed as the primary scientific contribution, and which are better understood as design choices that support the move to multiparameter inversion. This makes the contribution boundary somewhat diffuse. 3.Since no in vivo ground truth is available, the validation mainly relies on CNR and qualitative structural consistency. This is understandable in the application setting, but it also means that the practical significance of the impedance estimates is somewhat less firmly established than the framing of the paper may suggest. [1] Wang Z, Yan W, Liu Z, et al. P²INR-FWI: An Implicit Neural Representation Method for Speed of Sound Image Reconstruction in Ultrasound Computed Tomography. In: International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2025: 420–430.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 6.1 Novel formulation. The adaptation of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) for USCT is mathematically elegant, specifically the radially modulated Fourier features that cleverly incorporate the physical constraints of ring-array geometry. 6.2 Effective Disentanglement. The proposed dual-branch FACA module successfully mitigates the velocity-density crosstalk, which is a notorious challenge in traditional Full-Waveform Inversion (FWI). 6.3 Clinical Feasibility. The unsupervised nature of the framework means it can operate without paired training data or ground truth labels. It demonstrates superior performance over standard FWI and DIP methods on both synthetic and in vivo data.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 7.1 On page 2, the manuscript states that recent work adapted “DIP” to USCT sound-speed inversion [22,26], but this conflates two rather different ideas: the original Deep Image Prior of Ulyanov et al. [22], which is a general untrained convolutional image prior for image restoration, and Yan et al. [26], which describes a USCT-specific untrained neural network integrated into an FWI framework for breast sound-speed imaging. The experimental section then refers to “DIP [26]” as a baseline, which makes it unclear whether the comparison is against the original DIP, Yan et al.’s USCT-specific UNN/FWI method, or an in-house variant. This ambiguity matters because baseline identity directly affects the interpretation and fairness of the reported gains. In addition, Wu et al. [25] is cited in the introduction, but the manuscript does not explicitly discuss it as the closest prior on multiparameter USCT FWI, nor explain why it is not included as an experimental baseline. I therefore suggest adding a short paragraph that explicitly distinguishes InSPIRE from (i) Yan et al., which focuses primarily on sound-speed-only untrained inversion within an FWI-style framework, and (ii) Wu et al., which addresses classical multiparameter USCT FWI without the proposed coordinate-based implicit representation, geometry-aware encoding, or dual-branch decoding. If Wu et al. is not used as a baseline, the reason should also be stated clearly. 7.2 A central claim of the paper is reduced multiparameter crosstalk. I think this concern should be evaluated more directly than by image quality metrics alone. A feasible addition would be a controlled synthetic experiment with spatially separated sound-speed and impedance anomalies, together with a simple leakage/contamination metric that quantifies off-target energy mapped into the wrong parameter image. A more advanced sensitivity/Hessian-style analysis would also be valuable, but I would view that as optional rather than mandatory for this paper. 7.3 The manuscript explicitly motivates the sequential frequency-progressive strategy as a way to stabilize convergence in the presence of cycle-skipping, and the current results do suggest improved convergence behavior. However, the evidence is still obtained under a relatively mild synthetic setup: homogeneous initialization, fixed 40 dB noise, and a single frequency schedule starting from 400 kHz. I therefore think the cycle-skipping claim would be much more convincing with one targeted stress test, preferably by varying the initial model error and/or the available low-frequency content. For example, the authors could perturb the homogeneous background model more aggressively, or repeat the experiment with the lowest frequency band removed. An SNR sweep would also be useful as an additional robustness check, but I would view that as secondary. 7.4 An important methodological clarification concerns the chosen parameterization. Eq. (1) is written in terms of sound speed and density, whereas the inversion variables are defined as sound speed and acoustic impedance. This is a valid choice in principle, since acoustic FWI can indeed be formulated in a velocity–impedance parameterization, but the manuscript should state this explicitly and explain how the forward model and gradients are implemented under (c,z). At present, it is unclear whether Eq. (1) is re-expressed directly in (c,z), or whether density is derived internally from z/cfor the solver. Because parameterization strongly affects sensitivity, trade-off, and crosstalk in multiparameter FWI, a brief justification for choosing (c,z) in this ring-array USCT setting would make the method section substantially clearer [5,11–13]. 7.5 The ablation study in Table 3 is currently difficult to interpret because its description appears inconsistent with the reported numbers. The text states that “the baseline uses a DIP network without Geometry-Aware Positional Encoding (GAPE) or attention modules (FACA),” which suggests that the ablation should start from a DIP-based configuration and then incrementally add the proposed components. However, the first row of Table 3 (“Base ×, GAPE ×, FACA ×, Freq-Progressive ×”) reports exactly the same quantitative results as the FWI baseline in Table 1, whereas the second row (“Base ✓, GAPE ×, FACA ×, Freq-Progressive ×”) matches the DIP results in Table 1.This creates ambiguity about what “Base” actually denotes and how the ablation sequence should be interpreted. I therefore suggest that the authors clarify whether Table 3 is intended to represent an incremental progression from FWI → DIP-style base network → +GAPE → +FACA → +frequency-progressive optimization, or instead an ablation entirely within the neural-prior family. As currently written, the table mixes baseline definitions in a way that makes the contribution of each component harder to assess. Since the ablation study is one of the main pieces of evidence supporting the paper’s claims, this inconsistency should be resolved explicitly. 7.6 The in vivo results are promising, but some of the manuscript’s clinical wording appears stronger than the current evidence supports. In particular, the conclusion states that the method provides information for “clinical diagnosis” and is “particularly suitable for clinical applications,” while the in vivo validation consists of only three volunteer cases evaluated mainly by ROI/background CNR and qualitative structural correspondence. I therefore suggest framing the in vivo study more explicitly as preliminary feasibility evidence, and softening claims of clinical diagnosis, clinical robustness, or clinical utility unless additional lesion-level, pathological, or reader-based validation is provided. 7.7 The manuscript provides enough information to understand the overall framework, but a few implementation details still seem necessary for reproducibility. In particular, it would be helpful to state explicitly either in the paper, the supplement, or released code: (i) the exact frequency-stage schedule used by InSPIRE itself, (ii) the noise scale σ in Eq. (10), (iii) the key Fourier-feature settings (at least the dimensionality and scaling of B), and (iv) the numerical specification of the shared encoder / dual-decoder architecture, or a clear pointer to an exact standard implementation if one is used. These items appear important because the reported gains depend on the interaction between architectural bias and staged optimization. 7.8 The geometry-aware radial modulation is intuitively motivated, but the current justification remains largely heuristic. Because the manuscript explicitly attributes the radial weighting to reduced illumination / spectral coverage in the central region of the ring-array setup, I would encourage the authors to provide at least one more direct supporting analysis or experiment. This does not necessarily require a heavy Hessian-based study; even a simple geometry- or radius-dependent sensitivity/illumination analysis, or an empirical radial ablation showing that central emphasis is specifically beneficial in this acquisition setup, would make the physical motivation more convincing. author_feedback: We are grateful for the acceptance of our paper and the reviewers’ valuable feedback. We address the main concerns as follows: 1.Methodological Novelty (R1 and R2): We clarify how InSPIRE differs from Wang et al. and Yan et al. Wang’s P2INR-FWI uses point-wise MLP processing individual coordinates, while InSPIRE employs field-wise U-Net processing the entire coordinate field. This is critical for multiparameter inversion: our shared encoder captures global spatial context, enabling dual-branch decoders to independently reconstruct sound speed and impedance while mitigating crosstalk. Point-wise processing lacks spatial context to model distinct parameter characteristics. Yan et al. uses DIP mapping noise to images, whereas InSPIRE maps coordinates to physical parameters, providing continuous representation and stronger high-frequency modeling via Fourier features. Wu et al. [25] uses discrete FWI with optimal transport, a different paradigm from our coordinate-based continuous representation, making direct comparison less meaningful. 2.Experimental Design and Ablation (R2 and R3): We clarify Table 3’s ablation design. Row 1 is classical FWI. Row 2 uses DIP [26] as baseline for comparison with prior untrained neural USCT work. Rows 3-5 incrementally add our components. The transition from Row 2 to Row 3 includes shifting to coordinate-based input and adding GAPE. Coordinate-based formulation is a core design enabling our geometry-aware and frequency-adaptive modules. We note that coordinate-input U-Net without GAPE/FACA/frequency-progressive performs comparably to DIP, confirming coordinate-input provides similar regularization while enabling our proposed modules. This will be clarified in the final version. Regarding R3’s concern about GAPE’s modest gain, in synthetic experiments the ring-array geometry degradation is relatively mild, making radial weighting less pronounced. GAPE’s value is demonstrated through cumulative effects and becomes more critical in real scenarios with stronger illumination inhomogeneity. 3.Technical Details and Reproducibility (R2 and R3): Regarding the parameterization in c and z, our forward solver internally derives ρ=z/c, then solves Eq.(1) with gradients backpropagating to c and z. We chose this parameterization because impedance directly corresponds to tissue interfaces, facilitating dual-branch disentanglement. We will clarify this and provide complete implementation details in the final version. For computational cost, InSPIRE requires approximately 119 minutes on synthetic data using A100 GPU versus 170 minutes for DIP and 100 minutes for FWI. InSPIRE is faster than DIP and only moderately slower than FWI while delivering substantially improved reconstruction quality. 4.Clinical Validation (R1 and R2): We agree our in vivo study represents preliminary feasibility evidence on healthy volunteers rather than definitive clinical validation. Regarding impedance practical significance, acoustic impedance reveals tissue interfaces complementary to sound speed. While ground truth is unavailable, we validated structural consistency by comparing impedance gradients against USCT reflectivity maps in Fig. 5, demonstrating physically meaningful tissue boundaries. Additionally, quantitative characterization in healthy populations establishes baseline references for early screening protocols critical for preventive healthcare. InSPIRE shows promise for clinical applications, though further validation with patient cohorts and pathological correlation is needed.

title: Interaction-Aware Contrastive Multi-task Learning for Joint Segmentation and Malignancy Classification in Thyroid Ultrasound
reviewer_1_strengths: The framework explicitly addresses the inherent clinical interdependence between anatomical delineation and pathological diagnosis. The CI module formalizes bidirectional message passing as a mathematically clear, gated residual update. Applying supervised contrastive objectives symmetrically on post-interaction features successfully shapes feature separability at multiple granularities.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The CI gating formulation lacks algorithmic novelty and conceptually duplicates established multi-task paradigms like cross-stitch networks, sluice networks, and FiLM-like modulation. The evaluation completely omits mandatory quantitative comparisons against these classic feature-exchange architectures and recent thyroid-specific joint models. The methodology leaves critical technical details undefined, including backbone architecture, SCMR projection head dimensions, and pixel-level subsampling strategies for managing foreground/background imbalance. The dynamic loss reweighting scheme relies on an arbitrary Dice score threshold, introducing unfair training heuristics. The study lacks statistical significance testing and fails to report computational overhead, inference time, or memory consumption constraints.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Principled bidirectional cross-task interaction with clearly defined roles for each direction. The central contribution of IC-MTL is the explicit formalization of information flow between the segmentation and classification branches in both directions. The design is grounded in a clear clinical rationale: boundary and shape cues from segmentation are informative for malignancy assessment (per TI-RADS morphological descriptors), and malignancy-related semantics can sharpen segmentation by refining attention to lesion-relevant regions. This bidirectionality is not merely architectural but is implemented with role-specific message-passing operators and validated through direction-specific ablation. Removing Seg→Cls reduces AUC by 5.53 percentage points (85.92 → 80.39), and removing Cls→Seg reduces DSC by 0.66 points (92.38 → 91.72), confirming that each direction contributes to its intended target task in the expected direction. 2.SCMR applies contrastive regularization at both task-appropriate granularities. The supervised contrastive regularization is applied at the image level for classification (pulling benign/malignant embeddings together within class and apart between classes) and at the pixel level for segmentation (pulling foreground/background pixel embeddings apart). This dual-granularity contrastive framework is conceptually consistent with the different feature geometries required by each task and is supported by the ablation: removing SCMR (Cls) drops ACC from 90.00 to 84.67, and removing SCMR (Seg) drops DSC from 92.38 to 90.72, suggesting that the two contrastive terms have complementary and largely non-overlapping effects. 3.Thorough ablation study with component-level granularity. Table 2 includes ten experimental conditions covering: classification-only baseline, staged pipeline baseline, full joint model without proposed components, removal of CI entirely, removal of each CI direction independently, removal of SCMR entirely, and removal of each SCMR term independently. This level of ablation granularity significantly strengthens confidence in the contribution of each proposed component and provides clear evidence for both CI and SCMR as necessary elements. 4.Rich qualitative analysis supporting mechanistic interpretation. Figure 3 provides t-SNE feature visualization comparing class separability across competing methods (Chowdary et al., Luo et al., He et al., and IC-MTL before and after CI), Grad-CAM attention maps for both DDTI and local datasets, and segmentation feature map comparisons before and after CI. Together, these analyses provide an intuitive and multi-faceted verification that CI improves feature separability, attention-boundary alignment, and lesion-focused segmentation activations in the expected ways, going beyond what tables alone can convey. 5.Evaluation on two datasets with different characteristics. Testing on both the public DDTI benchmark and an independent clinical dataset collected at a separate hospital provides a reasonable assessment of generalization under scanner and population shift. The two-dataset evaluation is particularly valuable because the local clinical dataset includes ultrasound video sequences rather than static images, adding a degree of real-world complexity. 6.Dynamic loss re-weighting strategy is practically sound. The two-stage training schedule that prioritizes segmentation until DSC ≥ 0.8, then shifts emphasis to classification, is a pragmatic solution to the common problem of task imbalance in multi-task learning. The rationale — stable spatial representation first, then discriminative semantic learning — is aligned with how clinicians sequentially assess thyroid nodules (first locate, then characterize), and it reduces the risk of classification branch overfitting on unreliable segmentation features early in training.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Both evaluation datasets are relatively small, limiting the generalizability of conclusions. The DDTI dataset contains 347 images from 299 patients, and the local clinical dataset contains 4,598 images from 116 patients. While five-fold patient-level cross-validation is used to prevent leakage, the effective validation set per fold is approximately 60–70 images for DDTI and approximately 23 patients for the local dataset. The AUC standard deviations of ±6.77 (DDTI) and ±6.95 (local) reflect this limited sample size and indicate that performance estimates are not stable across folds. For a malignancy classification system intended for clinical use, validation on 100+ independent test cases would be a more credible basis for clinical conclusions. Furthermore, neither dataset constitutes a prospective or multi-center cohort. 2.Hyperparameter sensitivity is not analyzed. The model involves several hyperparameters with non-trivial impact on performance: the DSC threshold (0.8) that triggers the loss re-weighting stage transition, the two sets of loss weights (α, β, γ, γ_seg, γ_cls) for each training phase, and the contrastive temperature τ = 0.5.The paper states these were “chosen empirically on the validation folds,” but no sensitivity analysis is provided. It is not clear whether the reported performance gains are robust to moderate perturbations of these values, or whether they depend critically on the specific configuration. A brief sensitivity sweep over at least the DSC threshold and τ would strengthen the reproducibility and robustness claims. 3.Performance on the local dataset shows non-negligible DSC degradation relative to the best baseline. On the local clinical dataset, IC-MTL achieves DSC 87.77%, whereas He et al. achieves DSC 88.28%. While the paper characterizes this difference as “marginal,” it is worth noting that the local dataset represents a more challenging real-world setting (acquired from video sequences, different scanner characteristics, independent clinical site), and that the segmentation branch in IC-MTL is jointly optimized with classification, which may introduce trade-offs. A more detailed analysis of the cases where IC-MTL’s segmentation falls behind — e.g., whether these are systematically the difficult malignant nodules with irregular boundaries — would inform the clinical interpretation. 4.No investigation of the interaction between CI and different encoder architectures. All experiments use the same shared encoder backbone. The generalizability of the CI mechanism across different encoder architectures (e.g., transformer-based vs. CNN-based encoders) is not assessed. As the field moves toward foundation model backbones for ultrasound, it would be valuable to know whether the gated residual CI operator remains effective when features are extracted from, e.g., a pretrained SAM or MedSAM encoder. 5.Code and data release is not planned. The paper does not mention any plan to release code or dataset. While the local clinical dataset cannot be released for privacy reasons, the code for IC-MTL should be made available for community use and reproducibility. The lack of a code release commitment limits the practical impact of this contribution. 6.The Grad-CAM visualizations in Figure 3b are presented on a small scale. The qualitative results in Figure 3b are presented at a resolution that makes it difficult to verify the claimed attention-boundary consistency improvements, particularly for the local dataset examples. Enlarged selected examples with clearer visual comparisons would substantially improve the interpretability of these qualitative results.
