title: Self-supervised Learning on Lingual Ultrasound Video Encodes Clinically Meaningful Articulatory Structure of Rhotic Production in Residual Speech Sound Disorder
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The integration of an adversarial speaker classifier into a BYOL framework is a practical and highly effective strategy to explicitly handle the high inter speaker variability inherent in pediatric ultrasound data. 2.The quantitative results are impressive. The proposed BYOL-VS significantly outperforms strong SOTA baselines like VideoMAE and RESA on both downstream classification tasks using a simple k-NN probe. 3.The qualitative analysis is a strong point, particularly the extraction of mean tongue contours from the learned clusters (Figure 3). This provides excellent clinical interpretability, validating that the representations capture true, recognizable articulatory geometry.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The downstream evaluation relies entirely on k-NN probing of the frozen representations. Providing results with standard linear probing or end-to-end finetuning would give a more comprehensive picture of the embeddings utility for standard clinical pipelines. 2.The ablation study primarily focuses on the adversarial weight (\lambda_{grl}). Additional ablations on the choice of the spatiotemporal encoder itself (e. g. , comparing ViViT against standard 3D CNNs) would help isolate the specific contributions of the transformer backbone. While the PERCEPT-US dataset is large for this specific domain, the paper does not extensively detail the demographic distribution of the 70 child speakers. It remains somewhat unclear how well the model might generalize to different age groups (e. g. , adults) or more diverse clinical populations. 4.As the authors briefly acknowledge in the conclusion, speech production is inherently multimodal. The current framework relies solely on ultrasound video, missing out on synchronized acoustic signals that could provide strong supervisory signals for disambiguating articulatory shapes.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper targets a highly specific and valuable clinical application: evaluating distinct articulatory strategies (e.g., retroflex vs. bunched) that produce perceptually equivalent rhotic sounds, which is notoriously difficult in clinical practice. The use of the PERCEPT-US corpus represents a strong empirical foundation, as it provides a large-scale, expert-labeled resource for within-rhotic child ultrasound analysis. The proposed method achieved high classification accuracy (mean 0.974 for accuracy, 0.961 for rhotic subtype) purely through a k-nearest neighbor probe without task-specific encoder fine-tuning, demonstrating the quality of learned representations.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.From a methodological standpoint, the paper is primarily an application-driven integration of existing techniques. It concatenates BYOL, ViViT, and a standard gradient reversal layer for domain adaptation (speaker adversarial network). It lacks a fundamental algorithmic innovation specifically tailored to the physics or dynamics of tongue ultrasound imaging. 2.The abstract highlights the ability to perform downstream tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. However, the Method section (Section 2) completely omits how the downstream classification is technically executed. The reader only discovers in the Experiments section (Section 3) that a kNN probe is utilized. This disrupts the logical flow and clarity of the proposed framework. 3.The experimental setup reveals critical inconsistencies in hyperparameter tuning across the compared state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. For instance, VideoMAE uses a batch size of 32, while BYOL and BYOL-VS use 16.Learning rates also vary significantly ($1 \times 10^{-4}$ vs $2 \times 10^{-4}$). These discrepancies severely undermine the fairness of the benchmark comparisons. 4.The evaluation is restricted to only two SSL baselines (VideoMAE and RESA). A broader comparison with other contemporary temporal/video SSL frameworks would better substantiate the superiority of BYOL-VS.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is well-written and technically solid. The authors clearly explain their methods and the experimental setup appears to be correct. The inclusion of the speaker adversarial approach seems to yield considerable performance gains on the downstream task and also demonstrates how it improves the embedding space.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The medical application is unclear or not properly motivated. I’m not an expert in linguistics, so I can’t comprehend how important rhotic analysis is, but it seems the proposed approach addresses a very specific component of the English language, even though speech development also concerns the correct production of plosives and even vowels. Although I believe the same architecture could be easily extended to other phonemic groups. To me, it is still unclear why speaker-dependent information should be suppressed. If the idea is to build a system that ultimately would support speech therapy, so shouldn’t the model be adapted to the speaker? The ablation study shows that suppressing some of the information improves performance in the downstream tasks. I think some clarification is needed. It’s not explained in the paper in what context the rothic sounds are analyzed. I suppose there is a specific speech elicitation task, and rhotics are extracted from specific words, but the paper doesn’t clarify where. I’m asking because the context of the frames is 12, so I wonder if you actually catch enough articulatory movement in such a short context to properly analyze articulatory problems. Regarding the methods, I wonder why the authors did not try to incorporate other methods such as MoCo, SimCLR, or DINO? Also, I wonder if the speaker adversarial actually improves the performance so much, wouldn’t this also improve the performance of the other methods?
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their feedback and respond as follows. The addressed points will be clarified in the final version. Meta C1, Novelty: Our core contribution is meaningful to MICCAI. Although BYOL, ViViT, and GRL are established components, our integration of them is tailored to lingual ultrasound via spatiotemporal modeling, anatomically constrained augmentations, speaker-adversarial regularization, and speaker-disjoint evaluation to assess generalization. The careful design outperforms existing methods and recovers clinically interpretable embeddings. This is the first SSL study for within-rhotic articulatory structure and for using the newly curated PERCEPT-US, the largest American English child speech corpus. Our work contributes to the translational goal of an accessible, take-home speech therapy system. Meta C2, Benchmark: Based on our initial experiments, GRL is not BYOL-specific: adding GRL to VideoMAE and RESA improves mean ACC by 2–3% and mean MCC by 7–9%. The paper only reported BYOL-VS not VideoMAE/RESA + GRL, because it gives the best results, and its BYOL backbone has already beaten VideoMAE and RESA on our data. We only consider VideoMAE/RESA/BYOL as baselines rather than MoCo/SimCLR/DINO because pair construction for contrastive methods (MoCo/SimCLR) is hard for sensitive articulatory data (papers [4][11]), and RESA is already a SOTA baseline that outperforms MoCo, DINO, SimCLR, and 8 others in clustering and downstream classification (paper [21]). R1 C1, Probing: We only reported kNN due to page limit. In our initial experiments, linear probing result is directionally consistent but smaller in values, where BYOL-VS is still the best in both tasks (mean ACC = 0.793 & 0.753, mean MCC = 0.657 & 0.558; cf. Table 1). Finetuning is excluded as our goal tests whether SSL yields clinically useful, annotation-free representations. R1 C2, Ablation: Due to page limit, we only include the key ablation: whether adversarial regularization encourages interpretable embeddings. We use ViViT as vision transformers have shown better performance than CNN-based models in literature (paper [2]). R1 C3, Scope: PERCEPT-US targets the children population central to RSSD therapy: ages 8–17, sampled from CT/NJ/NY and balanced by sex and age (see paper [5]). It is the largest child speech corpus with ultrasound data for this clinical aim. Thus, findings should generalize to the target children population, while extension to adults requires further validation. R1 C4, Multimodal: Multimodal alignment with acoustics is the next step. An ultrasound-only model is the necessary first step to confirm that the learned representations encode tongue-shape structure needed for visual biofeedback. R2 C1, Novelty: See Meta C1. R2 C2, Protocol: We will revise Section 2 to explicitly describe the downstream evaluation protocol. R2 C3, Fairness: All models used the same 5-fold CV protocol and comprehensive search space (e.g. LR 0.0001–0.0005; BS 2–256). Reported settings are each model’s best validation configuration. R2 C4, Benchmark: See Meta C2. R3 C1, Motivation: In the U.S., the American English rhotic sound is the highest prevalence therapy target in older children (Farquharson et al, 2026, CLP). This combined with SLP staffing shortages and heavy caseloads (ASHA 2024 Schools Survey) motivates our project. R3 C2, Speaker: The motivation is to prevent models from exploiting speaker-specific artifacts over articulatory subtypes. The ablation study shows that moderate regularization improves performance and embedding separability, but excessive suppression leads to degradation. R3 C3, Context: The task is syllable repetition: 15 syllables, repeated 3 times, spanning consonantal r (e.g. ‘ru’), coda/vocalic r (e.g. ‘ear’), syllabic r (e.g. ‘er’), and vowel contexts. Productions are 50–60ms; 12 frames capture suffice rhotic movement while limiting neighboring coarticulatory influence (paper [5]). R3 C4, Benchmark: See Meta C2.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend rebuttal, broadly consistent with the reviewer signal (4, 4, 3 — two Weak Accepts and one Weak Reject). Per MICCAI guidelines, the strict “all ≥4” rule for early accept is not satisfied (R3 = 3), so rebuttal is the appropriate choice rather than early accept. The paper proposes BYOL-VS, a self-supervised framework for lingual ultrasound video built from BYOL + ViViT spatiotemporal encoder + a gradient-reversal speaker-adversarial branch, and evaluated on PERCEPT-US for two clinically meaningful tasks: rhotic perceptual accuracy (correct vs incorrect) and within-rhotic subtype (retroflex vs bunched). Speaker-disjoint 5-fold CV is correctly enforced. Paper-level inspection confirms two real strengths that justify reconsideration after rebuttal: (1) The empirical gains are unusually large. (2) The qualitative validation is genuinely interpretable. Spectral clustering of frozen embeddings yields cluster-mean tongue contours that match expert-traced ground truth (Fig. 3 right) with low RMSE. However, the paper has two issues that the rebuttal must address before acceptance: (a) Methodological novelty is integrative. BYOL + ViViT + GRL are all standard, off-the-shelf components; there is no domain-specific algorithmic modification. (b) Only VideoMAE and RESA are compared as video-SSL baselines. There is no MoCo/SimCLR/DINO comparison and no apples-to-apples test where the speaker-adversarial GRL branch is added to a baseline. | I recommend accept. In essence, BYOL-VS (BYOL + ViViT + speaker-adversarial GRL) achieves unusually strong empirical results on lingual ultrasound video for residual speech sound disorder, with interpretable cluster-mean tongue contours that match expert tracings and a complete ablation study supporting the design, justifying acceptance over R3’s lowest-confidence concern on novelty/baseline breadth, Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although the technical contribution of the paper is limited, it targets a clinically important problem of articulatory structure learning from lingual ultrasound videos for children with speech sound disorders. The paper presents a BYOL style SSL approach, making it label efficient and generalizable. The paper should be of interest to the MICCAI community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend Accept. The paper studies a narrow but well-defined clinical problem: learning ultrasound video representations for rhotic production in children with residual speech sound disorder. The method is not a new SSL objective. It combines BYOL, a video transformer encoder, and a speaker-adversarial branch. The value of the paper is that this combination matches a real structure in the data: tongue motion should be retained, while speaker-specific ultrasound variation should be reduced. The empirical results support this design. BYOL-VS performs well with a frozen encoder and a simple kNN probe, which suggests that the representation itself carries useful articulatory information. The cluster analysis is also helpful. The recovered mean tongue contours are not just performance numbers; they show that the embedding separates recognizable rhotic tongue shapes. This makes the result easier to interpret clinically. The original concerns were fair. The method has limited algorithmic novelty, the first version did not describe the downstream kNN protocol clearly enough, and the baseline comparison needed more explanation because the training settings differed across methods. The rebuttal addresses these points sufficiently for me. Broader SSL baselines and linear-probe or finetuning results would still make the paper stronger, but they are not necessary for acceptance here. I therefore support acceptance. The paper is application-driven, but the application is specific, the nuisance factor is handled in a direct way, and the learned representations show both quantitative and anatomical evidence of usefulness.

title: Self-supervised Spline Autoencoder for Smooth Latent Dynamics in Echocardiography
reviewer_1_strengths: The main strengths of the paper are the relevance of the problem, the coherent methodological pipeline, and the zero-shot evaluation on pediatric echocardiography. In particular, the idea of combining smooth spline-based latent trajectories with a dynamical phase discovery procedure is conceptually clear and reasonably well motivated. The zero-shot transfer results across populations and views are also a positive aspect of the experimental evaluation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: While the latent trajectory learning and phase discovery stages are unsupervised, the final ED/ES semantic assignment uses a global ED–ES alignment axis computed from training-set ED and ES embeddings, which relies on label information. The paper’s technical description could also be improved. For example, the encoder architecture is not described clearly enough in the main text, which weakens reproducibility. Finally, although the results are competitive, the gain over the strongest prior unsupervised baseline is limited. author_feedback: We are grateful for the valuable feedback from all reviewers. We respond to the suggestions and concerns below: (R1/R2/R3) Unsupervised claim and paper positioning We agree that wording around “unsupervised” should be framed more cautiously. While SplineAE training and localizing trajectory extrema are label-free, resolving the semantic ambiguity of ED/ES on detected extrema requires label information. We clarify that there is no fine-tuning or gradient-based optimization on labels. Instead, we compute the sign of the dot product between the extrema axis and the training-set global ED/ES axis, as described in Section 2.3. Our intended contribution is primarily representational, as described in Section 1: Our self-supervised SplineAE discovers low-rank loop-like latent dynamics from echocardiography. Moreover, instead of enforcing a fixed 2D latent bottleneck [15] or explicit periodicity constraints [6], we rely only on temporal smoothness and consistency. Label-free latent geometry discovery of cardiac phase is supported by topology analysis, qualitative observation of latent loops, cardiac event localization, and zero-shot pediatric transfer. ED/ES detection is a downstream task to evaluate clinical relevance of learnt representations. To reflect this positioning, we will rephrase the title to: “Self-supervised Spline Autoencoder for Smooth Latent Dynamics in Echocardiography”. We will revise the wording of manuscript content accordingly, to clearly explain self-supervised training, label-agnostic phase extraction with event localization, and label-informed ED/ES semantic assignment. (R1) Performance margin and ES error In addition to relaxed constraints during representation learning, our label-free localization performance is competitive. Localization error is equal to pooled error with perfect ED/ES labelling. Meanwhile, ED/ES MAE degradation are caused by semantic label flips after otherwise accurate localization, where errors are as large as the ED-ES interval. (R2/R3) Failure case We observe localization failure when a coherent latent loop does not emerge, often in low-quality videos with chambers moving out of view. Pediatric PSAX ED/ES MAE rises due to the 10% reduction in label assignment accuracy from A4C, as semantic directions in latent space may shift with view. However, the label-agnostic localization derived from trajectory geometry remains stable, as the MAE remains at 3.0 frames. (R2/R3) Hyperparameter choices Cubic splines balance smoothness and expressivity, while nctrl=16 for 64-frame partitions, approximately 1 control point per 4 frames, captures curvature without fitting frame-level noise. K=15 empirically balances preserving cross-cycle semantic neighbours against over-connecting temporally adjacent samples, which depends partly on frame rate. We clarify that splines are only used in training; inference uses encoder embeddings directly in Algorithm 1. (R1) Reproducibility The full architecture and implementation will be included in the code repository release. Briefly, the encoder uses residual blocks [3×3 conv, GroupNorm, GELU, 3×3 conv], with 2 residual blocks before each downsampling stage, and 5 such stages before average pooling. (R2) Nearest-hit localization The reviewer’s interpretation is correct. This protocol follows LMP [15] for EchoNet Dynamic under the same sparse-label limitation, so the comparison is like-to-like. Qualitative inspection of videos and Fig.3 suggest that our method aligns trajectory extrema to ED/ES events without dense over-prediction. (R3) Other concerns We reported mean±SD, that could be reported as 95CI for clarity. Cross-partitions are mutually exclusive if the video is longer than 127 frames, but may randomly overlap if the video is too short. We also hypothesize that model errors or geometry irregularities may correlate with clinical pathologies. However, the EchoNet datasets lack pathology labels. We believe this is an important direction for future work.

reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper proposes a self-supervised temporal regularization framework that improves the temporal consistency of cardiac segmentation and motion estimation without requiring frame-by-frame annotations. 2.The method leverages the learned anatomical correspondences to automatically map landmarks to the AHA 17-segment clinical standard, which supports standardized regional analysis and improves the clinical interpretability of the model. 3.The paper introduces a jitter metric to quantify the temporal regularity of landmark trajectories, which is used to capture high-frequency perturbations in motion trajectories.

author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for recognizing the conceptual clarity [R2], translational potential [R2, R3], and the relevance of our self-supervised temporal regularization [R1, R3]. All reviewers highlighted the AHA regional mapping as a major strength [R1, R2, R3], alongside our Jitter metric [R3] and the potential to quantify clinical biomarkers [R2]. SELF-SUPERVISION [R3]: Apologies for the confusion caused to R3 about the first training stage using T independently annotated frames (R3 comment 7.4). Confusion was caused by a typo duplicating the variable T in Sec. 2.2 Training Procedure. The refinement objective L_refine is composite. Each iteration first processes N independent annotated ED/ES frames to compute the spatial loss L_base, which anchors the model and prevents collapse to a trivial zero-velocity solution. In a second stage, T consecutive unannotated frames are used to compute temporal losses L_vel and L_accel self-supervisedly, since no GT masks are used in this temporal regularization step. METHODOLOGICAL NOVELTY & CLINICAL UTILITY [R2, R3]: [R3] describes AHA mapping as an “engineering application.” We clarify that it is enabled by our methodological contribution: integrating implicit anatomical correspondences with temporal regularization. Unlike pixel-based models such as nnU-Net, which lack inherent anatomical consistency, our graph-based approach tracks the same anatomical points throughout the cardiac cycle. The node-to-AHA mapping is computed once on a population-averaged reference atlas and propagated across sequences (Sec. 2.3). Mask-based methods require ad-hoc frame-wise partitioning, which reduces temporal consistency and produces noisier motion traces. As [R2] notes, our mapping bridges algorithmic outputs and clinically interpretable standards. BASELINES & EVALUATION METRICS [R1, R3]: [R1, R3] question the nnU-Net comparison. Because temporal consistency is difficult to compare between landmark- and pixel-based methods, we generated “pseudo-landmarks” from nnU-Net masks via post-processing; otherwise, temporal quality could not be assessed. Direct comparison is limited by the lack of echo-video segmentation methods with implicit anatomical correspondences. We will cite [Tziritas 2024, Wu 2023] for context and correct the typo in Ref. [14]. Regarding metrics [R1], standard Dice/HD95 assess static quality but cannot quantify temporal jitter or motion smoothness. In the absence of standard temporal-consistency metrics, we use Jitter, FTD, and Jerk to quantify high-frequency disturbances and physics-based motion, clinically critical aspects common metrics ignore. DATASET AND GENERALIZATION [R1, R2, R3]: [R3] notes the use of a single dataset. CAMUS is currently the only public 2D echo dataset with both A2C/A4C views and epicardial/endocardial contours, which are required to use AHA segments. Other datasets, like EchoNet-Dynamic, lack myocardial masks, limiting their usefulness. We are working with the TED dataset [R1] as a CAMUS subcohort to further validate temporal consistency. Regarding robustness [R2], Fig. 3 includes both low-EF and normal patients; the final manuscript will clarify this and stratify existing results by CAMUS quality scores and risk. We will mention in future works that we will consider temporally labeled data (as TED) and extend regional strain analysis to hypokinesis and dyssynchrony detection. REPRODUCIBILITY [R2]: For hyperparameters [R2], a linear scheduler (0.01 to 0.001) was used for λ_v and λ_a, training over 500k iterations (~600 epochs). T was set to 20 random continuous frames per batch due to 24GB NVIDIA RTX 3090 limits. Code, optimized hyperparameters, and a demo will be released with camera-ready version to ensure full reproducibility. SUMMARY: Our self-supervised, temporally stable tool provides anatomically consistent regional tracking that pixel-wise methods cannot, supporting MICCAI’s translational goals through clinically interpretable myocardial motion analysis.

title: Shape-Aware Registration Without Pretraining: CT-Ultrasound Bone Surface Alignment via Instance-Level Shape Completion
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper is well written and the proposed method is explained clearly. This is a well reasoned method for bone alignment that promises to enhance surgical navigation. The method archives better accuracy than RANSCAC-based alignment procedures.

The authors make a point that such models require paired ultrasound-CT data in a large number of subjects for training, and don’t generalize to new bone structures. No empirical evidence for this lack of generalization is offered. At the same time, the authors rely on the shape completion methods that might also fail for more complex bones, such as vertebrae and ribs. So the advantages of the proposed approach are not clearly demonstrated. reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: Dear reviewers, Thank you for very positive (R3), positive (R1, R4), and constructive reviews (R2). Regarding RRE standard deviation (SD) and resulting clinical reliability (R2): R2 identified this as the primary reason for rejection, and we appreciate to provide a more detailed analysis and concrete manuscript additions that we hope fully addresses this concern. The RRE percentiles are 0.30° (5%), 1.47° (25%), 2.55° (50%), 4.06° (75%), and 10.92° (95%), showing low RRE in the majority of runs. An in-depth analysis reveals that the large SD stems primarily from rare flip cases (~1.46% of runs). Due to long-bone symmetry, shape completion can flip to the opposite cortical side or wrong proximal-distal direction, producing flipped registration and ~180° RRE. Evaluation without flip cases reduces RRE SD from ~19° to ~8°. We believe that this is acceptable for pre-clinical work, given the pressing clinical need and the inherent challenges of ultrasound (US) data collection. Flip cases are a detectable failure mode rather than a general registration instability that we can address through shape priors or flip-consistency checks in future work. We will report these observations and statistics, as well as discuss flip cases explicitly as a limitation that can motivate future MICCAI research. Regarding population-scale learning and the concern that n=14 is not “large” (R2): We acknowledge that the “large” vs. “limited” framing needs more justification and want to emphasize that our argument is about annotation feasibility, not clinical coverage. Annotation remains the bottleneck for robust US-based registration. First, expert annotation of one US slice takes several minutes, making population-level annotation across anatomies and pathologies not only costly but infeasible. Second, UltraBones100k is, to our knowledge, the only approach providing automatic annotations. However, it does not scale to different anatomies, pathologies, or in-vivo settings, as it requires very costly cadaveric experiments (~$30,000 for 14 specimens). Thus, n=14 is not large for population-level learning, but reflects the current practical ceiling of annotation infrastructure. This motivates our patient-specific formulation which adapts to the target bone model using synthetic US, avoiding dependence on unavailable large annotated datasets. We will rename the table settings from “patients” to “annotations”, using full annotations (n=14), limited annotations (n=5), and instance-based and will explain that the annotation bottleneck is a fundamental infrastructural limitation making population-scale supervision currently out of reach. Regarding segmentation quality, noise modeling, and generalizability (R3/R4): We agree that advanced noise modeling and US simulation could further improve robustness and generalizability, and will describe them as future work in the revision. We will also weaken broad generalization claims. Although our method is anatomically agnostic in principle, cross-anatomy generalization remains untested, what we will state as a limitation. Regarding methodological novelty (R1/R4): MICCAI guidelines explicitly state that “a novel algorithm is only one of many ways to contribute” and that “an application of existing methods to a new problem” constitutes a valid contribution. Our main contribution is a novel CAI formulation for a relevant clinical problem. Beyond known components, the paper contributes joint end-to-end optimization of completion and registration under partial US observations, differentiable ICP embedded in the learning pipeline, and patient-specific self-supervised US simulation that adapts to each preoperative bone while avoiding paired CT-US training data entirely. We will clarify this positioning in the Introduction. Finally, we will add RANSAC details (R2), clarify training from scratch and patient-specific training/inference (R4), report runtime/hardware, and add US simulation references (R3).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a unified framework for CT–ultrasound bone surface registration that jointly performs shape completion and rigid alignment, leveraging patient-specific synthetic ultrasound simulation to address the scarcity of paired data. The work is positioned in a clinically relevant CAI setting, with an emphasis on robustness under partial observations and efficiency at inference time. The paper is well motivated and addresses an important problem in computer-assisted surgery. Its associated strengths include: (i) the joint optimisation of shape completion and registration, which provides a coherent alternative to multi-stage pipelines; (ii) the use of patient-specific synthetic data to alleviate limited data constraints; (iii) promising runtime characteristics compatible with intraoperative use; and (iv) generally clear writing and structured presentation. However, consistent limitations have been raised by the reviewers. The primary concern is about the reported results. Indeed, the comparison to learning-based baseline is not convincing, and the justification might overlook some limitations of the proposed method in terms of generalisation. Moreover, large standard deviations raise serious concerns about potential instability (including catastrophic failures) that limit clinical reliability. I would also like to add that no statistical testing is performed whatsoever. Another weakness is the limited methodological novelty, with the framework largely integrating existing components rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques. Finally, other concerns include missing details about baselines, overstatements, studying the impact of erroneous input segmentations, evaluation limited to one dataset, missing citations, and commenting on generalisation issues. Overall, this CAI paper presents a well-motivated method with practical advantages. However, the authors need to address important concerns raised about comparison to learning-based methods, robustness, and clarifications of many issues. | The authors have convincingly answered concerns about the size of the test dataset (very expensive) and why they haven’t tested on other organs (organ-specific problem). In my opinion, they also addressed concerns about novelty, by introducing a framework that takes on a problem with a new, promising technique. Finally, they have clarified a few methodological points, and agreed to soften the unsupported generalisation claims. However, the main concern about empirical results remains unconvincingly addressed. The authors claim that the much larger standard deviations obtained by their method wrt previous works primarily stem from an easily detectable failure mode. However, when they remain the corresponding cases, the std devs remain at a much higher level wrt other baselines (8 vs. 1.12 degrees). This adds up to mean scores that are on average worse than the baselines (2.93 vs. 1.43 degrees). Thus, evaluation results do not support gains in terms of accuracy or robustness. Overall, this CAI paper is borderline accept/reject. Despite the limited empirical gains, I still recommend acceptance (in agreement with 3 out of 4 reviewers) due to the interesting proposed framework and the discussions it will foster at MICCAI during a CAI session. I also strongly encourage the authors to add the much needed statistical tests. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This is a very painful decision to me as the idea and the clinical problem are both very good. After a very careful consideration, I believe the present shape of the manuscript can’t support its headline claims. This is intraoperative ultrasound to preoperative CT bone registration, and it trains without a costly paired CT-US dataset, which is a real strength. But the paper fails on one hard point. Its selling claim is that it is “more robust,” yet its own Table 1 reports a rotation error of 2.93 +/-19.98 degrees against the baseline’s 1.43 +/- 1.12.The mean is worse and the standard deviation is about ten times larger, which means the method breaks down badly on a real share of cases. On top of that, there is no significance test anywhere in the paper. The rebuttal says most of that huge spread comes from about 1.46 percent of “symmetry flip” failures, and that removing them brings the std down to about 8 degrees. But that analysis is not in the submitted paper, so under MICCAI no-new-experiment rule I do not credit it. Even if I did, 8 degrees still loses badly to the baseline’s 1.12, so the “more robust” claim is still false. The present results cannot prove a method is reliable by deleting its own failure cases. The two Faculty reviewers who read the original table were not convinced, while the two who scored it high never addressed the variance problem at all. So this is the submission failing on its own evidence, not the rule blocking it. The headline claim is contradicted by its own data, and nothing is backed by statistics, which puts it below the MICCAI bar. I do want to encourage the direction, and the quick fix is cheap: drop the overclaim, disclose the symmetry-flip failure mode, and run a significance test on the results they already have. As a result the decision is reject, but with strong encouragement to resubmit a clean version to top tier confs and journals. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This submission proposes a joint shape completion and registration framework for CT-ultrasound bone alignment. R3 and R4 liked the clinically relevance. R1 and R2 noted a limited methodological novelty and high error variance. The rebuttal has successfully clarified that the standard deviations mostly comes from rare symmetrical flip bones, justifying their limited dataset size. Consensus is on a possible clinical impact, despite limited novelty. For all these reasons, and with respect ot the other submissions, the recommendation is towards Acceptance.

reviewer_3_strengths: (1) Strong clinical motivation and concept-driven design. The paper addresses an important problem—improving interpretability in fetal ultrasound standard plane classification, where clinical trust is essential. The proposed framework introduces anatomically meaningful concepts and models their spatial relationships via a graph structure, aligning well with clinical reasoning and going beyond pixel-level explanations. (2) Comprehensive evaluation and clinical utility. The method is validated through a multi-level evaluation protocol, including multi-center datasets, perturbation-based fidelity analysis, and a blinded expert user study, which strengthens the empirical evidence. Additionally, the framework provides concept-level explanations and failure-aware signals, enhancing its potential clinical usability and trustworthiness.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: (1) Limited novelty with respect to prior work. While the paper is well-motivated, the overall research direction is not entirely novel. Prior studies have explored concept-based interpretability and graph-based reasoning in medical imaging, including works that integrate anatomical concepts with graph neural networks for ultrasound plane analysis (e.g., A Cognitive Explainer for Fetal Ultrasound Image Classification Based on Medical Concepts and Concept-Induced Graph Perception Model for Interpretable Diagnosis). In this context, the core idea of combining concept extraction with GCN-based relational modeling has already been investigated, suggesting that the current work represents an incremental extension rather than a fundamentally new contribution. (2) A key limitation of SONIC is its strong reliance on manually defined anatomical concepts, which limits generalizability. First, it strongly depends on accurate ROI localization and segmentation. Since the pipeline begins with U-Net-based ROI extraction, failures at this stage—such as under poor image quality, extreme fetal poses, or abnormalities—can propagate through the pipeline, causing cascading errors in concept extraction and graph reasoning. Second, the concept extraction process requires manual intervention. As noted in Section 2.1, sub-region-to-concept pairings must be manually verified to remove incorrect matches, meaning the framework is not fully end-to-end. This reliance on expert input introduces scalability challenges and high annotation costs, making the approach less practical for large-scale or multi-task deployment. (3) Another limitation of SONIC is its complex multi-stage pipeline, which introduces cumulative error propagation. The framework consists of sequential components—ROI segmentation, superpixel generation, concept matching, and graph-based reasoning—where each stage is susceptible to its own errors. As these components are tightly coupled, inaccuracies in earlier steps can propagate and amplify through the pipeline, ultimately degrading the final prediction. This design increases the system’s sensitivity to intermediate failures and raises concerns about its robustness in real-world settings. (4) There is a lack of analysis on real-time performance and engineering complexity. The multi-stage pipeline—CNN, concept matching, GCN, and attribution—may introduce non-trivial inference overhead, yet no latency or resource metrics are reported. This raises concerns about its suitability for real-time ultrasound workflows, especially for continuous video analysis.

title: Structure-Aware Sensorless 3D Ultrasound and Photoacoustic Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: A. Important and clinically relevant problem Sensorless freehand 3D reconstruction is practically important because removing external trackers improves workflow simplicity, cost, and compatibility. That is a meaningful direction for both US and PA, especially for handheld scanning and procedural settings. B. Good problem framing around modality-specific failure modes A real strength is that the paper is not just “another motion estimator,” but explicitly frames the challenge around physical degradation mechanisms: decorrelating US speckle, cluttered PA patterns, out-of-plane motion, and probe compression. That framing is well aligned with the real problem and makes the method design more coherent. C. Cross-modality evaluation is valuable Testing on both US and PA is stronger than a single-modality paper. The US dataset is reasonably large (50 subjects / 1200 scan sequences per the paper), and the PA experiment is valuable because PA tracking is harder and less explored than standard B-mode US. Even if the architectural novelty is somewhat incremental, showing one method that transfers across these two domains is useful. D. The paper appears to improve long-range stability, not just local pose The reported gains are not only on local relative errors but also on more reconstruction-relevant metrics such as ATE, final drift, and FDR. That is the right direction for this problem, because in tracker-free 3D reconstruction the real bottleneck is accumulated drift over long trajectories. E. Practical significance of hardware-free PA reconstruction The strongest application-level point is the demonstration of purely image-based 3D PA reconstruction of palm vasculature without external tracking hardware. Prior literature has already extended freehand reconstruction to PA/PAUS settings, especially MoGLo-Net, but this remains a valuable demonstration because PA tracking is particularly difficult due to sparse vessels and clutter.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: A. The technical novelty looks limited / highly compositional The paper’s main modules appear to be built from already familiar ideas: the channel decoupling block is very close in spirit to SE-style channel attention, i. e. global pooling plus learned channel reweighting; the masked cross-attention idea is explicitly inspired by MAE and CroCo/cross-view completion; the motion-modulated loss resembles prior motion-weighted training losses already used in tracker-free US reconstruction, e. g. RecON. So the paper may be better described as a domain-tailored combination of existing mechanisms rather than a strongly new formulation. B. Novelty relative to prior tracker-free US literature is not fully convincing: The paper positions itself against “coarse-grained macro features,” but several recent works already addressed long-range dependency, sequence modeling, motion-aware learning, or stronger feature interactions in tracker-free US reconstruction. Examples include LongTerm for long-range dependency modeling, physics-guided deep learning for sensorless end-to-end reconstruction, and RecON for online/self-supervised refinement with motion-weighted losses. Because of this, the paper’s advance feels more incremental than foundational. C. The “PA novelty” claim should be stated more carefully The paper suggests novelty around applying 3D reconstruction to PA, prior study such as MoGLo-Net already studied freehand 3D photoacoustic and ultrasound reconstruction and explicitly reported PA/vasculature visualization. That means the claim should be narrowed to something like pure-PA tracking without auxiliary modalities/hardware, if that is what the authors truly mean. As written, the novelty statement risks overstating the case. D. Missing or insufficient ablation evidence This is the biggest experimental weakness for me. A paper with several components should show: SACD on/off masking on/off cross-attention on/off MMAE vs MAE bidirectional/self-supervised training on/off maybe US-only training vs cross-domain generalization Without these, it is hard to know which component actually matters and whether the gain comes mostly from architecture scale or training details. E. Limited detail on fairness / reproducibility The paper says comparisons are under “identical experimental settings,” but it is not fully clear whether all baselines were retrained with matched data augmentation, sequence length, curriculum, and hyperparameters. For a benchmark-heavy paper, that matters.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Structure-Aware Channel Decoupling (SACD) module: This component uses global spatial statistics to assess the temporal stability of feature channels, adaptively down-weighting those dominated by unstable acoustic patterns (e.g., US speckle decorrelation, PA clutter) and up-weighting channels encoding stable anatomical structures. This is novel because it explicitly decouples physical noise from useful structural information at the feature level, rather than relying on implicit learning alone. Cross-Attention mechanism with masked feature modeling: Unlike prior works that may overfit to local textures, the authors employ a low-ratio masked feature strategy in the latent space, forcing the network to recover missing information via global spatio-temporal context. This encourages robust, generalizable spatial correspondences across frames, which is especially important in the presence of motion and noise. The combination of these elements forms a new, principled approach to handling the specific physical degradations of freehand US/PA imaging. 2.Original Use of Data and Problem Setting​ The work is the first to demonstrate high-fidelity sensorless 3D reconstruction entirely in the pure photoacoustic domain, a much more challenging setting than ultrasound due to severe acoustic clutter and sparse vascular cross-sectional features. The authors also curate and utilize two large-scale, clinically realistic datasets: A forearm US dataset​ with diverse trajectories (straight, C-shape, S-shape) and scanning directions, including forward/backward and parallel/perpendicular motions. A palm PA dataset​ with reciprocating scanning paths, requiring stitching of multiple short trajectories. The use of these varied, unconstrained real-world sequences tests the method’s generalization far beyond controlled lab conditions. 3.Strong and Comprehensive Evaluation​ The evaluation includes multiple complementary metrics: relative translation error (RTE), relative rotation error (RRE), absolute trajectory error (ATE), final drift rate (FDR), and—for the complex PA data—the Fréchet distance (F-Dist) to assess curve similarity independent of speed. Results show consistent, statistically significant improvements: 13.72% reduction in final drift rate​ and 14.29% reduction in ATE​ on the US dataset compared to the best baseline. State-of-the-art performance on the PA dataset despite its inherent challenges. The analysis includes both quantitative tables​ and qualitative trajectory visualizations​ (Fig. 2), clearly illustrating how SCC-Net suppresses long-range drift in complex motion scenarios. 4.Clinical Feasibility Demonstration​ By achieving accurate 3D reconstruction without any external tracking hardware, the method offers a cost-effective, flexible solution compatible with a wide range of clinical environments. The ability to reconstruct large-scale vascular networks in PA without trackers highlights the potential for functional 3D imaging in interventional or point-of-care settings, where external sensors are impractical. 5.Innovative Training Strategy​ The progressive joint optimization​ approach combines: A temporal triplet loss​ to enforce smooth, physically plausible feature evolution. A Motion-Modulated Mean Absolute Error (MMAE) loss​ that dynamically emphasizes high-motion regions during training, improving accuracy where errors are most likely to accumulate. This two-stage training, along with bidirectional sequence self-supervision, mitigates directional bias and enhances long-range stability, which is often a weak point in prior sensorless methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Limited Innovation in Core Architectural Components​ The structure-aware channel decoupling (SACD) module​ builds directly on established channel attention mechanisms​ (e.g., Squeeze-and-Excitation Networks [10] and ECA-Net [23]), which are widely used in computer vision to recalibrate feature maps via global average/max pooling and learned gating. While the paper adapts this idea to filter unstable acoustic patterns, the novelty lies primarily in the application domain(US/PA imaging) rather than the fundamental formulation. Similarly, the cross-attention mechanism with masked feature modeling​ draws heavily from recent self-supervised learning paradigms, such as masked autoencoders [9] and cross-view feature completion [24]. The paper’s contribution is applying these ideas to spatio-temporal tracking in medical imaging, but the underlying methods are not new. Reference: [9] He et al., “Masked autoencoders are scalable vision learners” (CVPR 2022) [10] Hu et al., “Squeeze-and-excitation networks” (CVPR 2018) [23] Wang et al., “ECA-net: Efficient channel attention” (CVPR 2020) [24] Weinzaepfel et al., “Croco: Self-supervised pre-training for 3D vision” (NeurIPS 2022) 2.Incremental Improvement Over Recent Baselines​ The performance gains over prior methods (e.g., 13.72% reduction in final drift rate on the US dataset) are modest​ given the complexity of the problem. For example, the absolute trajectory error (ATE) of SCC-Net (21.53 mm) is only ~3.6 mm lower than MoGLo-Net (25.12 mm) on the US dataset, which may not translate to clinically significant differences in many applications. The paper does not compare against the most recent state-of-the-art methods (e.g., [26] Yan et al., 2024, which integrates multi-modal data and fine-grained context) in all experiments, limiting the comprehensiveness of the evaluation. Reference: [11] Lee et al., “Enhancing free-hand 3D photoacoustic and ultrasound reconstruction” (IEEE TMI 2025) [26] Yan et al., “Fine-grained context and multi-modal alignment” (MICCAI 2024)

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for recognizing the clinical relevance of sensorless US/PA reconstruction, the cross-modality evaluation, and the promising long-range stability. We address the main concerns below: 1.Fairness and protocol clarification (R1,R3). All results in Table 1 used the same split, data budget, augmentation policy, schedule, and evaluation protocol thus the gains do not come from longer training or more sampled data. The test set was not augmented: the “10 sequences” are temporal windows with different starting frames from the original scans, not image transformations. PA images received the same fixed brightness enhancement for all methods. We will clarify that the 5-frame input is a local motion window balancing temporal context and memory cost, not an optimality claim. We will also define H/W/C/D, anchors, latent features, stages, metrics, trajectory length, PA stitching, and Eq. 4 notation, and report p-values for existing runs. 2.Component effect and model capacity (R1,R4,AC). We appreciate the reviewers’ concern about component-level evidence. Since rebuttal guidelines do not allow additional experiments or substantial experimental changes, we focus here on the current evidence and design rationale. Table 1 provides a controlled full-model comparison under the same image-only setting and matched data traversal, directly evaluating accumulated drift. The observed gains are consistent with the intended role of each design: SACD preserves structure-related cues while reducing unstable responses from ultrasound speckle and photoacoustic artifacts,Latent masking reduces dependence on local textures,Cross-attention introduces neighboring-frame context, MMAE weights larger-motion samples and bidirectional learning reduces scan-direction bias. The gain is unlikely to come from model size, since our model uses a lightweight ConvLSTM and has 24.47M parameters, compared with 27.91M for MoGLo. Our variants are also close in size, from 24.30M to 24.47M. We will report model capacity and revise the module descriptions so that the claims remain aligned with the reported evidence. 3.Related work and comparison scope (R1,R2,R3,AC). We will better position our work with LongTerm, RecON, physics-guided reconstruction, and Yan et al. (FiMA). We do not claim a leaderboard ranking over tracker-free US literature, since methods differ in input modality, supervision, online refinement, or protocol. Table 1 instead provides a matched image-only comparison under the same split, data traversal, and training budget. FiMA uses ReMamba with multiple IMUs and multimodal alignment; including IMUs changes our setting, while removing them misrepresents FiMA. Thus, we do not claim superiority over FiMA. TUS-REC top entries use ensembles, pretraining, checkpoint averaging, and scan-direction/offset fusion; they are useful references, not direct competitors. 4.Novelty, PA claim, and clinical interpretation (R1,R2,R4,AC). We will make the novelty statement more precise. Some blocks relate to channel attention, masked feature learning, and bidirectional modeling. Our contribution is the task-specific organization of these designs for US/PA reconstruction under acoustic artifacts, local texture instability, and scan-direction bias. SACD will be described as motivated by ultrasound speckle and PA artifacts, not as proof of physical factor separation. The masking design is lightly inspired by CroCo and is not claimed as a new masking paradigm. Since MoGLo-Net has studied freehand PA/US reconstruction, our PA setting is pure image-based reconstruction without external tracking hardware or US structural priors. The ATE gap should be read with FDR and absolute errors under the same sampled data traversal and training budget, not as a standalone clinical margin. Our main claim is reduced drift and improved long-range stability in the image-only setting.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): The paper addresses the problem of sensorless freehand 3D reconstruction in ultrasound and photoacoustic imaging. The three reviewers acknowledge the relevance of the task and recognize some novelty in the proposed combination of blocks. The ability to perform well across modalities (ultrasound and photoacoustics) was welcomed, especially given the difficulty of the photoacoustic case. Experiments were conducted on several curated datasets (forearm, palm). Results reported across several metrics show improved long-range stability of pose estimation. The main drawbacks raised were the incremental novelty, the unclear improvement over the state-of-the-art tracker-free US literature, and a limited ablation study. Claims of novelty in photoacoustics should be tempered by acknowledging prior work. | The paper remains borderline after the rebuttal, with two acceptance and two rejection votes. The novelty is compositional but acknowledged, and generalization on two modalities is interesting. Several clarifications and indications to moderate certain claims have been addressed in the rebuttal. The rebuttal also explains how some of the related work being compared to had access to additional data or employed more complex post-processing strategies, which seems reasonable. The remaining remarks for R3 and R4 are the lack of an ablation study, and R3 also recalls a lack of clarity in their after-rebuttal comments. title: Toward Thyroid Cancer BRAF V600E Mutation Prediction via Multimodal Large Language Model: Dataset and Model Development
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The manuscript developed a valuable multimodal dataset for thyroid cancer BRAF V600E mutation prediction. The proposed dataset contains multimodal data, including ultrasound images, annotated tumor regions, ultrasound reports, BRAF mutation status, and clinicopathological records. 2.The dataset construction utilized LLM as a synthesis agent, which efficiently reduced human annotation effort.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Anywhere we can access the dataset? For the dataset articles, I strongly suggest that the authors include detailed information about dataset access in the article, or at least indicate whether the access link will be released in the future. 2.Missing single-modal baselines. I would suggest the author consider adding single-modal baselines in the future. It would be meaningful to first demonstrate that the multimodal method outperforms the unimodal baseline, then determine which type of multimodal method performs best. Otherwise, it is unclear whether the benefits come from multimodal data fusion or whether the unimodal baselines are good enough for BRAF prediction, while multimodal data fusion actually decreases the performance. 3.For dataset construction: (a) Could the author indicate the cost of using GPT-4o to synthesize and structure the raw data? It would be helpful for others to evaluate the cost of reproducing this dataset. (b) Are the LLM-synthesized ultrasound reports and clinicopathological information used directly for further model training? Could any data quality control and verification be considered to ensure the reliability of the data? 4.To better demonstrate the value of the dataset, I would expect a comprehensive evaluation across multiple VLMs rather than a single one. Ideally, the experiment in the article should be divided into two parts: (1) Methodology-wise comparison: providing multiple baseline models for the proposed method, which have been included in this article; (2) A comprehensive evaluation to show the performance of finetuning multiple VLMs using the proposed dataset, which is missing in the article.

reviewer_2_strengths: Multimodal dataset: The MM‑BRAF dataset is the first publicly‑oriented collection that integrates US imaging, textual reports, and pathology for BRAF V600E prediction, filling a clear gap in thyroid‑cancer AI research. First MLLM for this task: BRAF‑MLLM is the inaugural attempt to apply a large language model to multimodal mutation prediction, moving beyond conventional fusion networks. TMDA module: By decoupling features into intra‑tumoral and extra‑tumoral scales and performing dual‑scale cross‑modal alignment, TMDA directly addresses the challenge of subtle, localized ultrasound signatures, a design not seen in prior multimodal fusion or MLLM works. Comprehensive benchmarking: The authors evaluate a wide spectrum of baselines, several state‑of‑the‑art multimodal LLMs and supervised fine‑tuning variants, providing a transparent performance landscape. Open‑source intent: The authors intend to release both the MM‑BRAF dataset and the code, which would be a valuable resource for the community.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Marginal gains: Although BRAF MLLM achieves the highest numbers, the absolute improvements over the strongest baselines modest; the clinical relevance of such incremental gains is uncertain. Lack of statistical analysis: No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, making it impossible to judge whether the observed differences are statistically robust. Clinical acceptability: The reported accuracy (≈77 %) and recall (≈71 %) fall short of typical clinical decision thresholds for mutation testing, which often demand high sensitivity. Training details insufficient: The choice of “2 epochs” during fine tuning is not justified; a technical validation (e.g., learning curve analysis) demonstrating that 2 epochs is optimal is missing. Limited exploration of LoRA: The paper relies solely on LoRA based fine tuning of the MLLM. Prior work suggests that sequential fine tuning on other medical multimodal datasets can substantially improve downstream performance; a discussion or experiment on this would strengthen the methodology. Figure quality: Figure 1 contains cluttered elements, ambiguous color gradients, and unnecessary details that hinder interpretability. A cleaner redesign (manual or “controlled” AI assisted) is needed. Minor textual issues: – The abbreviation “MLLM” is introduced without its full form in the introduction (“…the first MLLM based framework…”). – A typo appears: “first omprehensive multimodal dataset” should read “first comprehensive multimodal dataset”. Broader disease relevance omitted:BRAF V600E also drives malignancy in other tumors (e.g., pediatric low grade gliomas). Discussing this broader relevance would enrich the impact statement and suggest future research avenues. Metric presentation: Results are reported with four decimal places, which exceeds clinical significance; rounding to three decimals would improve readability. Reproducibility details: Please confirm the dataset, codes, and models will be publicly available.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper studies a clinically relevant problem. Predicting BRAF V600E mutation from non-invasive multimodal data is meaningful for thyroid cancer risk stratification and treatment planning. 2.The dataset construction effort is valuable. The proposed MM-BRAF dataset integrates ultrasound images, tumor region annotations, reports, clinicopathological information, and mutation labels, which is richer than prior single-modal settings. 3.The proposed method is coherent. The tumor-centric dual-scale alignment design is intuitively motivated by the fact that mutation-related cues may reside both within the tumor and in surrounding context. 4.The paper includes baseline comparisons and ablation studies, and the proposed method shows improved performance over the reported baselines on the internal dataset.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The methodological novelty is limited. The proposed framework is largely a straightforward adaptation of an existing MLLM with LoRA fine-tuning plus region-level/text-level contrastive alignment. The main technical component, TMDA, is essentially a dual-branch alignment strategy based on clinician-provided tumor masks and LLM-parsed text entities, which feels more like a task-specific engineering integration than a substantially new methodological advance. 2.The experimental validation is not yet strong enough for a top-tier venue. All experiments appear to be conducted on a single internally collected dataset, and the paper itself acknowledges future work on multi-center validation. Without external validation or cross-center testing, it is difficult to assess robustness and clinical generalizability. 3.The benchmark design is not fully convincing. Several compared MLLMs are evaluated in a zero-shot or off-the-shelf manner, whereas the proposed model is fine-tuned on the target dataset using Qwen2.5-VL-7B with LoRA. This makes the comparison less balanced, especially when the strongest baseline is also the same backbone after SFT. The improvement over the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B baseline is relatively modest. 4.The dataset protocol and clinical details are insufficiently reported. The paper mentions 3120 samples from 1258 patients and patient-level splitting, but many important details remain unclear, such as class distribution in train/test, acquisition variability, inclusion criteria, annotation protocol and agreement, missing-value handling in clinicopathological records, and whether multiple views per patient may still introduce bias despite patient-level splitting. 5.The use of GPT-4o in dataset curation raises reproducibility and data-quality concerns. The paper states that GPT-4o is used to collate original records into ultrasound reports and clinicopathological information, but the prompting protocol, quality control, and possible error propagation are not described in enough detail. This is particularly important because these generated text fields are central inputs to the final model. 6.Clinical relevance is still somewhat preliminary. The reported gains are based on retrospective internal data only, and there is limited analysis of failure cases, calibration, subgroup robustness, or how the model would be used in realistic clinical workflows. For a clinically oriented MICCAI paper, this reduces the practical impact.

author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive suggestions. We are encouraged that they recognized the clinical importance of BRAF V600E prediction (R1, R2, R6), the value of MM-BRAF (R1, R2, R6), and the promise of TMDA (R1, R2). Below, we address key concerns: Common Concerns: Dataset Accessibility (R1,R2,R6): We will release the dataset, code, prompts, splits, and trained weights upon publication. GPT-4o structuring (R1,R6): GPT-4o was used only to map clinician-recorded numeric/categorical fields into standardized textual descriptions, not to infer BRAF status or generate new clinical findings. Mutation labels were excluded from all prompts. Outputs were checked against the original records and clinically verified; inconsistent cases were manually corrected. The total cost for 3,120 records was ~$15, and prompts/protocols will be released for reproducibility. Fine-tuned VLM comparisons (R1,R6): For a fairer benchmark, we additionally fine-tuned representative VLMs under the same patient-level split: InternVL2.5-8B: 0.7395 Acc, 0.6331 F1, 0.6571 Recall; Qwen2-VL-7B: 0.7268 Acc, 0.6294 F1, 0.6350 Recall; MiniCPM-2.6B: 0.7270 Acc, 0.6684 F1, 0.6728 Recall. BRAF-MLLM remains best on all metrics, showing the gain is not merely from VLM fine-tuning but from TMDA. #R1 Q2: Thanks for the suggestion. Table 2 includes image-only M1, text-only M2, and multimodal M3; M3 outperforms both M1 and M2, confirming the value of multimodal fusion. We will highlight these unimodal baselines more clearly. #R2 Q1: We appreciate this comment. The gain is moderate but consistent across Acc/F1/Recall, especially Recall, reducing missed mutation-positive cases. Our primary contribution is the MM-BRAF benchmark, with BRAF-MLLM as a strong reference model. Q2: 95% CIs (1,000 bootstraps): Acc 0.774[0.757-0.796], F1 0.698[0.670-0.720], Rec 0.713[0.702-0.731]. McNemar vs. best baseline: p=0.026<0.05. Q3: We agree BRAF-MLLM should not replace molecular testing. It is intended as non-invasive decision support for risk stratification and prioritizing confirmatory testing. We will clarify this positioning. Q4: We selected 2 epochs by validation Acc, which peaked at epoch 2: 0.7521/0.7714/0.7617/0.7459 for epochs 1/2/3/4, suggesting overfitting afterwards. Q5: Thanks for the guidance. LoRA was used for parameter-efficient adaptation under limited medical data. Sequential medical multimodal pretraining is complementary to TMDA and may further improve performance; we will discuss it. Q6-9: We will revise Fig. 1, define MLLM, correct typos, round metrics, confirm data/code/model release, and discuss broader BRAF V600E relevance. #R6 Q1: BRAF-MLLM introduces a clinically motivated TMDA module, not generic dual-branch fusion. By aligning intra-/extra-tumoral visual cues with corresponding clinical semantics, it targets subtle mutation-related ultrasound signatures. Q2: We acknowledge that multi-center validation is important for clinical generalizability. Given the scarcity of paired imaging-clinical-genomic data, our key contribution is the first open multimodal benchmark enabling such future validation. Q4: Dataset details: train/test contain 2,184/936 images, with 56.36%/66.99% positives. Inclusion required confirmed cancer, BRAF status, US images, and clinicopathological data; poor-quality images or missing labels were excluded. Tumor masks annotated by two clinicians were reconciled by a senior expert. Patient-level splitting prevents leakage across multiple views from the same patient. Q6: As the first multimodal BRAF benchmark, our study establishes MLLM feasibility for this task. BRAF-MLLM is intended to support risk stratification and prioritizing confirmatory testing, not replace molecular testing. We will add failure-case and subgroup analyses to clarify utility and limitations.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a potentially valuable multimodal dataset for BRAF V600E mutation prediction in thyroid cancer, along with an associated multimodal LLM for mutation prediction. The rebuttal should address concerns about both the model and the dataset: (1) baseline comparison is not fully balanced, as only one external model underwent supervised fine-tuning (R1R3); (2) the reported accuracy of 77% and recall of 71% may not meet clinical acceptability for mutation testing (R2); (3) validation is limited to a single site, leaving generalizability unclear (R3). Regarding the benchmark itself, (4) the use of GPT-4o for data generation raises concerns about cost, reproducibility, and data quality control (R1R3); (5) important dataset protocol and clinical details are missing (R3). Overall, it is unclear whether the paper’s primary contribution is the benchmark or the model development, and either direction requires more details and justification. | The paper proposes a multimodal dataset for thyroid cancer BRAF V600E mutation prediction, along with a task-specific multimodal LLM. The reviewers’ concerns were largely addressed in the rebuttal. Further validation, especially multi-center validation, is still needed. However, the paper represents an important first step in demonstrating the value of this new dataset for mutation prediction and risk stratification. title: Towards Unified Image–Video Modeling Across B-Mode and Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound for Multi-task Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely challenging problem – unifying image/video, segmentation/classification, and B-mode/CEUS modalities within a single model. The experimental scale is impressive, covering 27,804 segmentation images, 7,320 classification images, and over 1,400 videos across multiple organs. This level of comprehensive evaluation is rare and valuable. The design of SSCP is well-reasoned. By grouping five semantic attributes into structural and spatial priors and injecting them at different network depths, the model effectively handles heterogeneity without requiring task-specific branches or model duplication. Beyond standard performance metrics, the paper includes a detailed ablation study and a qualitative kNN purity analysis (Fig. 3). The kNN analysis is particularly interesting as it visually demonstrates the transition of features from domain-aware (encoder) to task-aligned (decoder).
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Major: The paper claims that “most existing approaches remain predominantly image-oriented or segmentation-focused, and explicit unification of image and video reasoning… remains limited. ” However, several prior works have already proposed unified or promptable frameworks for ultrasound that handle multiple tasks and modalities. USFM is cited but not further compare against it in the main experiments, nor explain how UIV-US differs or improves upon USFM. Other representative work like URFM, UltraFedFM, USF-MAE are not discussed. The paper states that the source code will be made available, but many details are omitted: What is the backbone architecture? Is it based on SAM, ViT, or a custom design? How are the five semantic attributes (Task, Target, Mode, Modality, Position) obtained for each sample? Are they manually annotated, derived from dataset metadata, or inferred? This is critical for reproducibility. MRTA take the segmentation results of previous frames as reference attention. If the results of previous frames contain significant errors, will error accumulation occur in subsequent segmentation processes, and are there any methods to eliminate this risk? While the model uses a “shared parameter space,” the introduction of memory banks (MRTA) with a length of up to K=10, and cross-attention mechanisms may introduce significant computational overhead during inference. The paper lacks a discussion or quantitative analysis of inference speed (FPS) or memory usage, which is crucial for the claimed portable advantages of ultrasound. reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has several major strengths. 1.Meaningful unified formulation. The work addresses an important limitation in current ultrasound analysis, namely that most existing methods are organ-specific, task-specific, or developed separately for images and videos. In contrast, this paper proposes a single shared-parameter framework that jointly supports segmentation and classification across image, video, B-mode, and CEUS settings. This unified design is interesting because it moves beyond narrowly specialized pipelines and is closer to how heterogeneous ultrasound data are encountered in practice. 2.Well-motivated method design. The proposed components are aligned with the problem setting. SSCP provides structured conditioning of shared features, while MRTA and FLA separately address temporal consistency for video segmentation and temporal aggregation for video classification. This makes the framework technically coherent rather than simply combining multiple tasks in one model. 3.Broad experimental coverage. The evaluation spans multiple organs, modalities, tasks, and temporal settings, including both public and private datasets. This makes the study more comprehensive than many prior ultrasound works that focus on only one organ or one task. 4.Empirical results with useful ablations. The method shows competitive performance across several settings, and the ablation study helps verify that SSCP, MRTA, and FLA each contribute to the final performance. This strengthens the credibility of the proposed design.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper has several important weaknesses. 1.The method description and figures are not sufficiently clear. Figure 1 is difficult to read and some design choices are not well explained. In particular, the “Yes/No” branches around the mask decoder in the segmentation pathway are confusing, and it is unclear why the corresponding outputs are routed into the video branch in the illustrated way. In addition, the variable P in Eqs. (3) and (4) is not clearly defined, and the implementation details of SSCP remain too abstract. The statement that “Task, Target, Mode, and Modality are injected via learnable feature modulation, while Position is modeled through spatial bias” is conceptually reasonable, but the paper does not explain clearly how these priors are encoded and inserted at different layers. This makes the method harder to reproduce and assess. 2.Some key parts of the segmentation-aware classification pipeline are under-specified. The classification branch is described as using segmentation-aware representations and mask-guided ROI features, but the paper does not clearly explain how the masks are obtained for all classification settings, especially when classification datasets may not naturally provide segmentation supervision. This point is important for understanding both the practicality of the method and the fairness of the comparison with baselines that may not use such intermediate structural cues. 3.The empirical comparison is not fully fair or fully complete. In Table 1, the proposed method is trained in a supervised/fine-tuned setting on the benchmark, while several baselines are reported under zero-shot or prompt-based settings, which makes the comparison less clean. At the same time, some key settings are not matched with sufficiently strong competing baselines in the main table, especially for CEUS and video classification. Therefore, the claim of strong superiority across all settings is not yet equally convincing everywhere. 4.The quantitative presentation hides important dataset-level details. The paper mainly reports mean DSC and mean AUC/Accuracy aggregated across datasets. Given the substantial heterogeneity across organs, modalities, and tasks, this presentation makes it difficult to judge whether the gains are consistent across datasets or driven by a subset of easier benchmarks. Similarly, Table 2 would be easier to interpret if segmentation and classification ablations were presented more separately and explicitly. 5.The qualitative and representation analyses are not sufficiently convincing in their current form. Figure 2 only shows qualitative results of the proposed method, without visual comparison to representative competing approaches, so it is difficult to visually assess the claimed superiority. Likewise, Figure 3 is not sufficiently explained: the definition of kNN purity is not provided clearly, and the claim that decoder features exhibit better cross-domain alignment is not easy to verify directly from the figure. Overall, these analyses would benefit from clearer definitions, stronger visual evidence, and more careful interpretation. 6.Some ablation findings deserve deeper discussion. The MRTA ablation shows that increasing memory length improves performance, with the best result at K=10.However, the difference between K=6 and K=10 is still noticeable, especially for CEUS segmentation, and the paper does not discuss sufficiently why this happens or what the computational trade-off is. A more thorough sensitivity analysis would strengthen the temporal modeling claim. 7.The reproducibility and external validity are limited by insufficient dataset characterization. The paper uses multiple private datasets for video classification and CEUS analysis, but provides limited detail about acquisition conditions, scanner/vendor diversity, patient composition, annotation protocol, and center-level variability. Since the paper emphasizes a general and clinically relevant unified framework, more information is needed to judge how robust and transferable the reported results really are. In addition, the external validation is only reported for segmentation, not for classification or CEUS classification, so the evidence for broad cross-domain generalization remains partial. 8.The paper does not fully establish that the benefit comes from true unified multi-task learning. Although the framework is presented as unified, the training is performed in two stages: segmentation is optimized first, and then classification is trained with the encoder and segmentation branch frozen. This staged design is practical, but it weakens the claim that the gains arise from end-to-end unified learning itself. More direct comparisons with separate task-specific models using the same backbone would make this claim stronger. 9.The main novelty appears more integrative than fundamentally new. The overall unification across image/video, B-mode/CEUS, and segmentation/classification is meaningful, but the key components are relatively close to existing directions already discussed in the paper, including prompt-conditioned modeling (e.g., SAM, SAM2, MedSAM, SAM-Med2D, SAMUS), and memory-based temporal modeling for video segmentation (e.g., MemSAM). Therefore, the contribution seems to lie mainly in combining and adapting existing ideas into a broader ultrasound framework, rather than introducing a clearly new methodological principle.
