title: WaCT-US: Cyclic-Alignment Scaled Contour Tubes for Efficient, Calibrated Uncertainty in Echocardiography
reviewer_1_strengths: The boundary-centric conformal approach is interesting and timely. This is a nice adaptation of the conformal approach to boundaries. Calibration is appropriate. The method is computationally efficient. The evaluation is thorough and the results are nicely interpretable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: It is unclear how this method could generalize to 3D surfaces. No discussion of the sensitivity to distribution shift. A qualitative illustration of the advantage of the tube approach over pixelwise analysis would be useful.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The methodology is novel and addresses an important problem (deriving efficient confidence regions around predictions with adequate coverage of the ground truth). The framework is sound.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: I am not certain that the paper conclusively demonstrates the superiority of the method over the SOTA. The methods seem to all have very similar performance with respect to all metrics, with a slight edge for the proposed method w.r.t. Scale, that may only be statistically significant for one of the two datasets (no direct significance test is performed). Part of my unease comes from the fact that the methods to derive the Scale metric for the proposed method and for the baselines might be fairly diverse and this might impact the reported numbers. I would be grateful if the authors can comment on this. One weakness is that despite deriving confidence sets that are geometrically more constrained (as contour tubes), the main segmentation head itself is unchanged. As in, it is still based on predicting a mask, trained with Dice+BCE, which for echo data will often lead to predictions that are both topologically incorrect and geometrically unconstrained. In my opinion this is a strong limitation for the practical usefulness of the work.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: significant speedup and reduced uncertainty with locality
reviewer_3_weaknesses: the “competing” baselines noted are older, and it’s unclear why several already-cited recent works would not make more meaningful comparison.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer (MR) for constructive feedback. We focus on fair comparison/statistical interpretation, recent echo baselines, and scope/practicality. Fair comparison, Scale, significance (R2/R3/MR). We do not claim Dice/HD superiority; the segmentation protocol is intentionally kept standard/comparable to isolate UQ. Bolding WaCT-US rows in Table 1 was intended only to mark the proposed method, not metric-wise dominance. The claim is coverage-efficiency: at nominal 0.9 conformal coverage, WaCT-US gives the smallest calibrated tube scale with one forward pass. Scale is comparable because all methods are converted to the same tube family: sample the method’s local uncertainty on the predicted contour, compute the same Eq.(3) score, calibrate a method-specific λ̂ by the same quantile rule on the same validation split, evaluate on the same test frames, and report Scale=mean_i[λ̂ mean_j s_ij]. Raw entropy/vacuity/std units are not compared; a global rescaling of any raw map is absorbed by λ̂, leaving λ̂s and Scale unchanged. Table 1 reports comparable coverage with exact 95% CIs; WaCT-US has the lowest mean Scale (CAMUS 8.09 vs 8.98 next; EchoNet 5.10 vs 5.27 next). We did not include a direct Scale significance test, and the EchoNet gap is modest; thus the claim is an observed Pareto advantage in Scale and compute, not formal statistical dominance. Recent/relevant baselines (R2/R3/MR). The baselines cover UQ regimes under protocol parity: post-hoc deterministic maps, evidential/temperature maps, and sampling/Bayesian approximations (MC dropout, Laplace, SWAG), all conformalized identically. Judge et al. is relevant and cited; however, it produces asymmetric contour-regression uncertainty, whereas WaCT-US produces a split-conformal prediction set around a standard segmenter with finite-sample marginal coverage. A fair comparison would require an adapter/conformalized contour-set variant, so we do not claim dominance over that line. Similarly, recent conformal segmentation works cited in the paper are mask/morphology based or contour objects in another setting; they do not evaluate the same closed-contour, learned-local-scaling, single-pass echo setting. Segmentation/topology and scale head (R2). We agree topology-constrained echo segmenters are valuable. WaCT-US is architecture-agnostic (Sec.2.3) and can wrap stronger/topology-aware backbones. The Dice+BCE U-Net keeps the center-contour model unchanged across UQ methods. R2 is correct that the scale head is not designed to improve Dice/topology or feed back to correct the center contour; it learns residual-dependent local scale so the output reports where/how much the contour may be wrong. Limitations of the chosen segmenter, including the CAMUS Dice concern, therefore affect absolute segmentation quality, but not the within-paper UQ comparison: WaCT-US is not given a stronger center-contour model than the baselines. Shift, 3D, practical advantage, reproducibility (R1/MR). The paper states the exchangeability requirement: Theorem 1 gives P_te(d_s≤λ̂)≥1−α−δ under TV shift δ, so we do not claim robustness to arbitrary shift; weighted conformal alternatives are noted for drift. In 3D, split-conformal validity could apply to a chosen surface score under exchangeability, but cyclic shift would need surface correspondence/alignment; our empirical claim is limited to 2D echo contours. Practical value is shown in Fig.2: WaCT-US has the lowest AURC and deferring the top 20% most uncertain CAMUS samples reduces retained contour MAE by 15.7%; Fig.2b shows contour-tube overlays where uncertainty tracks image quality/contour mismatch. For reproducibility, Secs.2.3/3.1-3.3 specify public datasets/splits, preprocessing, model, losses, optimizer/epochs, M=64, τ=0.9, scale weight, calibration quantile, baselines, and metrics; we intend to release code after acceptance.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Please prioritize responding on comparisons with more recent and relevant baselines and clarify whether the observed performance differences are statistically significant. Additionally, address concerns regarding the evaluation of the Scale metric and ensure fair comparability across methods. Finally, respond to limitations and generalizability concerns, including applicability to 3D settings, robustness to distribution shift, and evidence of the practical advantages of the proposed approach. | The paper presents WaCT-US, a contour-native uncertainty representation that outputs a conformally calibrated prediction set. The strengths and limitations of the work were both clearly discussed during the review process, and the benefits appear to outweigh the weaknesses. In particular, the boundary-centric conformal formulation is novel and practically appealing, especially given the significant speedup reported by the authors. The questions regarding relevant baselines were also adequately addressed in the rebuttal. Overall, the paper is recommended for acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers agreed that this paper is well prepared and of interest to MICCAI. R2 originally recommended borderline reject, but raised their score to accept after authors’ rebuttal. AC recommends acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a novel efficient uncertainty quantification in echocardiography segmentation around boundaries through scaled contour tubes. It adopts cyclic landmark alignment to address index inconsistency and split conformal calibration to ensure marginal coverage. Although there are some shortcomings in terms of generalizability, sensitivity analysis, and performance advantages, these do not undermine the contributions and potential impact of this paper’s methodological innovation. The method will provide a new perspective on uncertainty quantification in medical image segmentation and is expected to enhance the reliability and accuracy of diagnoses in clinical practice.

title: wBCAM: Windowed Bi-directional Cross-Attention with Mamba for Enhanced 3D Vascular Reconstruction in Free-Hand Photoacoustic and Ultrasound Imaging
reviewer_1_strengths: The strongest aspect is the good problem choice. Free-hand 3D PAUS without external tracking is clinically meaningful and technically harder than ordinary freehand US reconstruction because broken trajectory consistency directly degrades 3D vessel continuity. The paper explains this motivation clearly and the qualitative figures on page 8 support that the task matters. A second strength is that the method is reasonably well matched to the stated failure mode. The paper argues that frame-to-frame/local methods drift over long sequences, then proposes a design that explicitly couples local evidence with global memory. That architectural logic is coherent: local frame-pair tokens preserve discriminative short-range motion cues, while global tokens plus Mamba provide a mechanism for longer-range temporal consistency. The multi-level heads for relative, window, and full-sequence motion are also sensible for this task. A third strength is the empirical pattern of results, especially on absolute metrics. On the US dataset, wBCAM is best on all absolute metrics; on the PAUS dataset it is again best on all absolute metrics, even though it is not best on relative metrics. That pattern is consistent with the paper’s central claim that the method mainly helps by suppressing accumulated drift rather than by maximizing short-range alignment. The ablation also supports that global tokens, windowing, and token regularization each contribute incrementally. A fourth strength is the translation toward PAUS rather than only ultrasound. Prior sensorless freehand 3D reconstruction literature is mostly ultrasound-focused, including early deep learning approaches by Prevost et al. and DCL-Net, later online/self-supervised variants, IMU-assisted models, and more recent local+global or Mamba-based US reconstructions. Extending this line into free-hand PAUS and showing actual reconstructed vascular volumes is valuable.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The biggest weakness is limited methodological novelty relative to recent freehand US reconstruction literature. The paper’s individual ingredients are close to existing trends: sensorless freehand 3D reconstruction itself is not new, going back at least to Prevost et al. 2018 and DCL-Net 2020. explicit local/global context for sensorless 3D ultrasound is already central in DualTrack (2025). Mamba/state-space modeling for long-range freehand 3D ultrasound reconstruction was already used in FiMA (MICCAI 2024), which explicitly argues for SSMs to mine long-range spatiotemporal information.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The methods are described clearly, and the results are compelling. Combined with the code that will be released digitally, I have no doubt others could reproduce the work. The work is timely, relevant, and of high quality - both in experimental approach and its description. The inclusion of not one, but multiple, alternative DL networks is commendable - even if the comparison of their performances is somewhat limited. (Where are the data for the “SOTA methods”, for instance?)
reviewer_2_weaknesses: In a limited number of places, the text is a little short on detail. Specifically: Section 2.1, the beamformer algorithms for both US and PA have not been described or defined The PA acquisition was stated at 10 FPS, but what was the acquisition rate for US? The text confirms this was higher, allowing for more accurate pose estimation, but not HOW much higher. Section 3.1, ratio 12:3:4 - it is unclear to me whether this means the training set contains data from all 19 volunteers, or whether data from some volunteers were used exclusively to test the algorithm. The former might have introduced bias in performance, as arguably vasculature and anatomy do not change much between consecutive scans (which I assume were performed in rapid succession?) - meaning the desired geometry for all test cases would be near-identically included in the training data. How severe is this risk of bias? Section 3.1, EM tracker: if these data were available, and indeed used for supervised learning, a comparison of the tracking performance of all algorithms would have been very useful. I appreciate the 3D US and PA images look convincing, but I cannot judge the positional accuracy of the scan pattern based on just the plots in Fig. 3.* Fig. 3: the US images contain multiple trajectories (the yellow, green, white, pink, … squiggles) but it is not explained what these represent. As they all deviate strongly from the final volume, which one(s) is closest to the “truth”? In addition, the addition of scale bars in each panel would be very helpful.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The strengthen for this paper is that it will not need an extra device for motion recording. The trajectory can be predicted only from the B-mode scanning sequence, which supports better reconstruction. The authors provide real in-vivo data for testing the model, which was collected from human arms. The device setup is comprehensive.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Miss literature citations for “Many existing deep learning (DL)-based scan motion estimation methods primarily rely on local frame-to-frame alignment.” 2.The writing and figures are confusing, especially in the “Sequence Modeling”. Since there are different modules, many notations in text are not shown in the figure. I cannot find the temporal self-attention block that produces the temporally enhanced feature V. The V is also not shown. In Figure 2, I cannot infer from the text what the number above the arrow means. 3.The description of modeling is vague. The method of encoding the sequence frames using ViT is unknown; either treat the frame as a channel or another way. The number of learnable global tokens and the number of frames in the B-mode sequence are not explicitly stated in the text. The Mamba block is not closely explained in terms of its structure and fit for this task. The choice of coefficients of loss components is not stated. 4.If I understand correctly, the relative-level motion is a kind of frame-to-frame alignment, which may be vulnerable to long trajectories, as mentioned above. 5.The proposed wBCAM’s relative error performances are lower than those of the two other models, which raises the question about the local motion estimates, which may be considered noisy. And, how the absolute poses remain accurate. The absolute error is computed independently or by composing with relative steps. 6.No qualitative comparison with other methods. 7.The authors did not provide quantitative evaluation metrics on 3D vascular reconstruction, which is one aim in their abstract.
reviewer_3_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for their constructive comments. We address the main concerns below. Method novelty (R1,R4) Prior sensor-free freehand 3D reconstruction exists (Prevost’18, DCLNet’20). Our contribution is a long-range trajectory modeling mechanism for drift-sensitive 3D PAUS vascular reconstruction. Unlike DualTrack (separate local/global streams + fusion), wBCAM uses learnable global tokens as structured motion memory, iteratively written/read via windowed bi-directional cross-attention (L2G/G2L), enabling unified local/global modeling and drift suppression. Unlike FiMA (SSM on backbone features), wBCAM uses Mamba only to propagate compact global-memory tokens across windows while preserving attention-based local motion estimation. This design explicitly targets cumulative trajectory inconsistency that degrades long-range vascular continuity in freehand 3D PAUS reconstruction. Relative vs. absolute motion (R3,R4) We do not regress absolute poses independently. We compose predicted relative transforms to obtain the trajectory and compute absolute metrics against EM-tracker-derived ground truth. Better frame-to-frame metrics do not guarantee long-range stability: small but temporally biased/inconsistent step errors accumulate into drift. wBCAM enforces long-range consistency via windowed global-memory propagation, yielding better absolute metrics and more coherent 3D vascular reconstruction. This is particularly important in long freehand scans, where small but biased local errors accumulate and distort reconstructed vascular topology. Fig. clarity / qualitative comparison (R2,R3,R4) Fig. 3 overlays trajectories from multiple methods for space-efficient qualitative comparison; the legend was unintentionally omitted. In the US panels, the grayscale volume is the EM-tracker reference (“truth”) and colored curves are estimated scan trajectories. In Fig. 3, yellow, purple, blue, green, and red trajectories correspond to DCL-Net, MoGLo-Net, DualTrack, FiMA, and the proposed wBCAM, respectively. We will add legends/scale bars in Fig. 3 and clarify arrow numbers (processing order) in Fig. 2. Acquisition/beamforming details (R2) US/PA images use delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming; US additionally uses envelope detection and log compression for B-mode, whereas PA is reconstructed as initial-pressure maps without log compression. The PAUS sequence operates at 10 Hz (20 Hz laser PRF with interleaved full-aperture acquisition). The US-only dataset was acquired at 20 Hz (no laser). Split / bias (R2) The 12:3:4 ratio is subject-level (12/3/4 subjects out of 19). All scans from a subject belong to a single split; test subjects are disjoint from train/val, so within-subject similarity cannot bias test performance. EM tracker comparison (R2) Quantitative evaluation against EM ground truth is reported in Table 1, and Fig. 3 provides a trajectory-overlay comparison; we will make the EM reference and legend explicit. Missing citations (R3) We will add representative citations for DL-based frame-to-frame motion estimation/registration. Method details (R3) Temporally enhanced tokens V are produced by temporal self-attention applied after GAP (GAP → temporal self-attention → V); we will label this block and V in Fig. 2/caption. ViT encodes adjacent frame pairs (not the full sequence as channels). We will explicitly state hyperparameters (M=16, N=65 with random sub-sequences of length 64, w=16) and loss weights (λ1, λ2, λ3). 3D vascular metrics & code (R3,R4) We agree there is no dedicated quantitative metric on 3D vasculature; since 3D continuity is primarily governed by accumulated pose error, EM-GT motion metrics serve as a surrogate and are supported by consistent trajectory overlays and preserved vascular continuity in Fig. 3.Future work will validate geometry using external 3D references (e.g., CTA/MRA). title: When Views Disagree: Conflict-Aware Evidential Inference for Multi-view Mammography
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The work correctly identifies a critical limitation of existing multi-view fusion methods: they ignore view disagreement and produce overconfident, poorly calibrated predictions. The problem is clinically relevant. 2.The method is novel. 3.The paper is well-organized.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The paper is motivated by conflicting evidence between CC and MLO views, but the quantitative analysis mainly reports dataset-level AUROC, ECE, and NLL improvements, without stratifying performance by clinically important disagreement regimes such as low-quality views, partial breast coverage, dense breasts, subtle lesions, or artifact-heavy cases. As a result, the manuscript does not clearly demonstrate in which concrete clinical scenarios the proposed conflict-aware evidential inference is most beneficial, rather than simply improving average benchmark performance. 2.The whole framework relies on the assumption that inter-view disagreement can be adequately characterized by class-wise Jensen-Shannon divergence between per-view Dirichlet means and then moderated by a scalar conflict gate. However, the paper does not analyze whether this design remains reliable in harder cases such as severe asymmetry of lesion visibility, view-specific false positives, very weak evidence in both views, or anatomically inconsistent but still clinically meaningful complementary findings. Thus, the robustness of the core conflict-modeling assumption is still not fully demonstrated. 3.The method assumes consistent paired CC/MLO views and standard preprocessing, and although the paper includes a missing-view test-time ablation, it does not evaluate real-world issues such as view mispairing, acquisition mismatch, corrupted views, variable compression quality, or imperfect preprocessing and breast cropping. Since such factors are common in practical mammography workflows, the real clinical robustness and deployability of the framework remain unclear.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper is driven by a strong motivation, as effectively leveraging the multi-view nature of mammography is of clinically relevant. The proposed method cleverly learns from incorporating two types of uncertainty by extracting view-specific features via an encoder and tokenization, computing Dirichlet evidence for each view, and applying class-wise conflict weighting. Furthermore, a major strength of this work is its comprehensive evaluation, successfully demonstrating improved AUROC and statistical significance compared to various recent SOTA models.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The major weaknesses of this paper are as follows: Baselines for Uncertainty: The baseline models used for comparison are deterministic and rely solely on simple temperature scaling, which may not provide a sufficiently rigorous baseline for evaluating uncertainty estimation. Visualizations: In the lower section of Figure 2, the clinical focus is somewhat ambiguous. It is unclear which specific regions or features within the mammogram the reader is expected to observe.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The manuscript presents a well-motivated and methodologically sound approach to multi-view mammography classification. The major strengths of this work include: 1.Novel Problem Formulation (Evidential Reasoning under Disagreement): The paper elegantly reframes multi-view mammography from a standard deterministic feature fusion problem to an uncertainty-aware evidential reasoning paradigm. Instead of forcing a consensus at the feature level—which can lead to overconfident predictions —the CEI-Net models each view as a source of uncertain evidence via Dirichlet distributions. This appropriately translates inter-view diagnostic conflict into calibrated epistemic uncertainty, which is highly valuable for safety-critical clinical screening. 2.Methodological Elegance (Class-Conditional Conflict Gating): The proposed fusion mechanism uses Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence to quantify conflict at the class hypothesis level. This is particularly innovative because it selectively attenuates only the disputed diagnostic hypotheses, rather than indiscriminately penalizing the entire view. Furthermore, the model achieves this directly in the evidence space without relying on auxiliary routing or image-quality sub-networks, ensuring high parameter efficiency.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Q1: Risk of False Negatives Induced by the JS Gating Mechanism. The authors employ a Jensen-Shannon (JS) gating mechanism, defined as $g_k = \exp(-\gamma JS_k)$, to attenuate evidence when the CC and MLO views disagree. However, in clinical practice, it is common for a lesion to be visible in only one view (e.g., deep in the breast, captured only by MLO) due to anatomical occlusion. In this scenario, the CC view might confidently predict “benign” (seeing only normal tissue), while the MLO view confidently predicts “malignant.” This creates a high JS divergence, triggering the gating mechanism to strongly attenuate the “malignant” evidence, which could lead to a fatal false negative. How does the proposed method distinguish between “true asymmetric lesion visibility” and “spurious conflict caused by noise” to prevent the model from compromising and missing the diagnosis? Q2: Limited Spatial Interpretability of the Conflict Mechanism. While Figure 2 effectively demonstrates the interpretability of the JS gating mechanism at the mathematical and predictive level (showing how uncertainty increases in high-conflict cases like Fig. 2e), it lacks spatial/clinical interpretability. Since CEI-Net relies on extracting “Top-M salient spatial tokens” from each view, the model inherently possesses spatial information about where the evidence originates. Could the authors expand their qualitative analysis to visualize which specific spatial tokens or anatomical regions are driving the high JS divergence? Providing token-level heatmaps or spatial overlays alongside the probability charts would significantly bridge the gap between mathematical conflict resolution and actionable clinical interpretability. Q3: Dataset Discrepancy and Potential View Dominance. Could the authors explain why the proposed method achieves a significantly higher performance gain on CBIS-DDSM compared to VinDr-Mammo (whereas baseline methods perform relatively consistently across both)? Furthermore, in Table 2, the Deterministic Prob-Avg achieves an AUROC almost identical to the missing-MLO ( CC only ) setting. Does this suggest that the model’s decisions heavily rely on the CC view? Additionally, the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for CC only is lower than that of MLO only , which seems to contradict the textual claim regarding the higher discriminative value of the MLO view.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for recognizing the clinical motivation, novelty, clarity, and empirical evaluation of CEI-Net. We revised Fig. 2 and related text to clarify conflict behavior and spatial evidence. Safety under asymmetric visibility (R1/R2/R3). A lesion visible in only one view is an important safety case. CEI-Net does not force CC/MLO consensus or convert disagreement into a benign decision. Each view first contributes evidence according to its Dirichlet strength, r(v)=S(v)/(S(v)+K). The JS gate is then applied to reliability-weighted evidence, not directly to class probabilities or to an entire view. Thus, when one view is confident and the other is weak or uncertain, the confident view can still dominate. When two confident views disagree, the gate reduces Dirichlet concentration for the disputed hypothesis and increases epistemic uncertainty rather than suppressing malignancy. We now clarify that such cases are uncertain/high-risk for review/triage. For single-view inference, JS is set to zero, so no artificial conflict is introduced. Missing-view results support this: CC-only and MLO-only remain functional, while full model performs best. Disagreement regimes and robustness (R1/R2/R3). Dense breasts, partial coverage, artifacts, mismatch, corrupted views, and view-pairing errors matter in deployment. We do not claim full prospective robustness to all acquisition failures, and the conclusion now clarifies this limitation. The current evidence tests the central claim that conflict modeling improves inference under disagreement or shift. Fig. 2 stratifies cases by JS disagreement and shows that stronger disagreement is associated with higher error and NLL. Table 2 evaluates missing-view inference without retraining, and cross-dataset results show improved calibration and NLL under domain shift. We will study view mispairing, corruption, imperfect cropping, and dense/subtle-lesion cases in future robustness tests. Uncertainty baselines and ablations (R2). To separate temperature scaling from uncertainty modeling, we compare CEI-Net with evidential variants using the same backbone and tokenization, including equal-weight fusion, reliability-only fusion, JS-gating-only fusion, and removal of tokenized evidence. Temperature scaling is applied only for evaluation calibration, while the actual uncertainty mechanism is the Dirichlet evidence strength plus JS-based conflict modulation. We now state this explicitly. Spatial interpretability and revised Fig. 2 (R2/R3). The previous figure made belief-level conflict clearer than clinical localization. We revised Fig. 2 to overlay selected Top-M spatial tokens and distinguish malignant, benign, and disputed tokens in specific regions. The revised panels connect image regions selected by CEI-Net with per-view belief, JS disagreement, and class-wise gates, which links conflict to spatial evidence.s View dominance and dataset discrepancy (R3). The similarity between deterministic probability avg. and CC-only, especially on CBIS-DDSM, reflects naive averaging, not CEI-Net collapsing to CC. Full model outperforms CC-only, MLO-only, and deterministic avg. on both datasets. Compared with CC-only, full CEI-Net improves AUROC from 0.796 to 0.855 on CBIS-DDSM and from 0.804 to 0.829 on VinDr-Mammo, while reducing ECE from 0.135 to 0.109 and from 0.300 to 0.073.This indicates that fusion uses complementary information from both views. We corrected the wording about MLO being generally more discriminative: in these splits, CC has stronger standalone signal, while full CEI-Net remains best. Image resolution (R2). 224x224 downsampling can remove subtle findings. We used this resolution for controlled comparison with baselines and feasible multi-run evaluation. Since all methods use the same preprocessing, gains reflect conflict-aware evidential inference rather than a resolution advantage. We now state this limitation and will explore high-resolution patch or multi-scale extensions.

Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The three reviewers recognize a novel formulation of multi-view disagreement in terms of epistemic uncertainty, and note an elegant method and a strong contribution. Several of the issues raised by the reviewers were adressed in the rebuttal through an enriching discussion. This clarifications should be also included in the paper. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a novel method for handling multi-view conflict in breast mammography, a particularly relevant and frequent clinical case. To do so, the authors model this conflict as a source of epistemic uncertainty using Dirichlet distributions and propose a gating mechanism based on Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence. Experiments are conducted on two large-scale mammography datasets and demonstrate the framework’s benefits in managing conflicting cases. In the first round of reviews, the reviewers’ main concerns were: i) management of asymmetric visibility cases (when a lesion is not visible on a view), disagreement regimes, and treatment of single-view cases; ii) uncertainty baselines and interpretation; and iii) view dominance and potential bias. The authors clearly responded to all the reviewers’ points, promising to better clarify asymmetric visibility, single-view, and robustness to acquisition features in the camera-ready paper. In addition, the authors revised Fig. 2 to address R2 and R3 concerns about the spatial interpretability of tokens. R1 and R2 were satisfied with these answers and recommended acceptance. While R3 did not provide an updated recommendation, I believe the authors addressed his questions in the rebuttal and therefore also recommend acceptance.
